materials.prompt: 〜かたがた
materials.answer:
while also; combining the purpose of; partly in order to

〜かたがた marks that a single action serves two purposes at once — the main one, plus the かたがた one done along with it. It attaches to a noun, almost always a formal social act such as 挨拶かたがた (partly to pay one's respects), お礼かたがた (partly to say thanks), or お詫びかたがた (partly to apologize). The tone is stiff and old-fashioned, at home in letters and polite visits. One deed accomplishes both aims.
materials.reading: かたがた
materials.notes:
Attaches to a noun (usually a formal suru-noun like 挨拶・お礼・お詫び), not to a verb.

One single action fulfils both purposes at the same time; it is not two separate errands.

Formal and written; in casual speech がてら or ついでに are more natural.

Synonyms: gatera — がてら does two things on one outing too, but is more casual and often involves physically going somewhere; かたがた is formal and noun-only.

Related: tsuide-ni — ついでに frames the second action as an afterthought taken while doing the first; かたがた presents both purposes as intended together, in stiffer register.

Related: katawara — かたわら pairs two sustained activities over a long span; かたがた joins two purposes in one single act.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 先日のお礼かたがた、近くまで参りましたのでお立ち寄りいたしました。
examples.english: Partly to thank you for the other day, and since I happened to be in the area, I have dropped by.
examples.reading: せんじつのおれいかたがた、ちかくまでまいりましたのでおたちよりいたしました。

examples.japanese: 帰省かたがた、長らくご無沙汰していた恩師のお宅を訪ねた。
examples.english: On my trip back to my hometown, I also visited the home of the mentor I had long neglected to contact.
examples.reading: きせいかたがた、ながらくごぶさたしていたおんしのおたくをたずねた。

materials.prompt: 〜かたわら
materials.answer:
while; alongside (one's main occupation or activity)

〜かたわら presents two ongoing pursuits: while doing A as one's main occupation, one also does B on the side over the same period. 傍ら literally means 'beside', and the figure is of B running parallel to a central activity — 仕事のかたわら (alongside one's work), 教えるかたわら (while teaching). It attaches to a dictionary-form verb or a noun + の, and belongs to written, somewhat literary style.
materials.reading: かたわら
materials.notes:
Describes two activities sustained over a long period (a main one plus a side one), not two acts done on a single occasion.

The clause before かたわら names the main occupation; the side activity comes after.

Written and literary; heavier than everyday 〜ながら.

Synonyms: nagara — ながら links two actions happening at the same moment; かたわら links two ongoing pursuits carried on over a long stretch of one's life.

Related: katagata — かたがた joins two purposes within one single act; かたわら sets one long-term side activity beside a main occupation.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Alongside teaching economics at the university, he continues to write novels.
examples.reading: かれはだいがくでけいざいがくをおしえるかたわら、しょうせつをかきつづけている。

examples.japanese: 家業を手伝うかたわら、地域のボランティア活動にも力を注いできた。
examples.english: While helping with the family business, she has also devoted her energy to local volunteer work.
examples.reading: かぎょうをてつだうかたわら、ちいきのボランティアかつどうにもちからをそそいできた。

materials.prompt: かつて
materials.answer:
once; formerly; (with a negative) never before

かつて is a formal adverb pointing to some time in the past: 'once, formerly, in days gone by'. かつて栄えた町 = a town that once flourished. With a following negative it means 'never (up to now)', as in かつてない ('unprecedented, never seen before'). It carries a literary, retrospective flavour and is common in writing and formal narration rather than casual chat.
materials.reading: かつて
materials.notes:
Formal and written; in everyday speech 昔 or 以前 sound more natural.

Followed by a negative it means 'never before': かつてない規模 = a scale never seen until now.

Related: imada-ni — 未だに fixes on a state that still persists into the present; かつて points back to a moment in the past.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: This area is land that once flourished greatly as a castle town.
examples.reading: このあたりはかつてじょうかまちとしておおいにさかえたとちである。

examples.japanese: かつてないほどの大雪に、街の交通は完全に麻痺した。

examples.reading: かつてないほどのおおゆきに、まちのこうつうはかんぜんにまひした。

materials.prompt: 〜かった
materials.answer:
i-adjective past tense

To put an い-adjective into the past, drop the final い and add かった: 高い→高かった (was expensive), 楽しい→楽しかった (was fun). It works both as the sentence predicate (楽しかったです) and when describing a past state. In polite speech, add です after かった — never でした.
materials.reading: かった
materials.notes:
The polite past is 〜かったです, not 〜いでした: 高かったです, never 高いでした.

いい is irregular in the past — よかった, not いかった.

Related: kunai — 〜くない is the negative of the same い-adjectives (past: 〜くなかった).

Related: datta-deshita — だった・でした is the past for nouns and な-adjectives, where い-adjectives use 〜かった.

Related: i-adjective-noun — The same い-adjectives can modify a noun directly in their non-past form.

Source references: bunpro
structures: い-adjective［drop い］＋ かった ＋ です［polite］

examples.japanese: 先週の映画はとてもよかった。
examples.english: Last week's movie was really good.

materials.prompt: 代わりに
materials.answer:
instead of; in place of; in exchange for

〜代わりに carries two linked senses: 'instead of / in place of' (substitution) and 'in exchange for / to make up for' (compensation) — バターの代わりにオイルを使う = use oil instead of butter; 手伝う代わりに昼ごはんをおごる = treat someone to lunch in return for help. Context tells you which.
materials.reading: かわりに
materials.notes:
After a noun it takes の: 私の代わりに, not 私代わりに.

The same form covers both 'instead of' and 'in exchange for'; read the context to tell substitution from compensation.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 今日は父の代わりに、私が会議に出た。
examples.english: Today I attended the meeting in place of my father.

materials.prompt: けど・だけど
materials.answer:
but; although

けど joins two clauses with a contrast, meaning "but" or "although". It comes at the end of the first clause and is the casual, everyday choice in conversation. After a noun or な-adjective it appears as だけど.
materials.reading: けど・だけど
materials.notes:
けど is casual; in formal writing or speech, けれども or が are more appropriate.

It doesn't always mark strong contrast — it often just softens or introduces a statement, as in すみませんけど….

Synonyms: keredomo — けれども is the more formal version of the same connector.

Related: demo — でも starts a new sentence; けど joins two clauses within one sentence.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 傾向がある
materials.answer:
there is a tendency to; tend to

傾向がある states that something tends to happen or that people tend to act a certain way. 傾向 is 'inclination / trend', so the phrase describes a general, often statistical pattern rather than a one-time event — 若者は新聞を読まない傾向がある = young people tend not to read newspapers. Common in analytical and written Japanese.
materials.reading: けいこうがある
materials.notes:
It describes a broad, general tendency, so avoid it for a single occasion.

Attach it to the plain verb and negate the verb itself (減らない傾向がある), rather than negating the whole phrase.

Synonyms: gachi — がち is a colloquial 'tend to / prone to', usually negative; 傾向がある is neutral and more formal.

Synonyms: kirai-ga-aru — 嫌いがある is a literary 'has a bad tendency to' and is always negative; 傾向がある can be neutral.

Source references: bunpro

Noun ＋ の ＋ 傾向がある

materials.prompt: 結果
materials.answer:
as a result of; as the outcome of ~

〜結果 means 'as the result of ~', linking an effort or process to its outcome — 話し合った結果 = as a result of discussing it; 努力の結果 = as a result of effort. It presents what actually followed from the preceding action.
materials.reading: けっか
materials.notes:
After a verb use the た-form: 調べた結果, not 調べる結果; after a noun use の: 検査の結果.

It reports an outcome that genuinely followed; it is not a plain 'after (in time)' like た後で.

bunpro lists N2

Related: sue-ni — た末に also means 'after (much) ~, finally'; 末に stresses a long, hard process, while 結果 stresses the outcome that resulted.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: けっこう
materials.answer:
quite; fairly; rather

As an adverb, けっこう means "quite" or "fairly" and often carries the nuance of "more than I expected". It sits before an adjective or verb to boost its degree in a casual, conversational way.
materials.reading: けっこう
materials.notes:
けっこう also works as a set phrase meaning "no, thank you" or "that's fine"; context tells the two apart.

It is more casual than とても and hints that something exceeded expectations, rather than being a plain "very".

Related: totemo — とても is a stronger, more neutral "very"; けっこう is a softer "fairly / quite".

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 結局
materials.answer:
after all; in the end; when all is said and done

結局 is an adverb that sums up the final outcome after a stretch of effort, wavering, or twists and turns. You lay out the process, then use 結局 to state how it actually turned out — often against expectations. It frequently pairs with a result clause like 〜ことになった or a negative 〜なかった.
materials.reading: けっきょく
materials.notes:
結局 points to the end result of a process; it does not mean 'finally, after a long wait' with a sense of relief — that is やっと.

It usually reports how things settled out, so it often precedes a past-tense result (結局〜た／結局〜なかった).

Related: tsui-ni — ついに marks a long-awaited or feared point finally being reached; 結局 states the outcome after a process, often an unexpected one.

Related: sue-ni — た末に sums up the result reached after much effort or deliberation; 結局 simply states how things ended up, effort or not.

Related: tsumari — つまり restates a meaning in other words; 結局 reports how a situation actually ended up.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: けれども
materials.answer:
but; however (formal)

けれども links two clauses with a contrast, meaning "but" or "however". It carries the same job as けど but sounds more formal and complete, so it fits polite speech and writing.
materials.reading: けれども
materials.notes:
けれども, けれど, and けど are the same word at descending levels of formality (けれども most formal, けど most casual).

Like けど, it can also serve as a gentle lead-in rather than a strict contrast.

Synonyms: kedo — けど is the casual, shortened form of the same connector.

Related: shikashi — しかし is also formal, but starts a new sentence rather than joining clauses.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 決して〜ない
materials.answer:
never; by no means; not at all (strong, firm denial)

決して sets up an emphatic negative that follows later in the sentence, expressing the speaker's firm will or an absolute denial — 'never, no matter what.' It is stronger and more formal than ぜんぜん and often signals a promise or conviction.
materials.notes:
決して must be answered by a negative later in the sentence: 決して忘れない, never 決して忘れる.

It conveys the speaker's determination or a categorical 'no'; it is not a neutral 'not really,' which is ぜんぜん or あまり〜ない.

Synonyms: zenzen-nai — ぜんぜん〜ない is a neutral, conversational 'not at all'; 決して〜ない adds firm will and a formal, categorical tone.

Related: kanarazushimo — 必ずしも〜ない softens to 'not necessarily'; 決して〜ない is an absolute 'never.'

Related: nakanaka — なかなか〜ない means 'not easily / not readily'; 決して〜ない is a flat denial regardless of effort.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 気
materials.answer:
気 expressions: mind, feeling, inclination (気がする, 気になる, 気にする, and more)

気 ('mind, spirit, feeling') forms a large family of set expressions about one's mental state: 気がする (have a feeling), 気になる (be bothered or curious), 気にする (mind, worry about), 気をつける (be careful), 気が済む (feel satisfied). The noun 気 combines with a fixed particle and verb in each idiom to describe feelings and inclinations.
materials.reading: き
materials.notes:
気になる is spontaneous (something bothers you); 気にする is deliberate (you choose to worry) — same 気, different verb.

Each idiom fixes its particle (気がする, 気をつける, 気が済む); you cannot swap them freely.

Related: ga-ki-ni-naru — が気になる is one specific member: something weighs on your mind or draws your curiosity.

Related: you-na-ki-ga-suru — ような気がする is the fixed pattern 'have a feeling that ~', built from 気がする.

Related: ni-ki-o-tsukeru — に気をつける ('be careful about ~') is another everyday idiom in the 気 family.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: I have a feeling I've met him somewhere before.
examples.reading: どこかでかれにあったようなきがする。

examples.english: It's better not to worry about the little things.

materials.prompt: 聞こえる
materials.answer:
to be audible; can hear (spontaneously)

聞こえる means a sound reaches your ears on its own, without you trying to listen — 'can hear' in the sense of 'is audible'. The sound is marked with が: 音が聞こえる. It's the hearing partner of 見える, and it's distinct from 聞ける, which is about having the chance or ability to listen to something on purpose.
materials.reading: きこえる
materials.notes:
聞こえる = sound reaches you involuntarily; 聞ける = you get the chance/ability to listen on purpose (a concert, a recording).

Mark the sound with が, not を: 音が聞こえる, not 音を聞こえる.

Related: mieru — 見える is the sight counterpart — something naturally coming into view.

Related: rareru-potential — 聞ける is the plain potential 'can listen'; 聞こえる is sound reaching you on its own.

Source references: bunpro

examples.japanese: 遠くから電車の音が聞こえます。
examples.english: I can hear the sound of a train in the distance.
examples.reading: とおくからでんしゃのおとがきこえます。

examples.japanese: 隣の部屋から誰かの声が聞こえてきた。
examples.english: Someone's voice came through from the next room.
examples.reading: となりのへやからだれかのこえがきこえてきた。

materials.prompt: 〜嫌いがある
materials.answer:
to have a (bad) tendency to; to be inclined to

〜嫌いがある points out an unfavourable disposition — a tendency to do something the speaker regards as regrettable. 物事を悲観的に考える嫌いがある = to have a tendency to think about things pessimistically. It attaches to a dictionary- or ない-form verb, or a noun + の, and belongs to formal, written style. The 嫌い here means 'inclination', unrelated to the everyday word for 'dislike'.
materials.reading: きらいがある
materials.notes:
Describes a negative predisposition and carries mild criticism; not used for good tendencies.

嫌い here means 'inclination', not 'dislike' — don't read it as the emotion.

Formal and written; heavier and more judgmental than casual がち.

Synonyms: gachi — がち is casual and simply notes a frequent tendency; 嫌いがある is formal and pointedly critical of an ingrained inclination.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［dictionary form／ない form］＋嫌いがある

examples.japanese: 彼はどうも物事を大げさに考える嫌いがある。
examples.english: He does seem to have a tendency to think about things in an exaggerated way.
examples.reading: かれはどうもものごとをおおげさにかんがえるきらいがある。

examples.japanese: 最近の報道は、物事の一面だけを強調する嫌いがあるように思う。
examples.english: Recent news coverage seems to have a tendency to emphasize only one side of things.
examples.reading: さいきんのほうどうは、ものごとのいちめんだけをきょうちょうするきらいがあるようにおもう。

materials.prompt: 切れない
materials.answer:
can't finish; too much/many to ~ (all the way)

〜切れない is the negative potential of 〜切る — an action can't be carried through to the end, usually because the amount is too great. 数え切れない = too many to count, 食べ切れない = can't finish eating it all.
materials.reading: きれない
materials.notes:
It usually means 'too much/many to complete', not simply 'I chose not to'.

Attach it to the stem: 使い切れない, not 使う切れない.

Antonyms: kiru — 切る is the positive 'do completely'; 切れない is 'can't get through it all'.

Related: hodo — ほど 'to the extent' pairs naturally as 数え切れないほど 'so many you can't count'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: There's too much food; there's no way I can finish it all.
examples.reading: りょうりがおおすぎて、とてもたべきれない。

examples.japanese: 空には、数え切れないほどの星が見えた。
examples.english: Countless stars were visible in the sky — too many to count.
examples.reading: そらには、かぞえきれないほどのほしがみえた。

materials.prompt: きり
materials.answer:
only; just; (after た-form) ~ and nothing since

きり has two senses: after a noun it means 'only, just' (二人きり = just the two of us), and after a た-form verb it means 'since ~, and nothing has changed since' (出かけたきり = went out and hasn't come back). Both narrow things down to a single case.
materials.reading: きり
materials.notes:
With a た-form it implies the expected next action never followed: 寝たきり = bedridden (lay down and stayed that way).

In the 'only' sense it overlaps with だけ but feels more exclusive and is a bit colloquial.

Synonyms: dake — だけ 'only' is the neutral limiter; きり is more exclusive/colloquial and also has the た-form 'since' use.

Related: bakari — ばかり 'nothing but / just' overlaps in the 'only' sense; きり adds the 'and nothing since' meaning.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I met him just once, and I haven't seen him since.
examples.reading: かれとはいちどあったきり、そのごあっていない。

examples.japanese: 祖母は病気で、もう何年も寝たきりだ。
examples.english: My grandmother is ill and has been bedridden for years now.
examples.reading: そぼはびょうきで、もうなんねんもねたきりだ。

materials.prompt: 切りがない
materials.answer:
there is no end to; endless; no stopping point

切りがない says that something has no natural stopping point — pursue it and you could go on forever. It often appears as 〜ばきりがない: 数え上げればきりがない (there's no end to listing them). きり here means a cut-off or limit, so 切りがない is literally 'there is no cut-off'. It is used to break off an open-ended enumeration or to note that wants and demands have no ceiling.
materials.reading: きりがない
materials.notes:
Frequently framed as 〜ばきりがない ('if you start ~ing, there's no end to it').

きり here means a limit or stopping point, not the 'only' きり of 一人きり.

Often used to cut a discussion short by admitting the topic could go on endlessly.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.japanese: 欲を言えばきりがないが、今の暮らしに大きな不満はない。
examples.english: If I started listing wishes there'd be no end to it, but I have no real complaints about my life as it is.
examples.reading: よくをいえばきりがないが、いまのくらしにおおきなふまんはない。

examples.japanese: 細かい問題点を挙げていけばきりがないので、主なものだけ述べる。
examples.english: There's no end to listing minor issues, so I'll mention only the main ones.
examples.reading: こまかいもんだいてんをあげていけばきりがないので、おもなものだけのべる。

materials.prompt: 切る
materials.answer:
to do completely, all the way to the end (or to the limit)

〜切る attaches to the ます-stem to say you do an action completely, all the way to the end or the limit — 使い切る = use up entirely, 読み切る = read through to the finish. It can also stress reaching an extreme (疲れ切る = be utterly exhausted).
materials.reading: きる
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 食べ切る, not 食べる切る.

Beyond 'finish', it can mean 'to the utter limit' (困り切る = be at a total loss); the sense is completeness or extremeness, not just stopping.

Antonyms: kirenai — 切れない is its negative — 'can't finish / too much to get through'.

Related: owaru — 〜終わる neutrally marks finishing an action; 〜切る adds 'completely, to the very limit'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: The whole family finished off all the food we bought.
examples.reading: かったたべものを、かぞくみんなでたべきった。

examples.japanese: 長いマラソンを、最後まで走り切った。
examples.english: I ran the long marathon all the way to the finish.
examples.reading: ながいマラソンを、さいごまではしりきった。

materials.prompt: 〜きっての
materials.answer:
the best/foremost ~ in (a group, place, or field)

〜きっての singles someone or something out as the very best within a defined group, place, or field. The noun before きって names the domain, and the noun after is what ranks number one in it: この業界きっての実力者 = the leading figure in this industry, 当代きっての名優 = the finest actor of the age. It is a set adnominal form (きって + の + noun) with a somewhat elevated, admiring tone.
materials.reading: きっての
materials.notes:
The first noun is the group or arena within which someone is foremost; the second is the one who ranks highest.

Fixed as きっての directly before a noun; it always modifies a following noun.

Used for a superlative standing ('the best in ~'), generally in a positive, admiring sense.

Related: nara-dewa — ならでは points to a quality only that person or place could produce; きっての ranks someone as number one within a group.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: She is widely known as the most capable figure in this industry.
examples.reading: かのじょはこのぎょうかいきってのじつりょくしゃとして、ひろくなをしられている。

examples.english: The owner of that used-book shop has a reputation as the most knowledgeable person in town.
examples.reading: あのこしょてんのしゅじんは、まちきってのものしりとしてひょうばんだ。

materials.prompt: 〜極まる・〜極まりない
materials.answer:
extremely; utterly; in the highest degree

〜極まる and 〜極まりない both attach to a な-adjective stem and mean 'extremely, utterly ~', describing a quality pushed to its limit: 失礼極まりない (extremely rude), 危険極まる (utterly dangerous). Curiously, despite the ない, 極まりない means the same as 極まる — both are affirmative in force. The pattern is formal, emphatic, and often voices strong disapproval or strong feeling in written style.
materials.reading: きわまる・きわまりない
materials.notes:
極まりない and 極まる mean the same thing here ('extremely'); the ない does not make it negative.

Attaches to a な-adjective naming a quality taken to its extreme, not to ordinary verbs.

Formal, emphatic, and usually charged with strong (often negative) feeling.

Synonyms: no-kiwami — の極み attaches to a noun and names 'the very height of ~'; 極まる／極まりない attach to a な-adjective quality.

Synonyms: kagiri-da — 限りだ conveys the speaker's own feeling at its utmost (嬉しい限りだ); 極まりない more often condemns an external quality.

Related: no-itari — の至り expresses an emotion or state reaching its extreme, often in set humble phrases; 極まる rates a described quality as extreme.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: あのような公の場で騒ぎ立てるとは、失礼極まりない態度だ。
examples.english: To make a scene in a public setting like that is an utterly rude way to behave.
examples.reading: あのようなおおやけのばでさわぎたてるとは、しつれいきわまりないたいどだ。

examples.english: They kept up their extremely dangerous work at height without any protective equipment at all.
examples.reading: かれらはきけんきわまるこうしょでのさぎょうを、なにのそうびもなしにつづけていた。

materials.prompt: っけ
materials.answer:
what was it again? (casual ending to confirm a half-remembered thing)

っけ is a casual sentence-final particle you tack on when you're trying to recall or double-check something you've half-forgotten — 'what was it again?' It usually follows the plain past (〜たっけ) or だ→だっけ. It belongs to relaxed, friendly speech among close people.
materials.reading: っけ
materials.notes:
It's casual; in polite situations people say 〜でしたっけ / 〜ましたっけ instead.

With nouns and な-adjectives it becomes だっけ: 今日は何曜日だっけ.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: あれ、鍵はどこに置いたっけ。
examples.english: Huh, where did I put the keys again?
examples.reading: あれ、かぎはどこにおいたっけ。

examples.japanese: 明日の会議は何時からだっけ。

materials.prompt: っこない
materials.answer:
there's no chance of ~; definitely won't / can't

っこない attaches to the ます-stem to flatly deny that something could ever happen — 分かりっこない = 'there's no way I'd understand', 勝てっこない = 'we can't possibly win'. It is a casual, spoken way to voice the speaker's firm conviction that something is impossible, close in meaning to はずがない but far more colloquial.
materials.reading: っこない
materials.notes:
Attach it to the ます-stem, not the dictionary form: 勝てっこない, not 勝つっこない.

It belongs to casual, spoken Japanese; avoid it in formal writing, where はずがない or わけがない fit better.

It states the speaker's own strong belief that something is impossible, not an objective fact.

Synonyms: wake-ga-nai — わけがない also denies possibility but is neutral in register; っこない is distinctly casual and spoken.

Synonyms: hazu-ga-nai — はずがない reasons that something 'can't be so'; っこない is a blunter, colloquial 'no way it'll happen'.

Related: mai — まい is a formal/written negative conjecture ('surely won't'); っこない carries the same certainty in casual speech.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 込む
materials.answer:
to ~ into (inward); to ~ deeply / thoroughly

込む attaches to a verb stem in two related senses: moving something inward (飛び込む jump in, 押し込む shove in) and doing an action deeply, hard, or over a long stretch (考え込む sink into thought, 使い込む use extensively). Context makes clear which sense is meant. The compound conjugates as an ordinary う-verb.
materials.reading: こむ
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 飛び込む, not 飛ぶ込む.

It covers two senses — moving inward and doing thoroughly — so read the base verb and context to tell 押し込む (shove in) from 考え込む (become lost in thought).

Antonyms: dasu — 〜出す points an action outward or marks a sudden start; 込む (in the inward sense) moves things in.

Related: kiru — 〜切る stresses completing an action fully to the end; 込む (thorough sense) stresses doing it deeply or at length.

Related: nuku — 〜抜く means pushing an action through to the very end despite difficulty; 込む (thorough sense) is doing it intensively or repeatedly.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ことこの上ない・この上ない
materials.answer:
unsurpassed; in the extreme; couldn't be more ~

この上ない literally says 'there is nothing above this' — the degree is the highest possible. After an adjective plus こと it grades that quality to the extreme: 不用心なことこの上ない = careless in the extreme. On its own it modifies a noun (この上ない喜び = the greatest possible joy), and the adverbial この上なく intensifies a predicate (この上なく幸せだ). The tone is formal-written, and unlike 極まりない it works comfortably with positive qualities as well as negative ones.
materials.reading: ことこのうえない・このうえない
materials.notes:
It grades qualities, so it attaches to adjectives (via こと) or nouns — not directly to verbs.

極まりない leans heavily toward negative qualities; この上ない is equally natural with positive ones (この上ない幸せ).

Synonyms: kiwamaru-kiwamarinai — 極まりない also marks an extreme degree but attaches to な-adjective stems and skews negative; この上ない welcomes positive qualities.

Synonyms: no-kiwami — の極み attaches to nouns (感激の極み); この上ない grades adjectives and modifies nouns directly.

Related: no-itari — の至り expresses an extreme of emotion in fixed formal phrases (光栄の至り); この上ない is a more general superlative.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 頃
materials.answer:
around; about (a point in time)

ころ／ごろ marks an approximate point in time — 'around'. Voiced ごろ attaches to a specific clock time or date (八時ごろ = around eight), while ころ follows periods or events (子どものころ = when I was a child). It pins down 'roughly when', not 'how long'.
materials.reading: ころ・ごろ
materials.notes:
ごろ is for a point in time (八時ごろ = around eight). For an approximate amount or duration, use くらい／ぐらい: 三時間ぐらい = about three hours.

Don't add に after ごろ when it already means 'around a time' — 八時ごろ会う is natural; 八時ごろに also occurs but the に is optional.

Related: kurai-gurai — くらい／ぐらい gives an approximate amount or degree; ごろ gives an approximate time point.

Related: toki — とき names the occasion 'when' something happens; ころ softens it to 'around the time'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: こそ
materials.answer:
precisely; for sure; this very one (emphasis)

こそ spotlights the word right before it, singling it out as 'this one, precisely, and not another.' Attached to a noun or phrase it says 'this is the one that really counts' — 今度こそ (this time for sure), こちらこそ (no, thank YOU). It highlights rather than contrasts.
materials.reading: こそ
materials.notes:
こそ spotlights one item as 'precisely this'; unlike は it does not set up a topic-and-contrast, it simply emphasizes.

In reply exchanges こちらこそ means 'the feeling is mine, precisely' — the emphasis lands on こちら, not on thanking again.

Related: kara-koso — からこそ means 'precisely because'; here こそ is fused with the reason から, while plain こそ can spotlight any noun.

Related: sae — さえ emphasizes by giving an extreme example ('even this'); こそ emphasizes by singling one thing out as the very one.

Related: dake — だけ limits to 'only this'; こそ spotlights 'this, precisely,' without excluding others.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜こそあれ
materials.answer:
though there may be ~; there is ~, but

〜こそあれ concedes that A does exist or is the case, then goes on to a contrasting statement that discounts its importance — 'there may indeed be A, but ~'. 多少の違いこそあれ、本質は同じだ = there may be slight differences, but the essence is the same. It attaches to a noun (a な-adjective takes で before it) and uses the classical あれ. The tone is formal and literary, and the following clause often negates or minimizes.
materials.reading: こそあれ
materials.notes:
Concedes that A exists, then the following clause downplays or denies its significance — often 〜こそあれ、〜ない.

Uses the classical あれ (from ある); formal and literary.

Attaches to a noun; a な-adjective needs で before こそあれ.

Synonyms: koso-sure — こそすれ builds on a verb ('may well ~, but certainly not ...'); こそあれ builds on a noun ('there may be ~, but ...').

Synonyms: towa-ie — とはいえ concedes a whole statement then qualifies it; こそあれ concedes the existence of a specific thing then downplays it.

Related: koso-ga — 〜こそ〜が concedes a point then contrasts it with a heavier main claim; こそあれ concedes existence then minimizes its weight.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜こそ〜が
materials.answer:
it is true that ~, but; ~ indeed, yet

In the 〜こそ〜が pattern, こそ emphasizes a point that is then conceded, while が (or けれど) introduces the contrasting main claim. The shape is 'A こそ ~, が B' = 'A may indeed be the case, but B'. 規模こそ小さいが = small in scale it may be, but... The real weight of the sentence falls on the clause after が; the こそ part is granted only to be set against it.
materials.notes:
こそ marks the conceded point; the true emphasis lands on the clause after が/けれど.

It is a concessive 'A indeed, but B', not a plain listing of two facts.

Written and somewhat emphatic in tone.

Related: koso — こそ on its own simply emphasizes ('it is precisely ~'); 〜こそ〜が uses that emphasis to set up a concession before a contrast.

Related: koso-are — こそあれ concedes that A exists then downplays it; 〜こそ〜が concedes A then contrasts it with a weightier main claim.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜こそすれ
materials.answer:
may well ~, but certainly not ...

〜こそすれ concedes that one thing does hold — and then flatly denies the alternative the listener might expect. 感謝こそすれ、恨みはない = I may well feel gratitude, but resentment, never. It uses すれ, the classical conditional stem of する, after こそ, and the clause that follows must be a denial. The tone is formal and literary; in speech people would say 〜することはあっても instead.
materials.reading: こそすれ
materials.notes:
The second clause must deny something: 感謝こそすれ、恨むことはない — ending on an affirmative statement breaks the pattern.

すれ is the classical 已然形 of する, not the conditional すれば — write こそすれ, not こそすれば.

This is formal, written-style Japanese; it sounds stiff in casual conversation.

Related: koso — こそ simply spotlights one element ('precisely X'); こそすれ builds on it to concede X while denying the alternative.

Related: ba-koso — ばこそ emphasizes a reason ('precisely because'); こそすれ concedes one action and rules out another.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: あなたには感謝こそすれ、恨む気持ちなど少しもありません。

materials.prompt: こと
materials.answer:
nominalizer: turns a verb or clause into a noun

こと turns a verb or a whole clause into a noun so it can act as a subject or object: 泳ぐこと = swimming, 早く寝ること = going to bed early. The verb stays in plain form right before こと. It's the tool for talking about actions and facts as things — hobbies, what's important, what you like.
materials.reading: こと
materials.notes:
Both こと and の nominalize; こと leans toward abstract facts and general statements, while の suits concrete, directly perceived actions.

Keep the verb in plain form before こと: 撮ること, not 撮りますこと.

Synonyms: no-nominalizer — の nominalizes too, but favors concrete, perceived actions; こと favors abstract facts.

Related: koto-ga-dekiru — ことができる is this こと plus ができる to express ability.

Related: koto-ga-aru — ことがある builds on this こと to say something happens on occasion.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことだ
materials.answer:
should; the thing to do is to ~ (direct advice)

Attached to a verb, ことだ delivers direct advice or a recommendation — 'the best thing is to do X.' It sounds firm and a little instructive, as if handing down the sensible course of action. Use the dictionary form for what to do, the ない-form for what to avoid.
materials.reading: ことだ
materials.notes:
This advice sense attaches to a verb; when ことだ follows a feeling word (うれしいことだ) it is instead an exclamation, a different use.

It can sound top-down, like giving a lesson; for gentler suggestions use ほうがいい or 〜といい.

jlptsensei lists N2

Synonyms: hou-ga-ii — ほうがいい gently suggests one option is better; ことだ states more forcefully what one really ought to do.

Antonyms: koto-wa-nai — ことはない says there is no need to do something; ことだ says doing it is exactly what one should do.

Related: beki-da — べきだ frames a should as a matter of principle or duty; ことだ gives practical, situational advice.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ことだし
materials.answer:
since; seeing as (one reason among others)

〜ことだし offers one reason — while hinting there are others — as gentle grounds for a suggestion or decision: 雨も上がったことだし、出かけよう = the rain's stopped (among other things), so let's head out. The こと wraps the reason up as an established circumstance, and し adds the 'and other reasons too' flavor. It is conversational but slightly considered in tone, and the sentence usually ends with a proposal, intention, or request rather than a plain statement.
materials.reading: ことだし
materials.notes:
It implies the stated reason is not the only one — for a single, direct cause, use から or ので.

The main clause is typically a suggestion, decision, or request (〜しよう, 〜たらどう), not a neutral report.

Synonyms: shi — Plain し also lists reasons; ことだし is softer and frames the reason as a settled circumstance leading to a proposal.

Related: koto-mo-atte — こともあって reports a partial cause of a fact; ことだし gives a reason for what the speaker proposes to do.

Related: koto-dakara — ことだから reasons from someone's known character; ことだし cites a circumstance as one reason among several.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: ことだから
materials.answer:
since it's ~ (given what we know of them); knowing ~

〜ことだから builds a prediction on the known character of a person or group. Because we know what they are like, we can guess how they will act — 几帳面な彼のことだから遅れないだろう = knowing how punctual he is, he surely won't be late. It attaches to a noun (usually a person) + の.
materials.reading: ことだから
materials.notes:
The noun is normally a specific person or group you both know; the guess leans on their established character.

It sets up a prediction about that person's behavior, so it usually leads into だろう・にちがいない, not a plain statement of fact.

Related: dake-ni — だけに draws a heightened result from a known fact ('all the more because'); ことだから predicts behavior from someone's character.

Related: koto-mo-atte — こともあって states a contributing reason ('partly because'); ことだから predicts an action from what someone is like.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun［person／group］＋ の ＋ ことだから

materials.prompt: ことがある
materials.answer:
there are times when; sometimes

With a verb in dictionary form, 〜ことがある says an action happens now and then — 'there are times when...'. 遅れることがある = the train is sometimes late. It describes occasional occurrence, and it's often paired with たまに or ときどき. Watch the tense: the past 〜たことがある means something completely different (past experience).
materials.reading: ことがある
materials.notes:
Dictionary form 〜ことがある = 'sometimes happens'; past 〜たことがある = 'have done before'. 食べることがある is 'I sometimes eat it', while 食べたことがある is 'I have eaten it'.

It states occasional events, so pairing it with たまに or ときどき reads naturally.

bunpro lists N3

Related: ta-koto-ga-aru — 〜たことがある is the past-experience sibling ('have done'); this one is 'sometimes do'.

Related: koto — This pattern is the こと nominalizer plus がある ('there are occasions of').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことができる
materials.answer:
can; to be able to

Verb［dictionary form］＋ことができる expresses ability or possibility — 'can do'. 弾くことができる = can play. It means the same as the potential verb form (弾ける) but sounds a touch more formal and is common in writing and announcements. The verb before ことができる stays in plain dictionary form.
materials.reading: ことができる
materials.notes:
Keep the verb in dictionary form: 弾くことができる, not the potential 弾けることができる.

It's a little more formal than the plain potential form (弾ける), which is preferred in casual speech.

Synonyms: rareru-potential — The potential verb form says the same 'can do' more casually; ことができる is a bit more formal.

Related: koto — This is the こと nominalizer plus ができる ('be possible').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことごとく
materials.answer:
entirely; every last one; without exception

ことごとく is a formal adverb meaning that something applies to every single item with no exceptions: 提案がことごとく否決された = every last proposal was voted down. It typically sweeps over a set of things (plans, predictions, buildings) and very often the outcome is unwelcome — everything failed, everything was destroyed. In kanji it is 悉く, but it is normally written in kana. It belongs to written and news-report style; casual speech prefers 全部 or すべて.
materials.reading: ことごとく
materials.notes:
It strongly tends to appear with unfavorable outcomes (ことごとく外れる, ことごとく失敗する); for neutral 'all', すべて or 全部 is safer.

Despite the look, it has no connection to 〜ごとく ('like') — ことごとく is one word meaning 'without exception'.

Related: gotoku — 〜ごとく means 'like, as if' and is a different word entirely — don't let the shared kana mislead you.

Related: marukkiri — まるっきり means 'utterly, completely' about degree; ことごとく counts through every member of a set.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: ことか
materials.answer:
how …!; what …! (deep emotion)

ことか turns a statement into a heartfelt exclamation, usually paired with a question word like どんなに, どれほど, or なんと. It voices strong emotion — how happy, how worried, how long — rather than asking a real question. It has a slightly literary, emotional ring.
materials.reading: ことか
materials.notes:
It normally needs a degree word (どんなに, どれほど, なんと) to carry the exclamation; ことか alone does not do the job.

Despite the か, it is not a question — it is an emphatic outpouring of feeling.

jlptsensei lists N2

Related: koto-ni — ことに front-loads the emotion word to color a fact ('to my surprise, …'); ことか makes the whole line an exclamation of degree.

Related: mono-da — ものだ can voice deep feeling or fond recollection; ことか is specifically an exclamation of 'how much.'

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: どんなに／どれほど／なんと ＋ ［plain form］＋ ことか

materials.prompt: ことから
materials.answer:
from the fact that; judging from; owing to the fact that

ことから presents a fact as the grounds you reason from — 'from the fact that A, we can tell / it came about that B.' It often explains how a conclusion is reached, or how a name or reputation arose. The B clause is a judgment, result, or naming that follows from A.
materials.reading: ことから
materials.notes:
ことから frames A as evidence you infer B from; plain から simply gives a cause, without that 'judging from' nuance.

な-adjectives and nouns take な／である before ことから (静かなことから, 有名であることから).

Related: kara — から states a straightforward reason; ことから presents a fact as evidence you draw a conclusion from.

Related: node — ので gives an objective cause for a result; ことから emphasizes reasoning outward from a known fact.

Related: koto-dakara — ことだから reasons from someone's known character; ことから reasons from an observed fact or circumstance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: From the fact that the window was broken, we knew a burglar had gotten in.

examples.japanese: 空が急に暗くなったことから、もうすぐ雨になると思った。
examples.english: Judging from how suddenly the sky darkened, I figured it would rain soon.
examples.reading: そらがきゅうにくらくなったことから、もうすぐあめになるとおもった。

materials.prompt: 〜こともあって
materials.answer:
partly because; with ~ also being a factor

〜こともあって cites one contributing reason while openly signaling it is not the whole story: 駅から近いこともあって、いつも混んでいる = partly because it's near the station, it's always crowded. The も does the work — 'this factor, among others, exists'. It attaches to plain-form clauses (nouns take という or である) and suits neutral explanation in both speech and writing; the main clause states the resulting situation.
materials.reading: こともあって
materials.notes:
It presents a partial cause — if the reason is the sole, direct cause, use ので or ため instead.

The main clause reports an observed result, not a proposal; for reason-plus-suggestion, use ことだし.

Related: sei-ka — せいか guesses at an uncertain (often negative) cause; こともあって confidently names one factor among several.

Related: koto-da-shi — ことだし gives a reason for what the speaker will do; こともあって explains why a situation is the way it is.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: な-adjective＋な／である＋こともあって
Noun＋という／である＋こともあって

examples.reading: れんきゅうだったこともあって、ゆうえんちはかぞくづれでにぎわっていた。

materials.prompt: ことなく
materials.answer:
without ~ing; never once ~ing

〜ことなく attaches to a dictionary-form verb to mean 'without doing that action' — 休むことなく働いた = worked without resting. It is the more formal, written counterpart of 〜ないで／〜ずに, and often stresses that something carried on the whole time without that action ever interrupting it.
materials.reading: ことなく
materials.notes:
Attach it to the dictionary form (止まることなく), not the ない form.

It belongs to formal or written Japanese; in speech 〜ないで or 〜ずに is more natural.

Synonyms: zuni — ずに also means 'without doing'; ことなく is more formal and often more emphatic about continuity.

Synonyms: nashi-ni — なしに attaches to a noun ('without ~'); ことなく attaches to a verb ('without doing ~').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: This factory has run for thirty years without stopping even once.
examples.reading: このこうじょうはさんじゅうねんかん、いちどもとまることなくかどうしている。

materials.prompt: ことなの
materials.answer:
it means (doing) ~; it comes down to ~; what it is, is ~

ことなのだ (casual ことなの, polite ことなのです) restates a topic as what it fundamentally amounts to. It takes a plain clause, packages it as a こと — a matter or act — and equates the topic with it, explaining 'what X really is / what it means.' The な comes from こと being treated with the explanatory の.
materials.reading: ことなの
materials.notes:
The な is required because こと takes the explanatory の: ことなのだ, not ことのだ.

This is a defining 'it means that ~,' distinct from the advice ことだ that attaches to a verb ('you should ~').

Synonyms: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ also restates a meaning ('that is to say'); ことなのだ frames the whole thing as one defining matter with explanatory の.

Related: koto-da — ことだ after a verb gives advice; ことなのだ defines or explains what something amounts to.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ことなしに
materials.answer:
without doing; unless (one does)

〜ことなしに attaches to a dictionary-form verb and means the main action happens without that verb ever occurring: 誰にも相談することなしに決めた = decided without consulting anyone. In its second, more argumentative use, the main clause is negative or potential-negative and the whole sentence reads 'unless you do X, Y is impossible' — 努力することなしに成功はあり得ない. Both uses are formal and written in flavor; everyday speech would use 〜ないで or 〜ずに.
materials.reading: ことなしに
materials.notes:
Attach it to the dictionary form via こと: 相談することなしに, not 相談したことなしに.

It is distinctly formal; for everyday 'without doing', 〜ないで or 〜ずに is the natural choice.

In the 'unless' use, the main clause must be negative in sense: 犠牲を払うことなしに自由は得られない.

Synonyms: nashi-ni — なしに attaches directly to nouns (連絡なしに); ことなしに packages a verb phrase into the same construction.

Synonyms: naide — ないで is the neutral spoken 'without doing'; ことなしに is its stiff written counterpart.

Related: nakushite-wa — なくしては ('without ~, no ...') also builds an 'impossible without' argument, but from a noun.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: Success is impossible without steady, patient effort.
examples.reading: じみちにどりょくすることなしに、せいこうはありえない。

materials.prompt: ことに
materials.answer:
to my ~ (surprise, delight, regret); ~ enough

ことに puts a feeling word up front to color the fact that follows — 驚いたことに (to my surprise), 残念なことに (regrettably). The emotion is the speaker's reaction to what comes next, delivered as a lead-in before the main clause.
materials.reading: ことに
materials.notes:
Only emotion words fit (驚いた, うれしい, 残念な); a neutral verb like 食べた does not work here.

The feeling comes first as a reaction; the fact that caused it follows after ことに.

jlptsensei lists N2

Related: koto-ka — ことか makes the whole line an exclamation of degree; ことに tags one feeling onto a fact that follows.

Related: mono-da — ものだ voices general feeling or nostalgia; ことに names a specific reaction to a specific fact.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことになる
materials.answer:
it has been decided that; it turns out that

Verb［dictionary or ない form］＋ことになる says a decision or arrangement has come about, usually through circumstances or a group rather than your own will. 転勤することになった = it's been arranged that I'll transfer. Even when you were involved, it sounds more modest than ことにする. The form ことになっている describes a standing rule or fixed arrangement.
materials.reading: ことになる
materials.notes:
ことになる presents the decision as coming from circumstances or others; ことにする presents it as your own choice.

ことになっている (ongoing) states a standing rule or arrangement, not a new outcome.

bunpro lists N3

Related: koto-ni-suru — ことにする is a decision you make; ことになる is one that comes about around you.

Related: koto-ni-natteiru — ことになっている is the settled-rule form of this pattern.

Related: you-ni-naru — 〜ようになる is a gradual change reaching a state; ことになる is a decision being set.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことになっている
materials.answer:
it is a rule / arrangement / custom that ~; is supposed to ~

ことになっている describes a rule, arrangement, or custom that is already in place and expected to hold — a school regulation, a schedule, a standing plan. It presents the situation as an established norm rather than a fresh decision.
materials.reading: ことになっている
materials.notes:
ことになっている is a standing rule or arrangement in place; ことになる is a decision or outcome coming about at some point.

Do not confuse it with ことにしている, which is a personal habit you keep by choice, not an external rule.

bunpro lists N2

Related: koto-ni-naru — ことになる is the moment a decision or result comes about; ことになっている is the rule or arrangement that then stands.

Related: koto-ni-suru — ことにする is deciding to do something yourself; ことになっている is a norm set from outside.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことにする
materials.answer:
to decide to (do)

Verb［dictionary or ない form］＋ことにする marks a decision you make yourself. 走ることにする = I've decided to run; 飲まないことにする = I've decided not to drink. The past ことにした reports a decision already reached, and ことにしている describes a rule or habit you keep to on purpose.
materials.reading: ことにする
materials.notes:
ことにする is your own choice; ことになる is a decision made by circumstances or others.

ことにしている (ongoing) describes a habit you've resolved to keep, not a single fresh decision.

bunpro lists N3

Related: koto-ni-naru — ことになる is when things get decided for you; ことにする is deciding yourself.

Related: you-ni-suru — 〜ようにする is making an ongoing effort toward a state; ことにする is a one-time decision.

materials.prompt: ことにはならない
materials.answer:
it doesn't (automatically) mean that ~; that doesn't make it ~

〜ことにはならない rejects a conclusion someone might jump to — 'that doesn't mean ~'. It commonly follows からといって: 高いからといって、いい物だということにはならない = just because it's expensive doesn't make it a good product. It refuses to treat one fact as if it settled another.
materials.reading: ことにはならない
materials.notes:
It denies an inference ('doesn't mean'), not a fact ('didn't happen').

It is very often set up by からといって earlier in the sentence.

Related: kara-to-itte — からといって sets up the premise ('just because ~'); ことにはならない then denies the conclusion drawn from it.

Related: wake-dewa-nai — わけではない broadly denies an implied conclusion; ことにはならない specifically denies that one fact makes another true.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ことのないように
materials.answer:
so as never to; to make sure ~ never happens

〜ことのないように wraps a feared event in ことのない ('such that it never happens') and aims an action at preventing it: 二度と起こることのないように対策する = take measures so it never happens again. It is the formal, emphatic version of plain ないように, common in official apologies, announcements, and warnings, and frequently reinforced with 二度と ('never again'). The main clause states the precaution or request.
materials.reading: ことのないように
materials.notes:
It is more formal and emphatic than plain 〜ないように; in casual speech, 忘れないようにね is enough.

The verb before ことのない is in the dictionary form: 起こることのないように, not 起こったことのないように.

Synonyms: you-ni-so-that — Plain ように expresses the same purpose neutrally; ことのないように adds formal weight and the sense of 'never'.

Related: bekarazu — べからず bluntly prohibits on signs; ことのないように politely urges prevention.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜こととて
materials.answer:
because; as (formal, often apologetic)

〜こととて presents a circumstance as the reason for something — most often as an excuse when apologizing or asking for indulgence: 慣れぬこととて = as (I am) unaccustomed to it. It is markedly old-fashioned and formal, at home in business letters, formal apologies, and period fiction. It follows a plain-form clause or Noun＋の, and famously combines with the classical negative ぬ (知らぬこととて, 慣れぬこととて).
materials.reading: こととて
materials.notes:
It is archaic-formal; using it in casual conversation sounds theatrical. In speech, ものですから or ので fills the same role.

With negatives it characteristically takes the classical ぬ (慣れぬこととて); the plain ない (慣れないこととて) is also used but sounds less set.

The main clause is usually an apology or a request for understanding, not a neutral consequence.

Synonyms: mono-de — もので also gives an excuse-flavored reason, but is ordinary polite speech; こととて is archaic and ceremonious.

Related: koto-da-shi — ことだし casually offers one reason for a proposal; こととて formally excuses a shortcoming.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことは〜が
materials.answer:
it's true that ~, but; ~, yes, but ~ (partial concession)

By repeating the same predicate around ことは and following with が, you concede a point partway before qualifying it — 話せることは話せるが (I can speak it, sure, but…). It admits the first half is true, then adds a reservation.
materials.notes:
Repeat the same predicate on both sides of ことは (高いことは高いが), not two different words.

It grants the point only partly; the real message lands in the が clause that follows.

bunpro lists N2

Related: kedo — けど simply joins a 'but' clause; ことは〜が specifically concedes the point half-heartedly before qualifying it.

Related: monono — ものの concedes an established fact then adds a contrary result; ことは〜が repeats the predicate to grant it only partly.

Related: towa-ie — とはいえ is a formal 'that said'; ことは〜が is a colloquial 'true, but' built by repeating the word.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ことはない
materials.answer:
there is no need to ~; no reason to ~

Verb-dictionary + ことはない reassures someone that a certain action isn't necessary — 'you don't need to (do that).' It is gentle, encouraging advice, often used to talk someone out of worrying or overreacting.
materials.reading: ことはない
materials.notes:
Verb-dictionary + ことはない means 'no need to do'; do not mix it up with たことがない, which means 'have never done' (past experience).

It reassures or reduces a burden, so it pairs with actions the listener need not take on.

Antonyms: koto-da — ことだ says doing something is exactly what you should do; ことはない says there's no need to do it.

Related: hou-ga-ii — ほうがいい recommends doing something; ことはない reassures that you don't have to.

Related: beki-da — べきだ frames a duty to act; ことはない removes any such obligation.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: く・に
materials.answer:
turning adjectives into adverbs (〜く / 〜に)

To describe how an action is done, adjectives take an adverb form. An い-adjective changes its final い to く (早い→早く), and a な-adjective adds に (静か→静かに). The result modifies a verb: 早く起きる = get up early, 静かに歩く = walk quietly.
materials.reading: く・に
materials.notes:
い-adjectives use く, な-adjectives use に: 早く and 静かに, never 早に or 静かく.

いい is irregular: its adverb form is よく, not いく.

Related: ni-suru-ku-suru — 〜くする・〜にする uses the same く／に forms to make something become that way.

Related: ku-wa — くは adds は to the 〜く adverb form for contrast, mostly in negatives.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: くは
materials.answer:
〜く + は (contrast or qualified negation)

Adding は to the adverbial 〜く form of an い-adjective sets that quality apart for contrast or partial denial, most often before a negative: 高くはない = it's not exactly expensive (as for being pricey, no). The は hints that while one thing may not hold, something else might — a softer, more qualified statement than the flat 〜くない.
materials.reading: くは
materials.notes:
高くはない reads as a qualified 'not exactly expensive'; plain 高くない is a flat 'not expensive'.

This pattern almost always leads into a negative; a bare 安くは on its own sounds unfinished.

Related: ku-ni — 〜く is the plain adverb form; くは adds は onto it to mark contrast.

Related: kunai — 〜くない is the flat negative; くはない adds a contrastive, hedging tone.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: くない
materials.answer:
not ~ (i-adjective negative)

Makes an い-adjective negative: drop the final い and add くない to say something is "not ~". This is the plain present-negative form; add です after it for polite speech.
materials.reading: くない
materials.notes:
いい (good) is irregular: its negative is よくない, not いくない.

くない works only on い-adjectives; for nouns and な-adjectives use じゃない instead.

Related: kunakatta — くなかった is the past-tense version of this same い-adjective negative.

Related: janai — じゃない negates nouns and な-adjectives, where くない cannot be used.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: くなかった
materials.answer:
was not ~ (i-adjective past negative)

The past-negative form of an い-adjective: drop the final い and add くなかった to say something "was not ~". Add です after it to make it polite.
materials.reading: くなかった
materials.notes:
いい (good) is irregular here too: its past negative is よくなかった.

For politeness, add です → くなかったです; never say くないでした.

Related: kunai — くない is the present-tense form; くなかった shifts it to the past.

Related: janakatta — じゃなかった is the matching past negative for nouns and な-adjectives.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: くらい
materials.answer:
about; approximately

Placed after a number or amount to make it approximate, meaning "about" or "roughly". The variant ぐらい means exactly the same thing; the two are interchangeable.
materials.reading: くらい
materials.notes:
くらい and ぐらい are the same word — pick whichever sounds smoother after the preceding sound.

Use くらい for amounts and durations; for an approximate point in time use ごろ (三時ごろ = around three o'clock).

Related: hodo — ほど can also express an approximate degree, but is more formal and reaches beyond N5.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: くらい・ぐらい
materials.answer:
about, approximately; to the extent that ~

くらい・ぐらい has two jobs: with quantities it means 'about, approximately' (千円くらい = about 1,000 yen), and after a clause it marks a degree by example — 'to the extent that…' (泣きたいくらい = to the point of wanting to cry). くらい and ぐらい are interchangeable.
materials.reading: くらい・ぐらい
materials.notes:
In the extent sense it gives a vivid example of a degree (立てないくらい疲れた = so tired I couldn't stand), not a precise measure.

くらい and ぐらい mean the same thing; ぐらい just tends to follow certain sounds. Both are fine.

Synonyms: hodo — ほど also marks extent and approximation; it is a bit more formal and common in negative comparisons.

Related: kurai — The standalone N5 くらい covers just the basic 'about' (approximation) sense.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［plain form］＋ くらい・ぐらい

examples.english: It takes about fifteen minutes on foot to the station.

examples.japanese: お腹が痛くて、動けないくらいだった。
examples.english: My stomach hurt so much that I could barely move.
examples.reading: おなかがいたくて、うごけないくらいだった。

materials.prompt: 〜くらいなら・〜ぐらいなら
materials.answer:
rather than (do something that unpleasant); if it comes to ~, I'd sooner

〜くらいなら weighs the first option as something so unpleasant that the speaker would sooner take another, often drastic, alternative — 'rather than A, I'd rather B'. 途中でやめるくらいなら、最初からやらない = rather than quit halfway, I'd not start at all. It attaches to a dictionary-form verb and frequently pairs with むしろ or 〜ほうがましだ. It is a pointed comparison, not a neutral one.
materials.reading: くらいなら・ぐらいなら
materials.notes:
The くらいなら option is presented as bad or unbearable, and the alternative as the lesser evil — not an even-handed choice.

Often paired with むしろ or 〜ほうがましだ to point to the preferred, sometimes extreme, alternative.

くらい here downgrades the first option rather than estimating a quantity.

Synonyms: mushiro — むしろ marks the 'rather / sooner' side of the choice and often co-occurs; くらいなら packages the rejected option as an unbearable one.

Related: yori — より makes a plain comparison ('than'); くらいなら adds that the first option is bad enough to reject outright.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［dictionary form］＋くらいなら＋（むしろ）～ほうがましだ／～たい

examples.reading: まんいんでんしゃでつうきんするくらいなら、すこしとおまわりでもじてんしゃでいきたい。

examples.japanese: 人に頭を下げて頼むくらいなら、自分でやったほうがまだましだ。
examples.english: Rather than bow my head and beg someone, I'd be better off just doing it myself.
examples.reading: ひとにあたまをさげてたのむくらいなら、じぶんでやったほうがまだましだ。

materials.prompt: 〜くらいのものだ
materials.answer:
about the only ~; ~ is just about the only one

〜くらいのものだ narrows things down to essentially a single case — 'that's about the only one'. こんなことを言うのは彼くらいのものだ = he's about the only one who'd say such a thing. It attaches to a noun (often after a 〜のは clause), and the くらい softens a flat 'only' into 'more or less the sole case'. The tone is one of resigned or wry observation that scarcely anyone else qualifies.
materials.reading: くらいのものだ
materials.notes:
Singles out essentially the only case that fits — close to だけ but softer, with a nuance of 'that's about all'.

くらい here limits the scope, not approximates a quantity.

Commonly set up by a 〜のは clause naming what almost no one does.

Synonyms: dake — だけ states 'only' flatly; くらいのものだ softens it to 'about the only one', with a resigned or wry undertone.

Synonyms: ni-suginai — にすぎない downplays something as 'no more than'; くらいのものだ limits the field to essentially a single case.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［plain form］＋のは＋Noun＋くらいのものだ

examples.reading: あのみせのことをいまでもおぼえているのは、じもとのふるいじゅうみんくらいのものだ。

materials.prompt: くれる
materials.answer:
to give (to me / my in-group)

くれる describes someone giving something to you or to your in-group (family, close friends). The giver is the subject, and the sense of the verb points the gift toward the speaker's side.
materials.reading: くれる
materials.notes:
Use くれる only when the receiver is you or your in-group; when you give to someone else, use あげる.

The giver is marked with が／は, and the receiver (usually 私) takes に.

Antonyms: ageru-giving — あげる gives outward, away from the speaker; くれる gives inward, toward the speaker.

Related: morau — もらう describes the same exchange from the receiver's side ("to receive").

Related: te-kureru — てくれる extends くれる to doing an action as a favor for me/us.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Giver ＋ が ＋ （私に）＋ Noun ＋ を ＋ くれる

examples.japanese: 父が新しい自転車をくれた。

materials.prompt: くる
materials.answer:
to come (irregular verb)

くる (来る) means "to come" and is one of Japanese's two irregular verbs. Its stem vowel changes across forms, so it must be memorized rather than conjugated by the usual rules.
materials.reading: くる
materials.notes:
くる is irregular: it becomes き- (きます, きた, きて) and こ- (こない) in different forms, not the regular う-verb or る-verb patterns.

Written 来る, the kanji 来 is read き, こ, or く depending on the conjugation.

Antonyms: e-iku — へ行く moves away toward a place; くる moves toward the speaker.

Related: suru — する is the other irregular verb learned alongside くる.

Source references: bunpro
structures: くる ＋ ［polite: きます］／［negative: こない］
くる ＋ ［past: きた］／［て form: きて］

materials.prompt: くせに
materials.answer:
even though; despite (with blame or contempt)

〜くせに means 'even though', but always with a critical, reproachful edge — you are blaming or looking down on someone for the contradiction. 知っているくせに教えてくれない = he won't tell me even though he knows. Both clauses usually share the same subject.
materials.reading: くせに
materials.notes:
It carries blame or contempt, so it is rude toward the person described; for a neutral 'even though', use のに.

It connects to nouns with の and な-adjectives with な: 子供のくせに, 下手なくせに.

Synonyms: noni-although — のに is the neutral 'even though'; くせに adds blame and can't be used approvingly.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: しっているくせに、かれはなにもおしえてくれなかった。

examples.english: He does nothing himself, yet he's all complaints.
examples.reading: じぶんではやらないくせに、もんくばかりいう。

materials.prompt: くせして
materials.answer:
even though; and yet (with blame or scorn)

くせして is a colloquial, blunter variant of くせに. It joins two clauses where the second clashes with what the first would lead you to expect, and it carries criticism, contempt, or complaint aimed at the subject — 知っているくせして教えてくれない = knows it, and yet won't tell me. Normally used about someone else, not oneself.
materials.reading: くせして
materials.notes:
It carries a critical, faultfinding tone; for neutral concession use のに instead.

It normally judges another person's behavior, so it sounds odd applied to yourself.

Same meaning as くせに, just more colloquial and often harsher.

Synonyms: kuse-ni — くせに is the same critical 'even though'; くせして is the more colloquial, often blunter form.

Related: nagara-mo — ながらも is a literary concessive 'although' with no scorn; くせして adds blame or contempt.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: Deep down she's lonely, and yet she keeps pretending she's fine.
examples.reading: ほんとうはさびしいくせして、へいきなふりをしている。

materials.prompt: くて・で
materials.answer:
~ and ~ (linking adjectives and nouns)

Links two descriptions in one sentence, meaning "and". Change an い-adjective's ending to くて, and put で after a noun or な-adjective, to connect it smoothly to the next part. It lets you stack qualities without starting a new sentence.
materials.reading: くて・で
materials.notes:
いい (good) is irregular: it becomes よくて, never いくて.

The で here is the connective form of the copula joining nouns and な-adjectives — it is not the で that marks a place or a means.

Related: soshite — そして joins two whole sentences; くて・で links descriptions inside a single sentence.

Related: kunai — Same い-adjective conjugation family — くない is the negative, くて the connective form.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜強
materials.answer:
a little more than; just over (suffix on a quantity)

Placed right after a number or amount, 〜強 means 'a bit more than that figure'. It rounds down to a round number and signals that the true value sits slightly above it — 二年強 = just over two years, 五割強 = a little over 50%. Common in statistics, reports, and news.
materials.reading: きょう
materials.notes:
Here 強 reads きょう and means 'and a bit more'; it has nothing to do with 強い ('strong').

It marks a value just above the stated figure; the mirror suffix for 'a little less' is 〜弱.

Antonyms: jaku — 〜弱 is the mirror suffix, marking a value slightly below the stated figure.

Related: ijou — 以上 means 'that amount or more' inclusively; 〜強 means a bit above a rounded-down figure.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 真っ～
materials.answer:
intensifier prefix: completely; deep; right (in the middle)

真っ is a prefix that intensifies the word after it, meaning 'completely / deep / dead ~'. It attaches to a fixed set of color and position words: 真っ赤 (deep red), 真っ白 (pure white), 真っ暗 (pitch dark), 真ん中 (the very middle). The small っ (or ん) is part of the set form.
materials.notes:
真っ combines only with a fixed set of words; you can't freely attach it to any adjective.

Before some sounds it becomes 真ん: 真ん中 (dead center), 真ん前 (right in front), not 真っ中.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: まだ
materials.answer:
still; not yet

まだ means "still" with an affirmative verb (a state keeps going) and "not yet" with a negative verb (something expected hasn't happened). Either way, the situation has not moved on to the next stage.
materials.reading: まだ
materials.notes:
まだ (still / not yet) is the mirror image of もう (already); learners often confuse the two.

A bare まだです can answer "not yet" on its own.

Antonyms: mou — もう marks that the change has already happened; まだ marks that it hasn't.

Related: mada-te-imasen — まだ〜ていません uses the negative ている form to say an action hasn't been done yet.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I don't know the answer yet.

materials.prompt: まだ〜ていません
materials.answer:
have not done ~ yet

Says an expected action still hasn't happened, viewed as of now: pair まだ with the negative ている form (ていません). Japanese uses the negative present here, not the past, because you are describing the current unfinished state rather than a past event.
materials.reading: まだていません
materials.notes:
Answer with ていません, not ませんでした — ませんでした means "didn't do it (back then)", while まだ〜ていません means "haven't done it (but still might)".

In casual speech いません shortens to ない: まだ食べてない.

Related: mada — The adverb まだ on its own; this pattern pins it to the ている form.

Related: te-iru — The ている form that this pattern negates to express "not yet done".

Related: mou — もう plus a past verb is the affirmative counterpart: already done.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: まだしも
materials.answer:
would be acceptable by comparison; if it were only ~, fine, but ~

まだしも marks something as still tolerable compared with a worse alternative — 'X would be one thing, but Y is too much'. It very often appears as ならまだしも: X ならまだしも Y = 'if it were just X, fine, but Y…'. It concedes X grudgingly in order to condemn Y.
materials.reading: まだしも
materials.notes:
It is comparative: X is not good, only 'less bad' than Y; don't read まだしも as X being genuinely fine.

It very often appears as 〜ならまだしも, setting up the tolerable case before the intolerable one.

Synonyms: kurai-nara — くらいなら rejects an option in favor of a better one; ならまだしも grudgingly accepts the lesser one while condemning a worse one.

Related: nara — the なら here is the ordinary conditional; まだしも adds the 'that much would be tolerable' judgement.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: まで
materials.answer:
until; as far as

まで marks the end point of a span — a time ("until") or a place reached ("as far as, all the way to"). The action or state continues right up to that limit. It frequently pairs with から, which marks where the span begins.
materials.reading: まで
materials.notes:
まで means "continuously up until"; to give a deadline ("by a time"), use までに instead.

Pair it with から for a "from ~ to ~" range: 九時から五時まで.

Related: kara — から marks the start point, the "from" that pairs with まで.

Related: made-ni — までに sets a deadline ("by"); まで means continuously until.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜までだ・〜までのことだ
materials.answer:
merely; simply; that's all; nothing more than

〜までだ / 〜までのことだ plays an action down as nothing more than what is stated. After a dictionary-form verb it expresses calm resolve — 'if it comes to that, I'll simply ~' (だめなら、やり直すまでだ = if it fails, I'll just do it over). After a た-form verb it justifies — 'I merely ~, that's all' (事実を述べたまでだ = I only stated the facts, nothing more).
materials.reading: までだ・までのことだ
materials.notes:
Dictionary form gives resolve ('I'll simply ~ if need be'); た-form gives justification ('I merely did ~, no more than that') — pick the form for the sense you want.

It downplays the action as the only, modest option, without exaggeration.

Synonyms: nomi — のみ is a formal 'only'; までだ frames the action as the sole, modest recourse or as nothing more than stated.

Related: made-mo-nai — までもない ('no need to go so far as') is a separate までも construction, not this 'merely ~' までだ.

Related: dake — だけ limits scope to 'only ~'; までだ adds the nuance of a modest, final recourse or a bare justification.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［dictionary form］＋までだ／までのことだ
Verb［た form］＋までだ／までのことだ

materials.prompt: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
materials.answer:
there is no need to go so far as to ~; it goes without saying

〜までもない says an action isn't worth taking because the matter is too obvious or minor to require it — 'there's no need to go so far as to ~'. 言うまでもない = it goes without saying, わざわざ確認するまでもない = no need to bother checking. The 〜までもなく form links to a following clause: 説明するまでもなく = without even needing to explain.
materials.reading: までもない・までもなく
materials.notes:
It marks an action as unnecessary because the point is self-evident or trivial, not that the action is forbidden.

The very common 言うまでもない / 言うまでもなく means 'needless to say'.

Synonyms: koto-wa-nai — ことはない says 'there's no need to ~'; までもない adds that it isn't worth going so far because the point is obvious.

Synonyms: hodo-no-koto-dewa-nai — ほどのことではない downplays how serious a matter is; までもない says an action is superfluous given how self-evident the point is.

Related: made-da — までだ ('merely ~') is a different までだ construction expressing resolve or justification.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: It goes without saying that meeting the deadline matters above all.
examples.reading: いうまでもなく、しめきりをまもることがなによりたいせつだ。

materials.prompt: までに
materials.answer:
by; by the time (deadline)

までに marks a deadline — the point by which an action must be finished. Unlike まで ('until', for continuous actions), までに is for one-time actions completed at or before a limit: 5時までに帰る (be home by 5). It attaches to a time noun or a verb in dictionary form.
materials.reading: までに
materials.notes:
までに (deadline, one-time action) vs まで (continuous action up to a point): 5時まで待つ (wait until 5), but 5時までに来る (come by 5).

Don't use までに with a continuing action like 'wait' or 'stay'; those take まで.

Related: made — まで marks a continuous action lasting up to a point; までに marks a deadline for a one-time action.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: くらくなるまでにかえりましょう。

materials.prompt: 前に
materials.answer:
before doing ~; in front of

前に marks what happens before something else. After a dictionary-form verb it means "before doing ~"; after a noun plus の it means "before" that event or, in a spatial sense, "in front of" it.
materials.reading: まえに
materials.notes:
The verb before 前に stays in the dictionary (non-past) form even when the whole sentence is about the past: 寝る前に, never 寝た前に.

A noun needs の before 前に: 食事の前に, not 食事前に.

Antonyms: ato-de — 後で means "after"; 前に marks what comes before.

Related: te-kara — てから marks doing B after finishing A; 前に marks doing B before A happens.

Related: toki — とき marks "when / at the time of"; 前に pins the moment just before an event.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: まい
materials.answer:
surely won't ~; I have no intention of ~ (literary negative)

まい is a literary negative auxiliary with two senses: negative conjecture ('surely won't / probably not', ≈ ないだろう) and negative volition ('I will not / I refuse to', ≈ しないつもりだ). It attaches to the dictionary form; with ichidan verbs and する the stem is also used (見まい／すまい). It sounds formal or old-fashioned.
materials.reading: まい
materials.notes:
Two meanings: with a third person it is usually 'surely won't' (conjecture); with the speaker it is 'I won't / I refuse' (volition).

It is literary; everyday Japanese uses ないだろう for the guess and ないつもりだ for the intention.

Antonyms: you-to-omou — ようと思う states the intention to do something; まい (volitional sense) states the intention not to.

Related: darou — だろう is positive conjecture ('probably will'); まい is its negative literary counterpart ('surely won't').

Related: beki-dewa-nai — べきではない says one shouldn't (obligation); まい voices the speaker's own resolve not to, or a negative guess.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: する → するまい／すまい、来る → 来るまい／来まい

examples.english: With ability like hers, surely she won't fail this exam.
examples.reading: かのじょほどのじつりょくがあれば、このしけんにおちることはあるまい。

materials.prompt: 毎～のように
materials.answer:
almost every ~; practically every ~

毎 means 'every', and 毎〜のように adds 'as if', giving 'almost every ~'. It attaches to time words such as 日 (day), 週 (week), or 年 (year): 毎日のように = practically every day. The のように softens 毎 from a strict 'every' into 'so often it might as well be every'.
materials.notes:
The のように is what adds 'almost': 毎日 is literally 'every day', while 毎日のように is 'almost every day'.

Use it with recurring time nouns (日・週・月・年), not one-off events.

Related: goto-ni — ごとに marks a regular interval ('every X'); 毎〜のように means 'almost, but not strictly, every'.

Related: tabi-ni — たびに means 'every time (an event) happens'; 毎〜のように counts recurring time periods.

Source references: bunpro
structures: 毎 ＋ Noun［time period］＋ のように

examples.english: He eats out almost every day.

materials.prompt: 〜まじき
materials.answer:
unbecoming of; that must not be (literary)

〜まじき is a literary attributive meaning 'that must not be, unbecoming of' — it modifies a noun to condemn conduct as improper for a given role. 教師にあるまじき言動 = behaviour unbecoming of a teacher, 許すまじき罪 = an unforgivable crime. It descends from classical まじ (the negative of べし) and appears mostly in the set frame 〜にあるまじき.
materials.reading: まじき
materials.notes:
Literary and largely frozen in 〜にあるまじき (＋ 行為／言動 etc.); it is not freely productive.

It labels conduct as improper for a role or status, so a person or position is usually named with に.

Synonyms: bekarazu — べからず ends a clause as a prohibition; まじき modifies a noun attributively ('unbecoming ~').

Related: beki-da — べきだ ('should') is the affirmative; まじき functions as its literary negative counterpart.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜まくる
materials.answer:
to do like crazy; to do intensely and nonstop

The suffix 〜まくる attaches to a verb stem and means to do that action intensely, repeatedly, and without restraint — 'to do like crazy, to do nonstop'. 遊びまくる = to party nonstop, 買いまくる = to buy up like mad. It is colloquial and emphasizes the sheer volume or vigour of the action.
materials.reading: まくる
materials.notes:
Colloquial and emphatic; it suits casual speech, not formal writing.

It stresses doing something to excess or in great quantity with energy, not a single careful action.

Synonyms: houdai — 放題 marks doing something freely without limit; まくる marks doing it intensely and over and over.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: まま
materials.answer:
as it is; leaving/staying unchanged

まま describes a state left unchanged while something else happens — 'as it is / still in that condition'. Something stays the way it was instead of being set right: 窓を開けたまま出かけた (went out with the window left open). It attaches to た form, ない form, な-adjective＋な, or noun＋の.
materials.reading: まま
materials.notes:
The state carries over into the next action: 靴をはいたまま入る (enter with shoes still on).

Different from ながら: ながら is two actions happening at once; まま is one unchanged state persisting during another action.

bunpro lists N3

Related: nagara — ながら is doing two actions simultaneously; まま is keeping one state unchanged during another action.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ままに
materials.answer:
as ~; just as ~; at the mercy of; letting it happen

ままに means 'just as (something is or tells you)', going along with a force or desire rather than acting on one's own will — 気の向くままに ('as the mood takes me'), 言われるままに ('just as one is told'). It conveys yielding to whatever drives the action.
materials.reading: ままに
materials.notes:
This ままに means 'yielding to / just as', driven by an outside force or impulse; it differs from plain まま ('an unchanged state'), though they share the word まま.

It appears in set phrases: 足の向くままに, 思いのままに, 言われるままに.

Related: mama — まま states that a condition stays unchanged; ままに adds the sense of yielding to a force or instruction.

Related: toori-ni — とおりに follows a specified way exactly; ままに passively goes along with whatever drives it.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜まみれ
materials.answer:
covered in; smeared all over with

〜まみれ marks a surface covered or smeared all over with something — almost always a dirty, wet, or unpleasant substance. 泥まみれ = covered in mud, 汗まみれ = drenched in sweat, 血まみれ = covered in blood. It attaches to a noun and can extend to abstract unpleasantness clinging to someone: 借金まみれ = mired in debt.
materials.reading: まみれ
materials.notes:
The covering substance is typically unpleasant — mud, sweat, blood, dust, debt — not something clean or desirable.

It stresses being smeared all over a surface, unlike だらけ, which stresses 'full of lots of ~' (mistakes, people).

Synonyms: darake — だらけ stresses 'full of many ~'; まみれ stresses a substance smeared all over a surface.

Synonyms: zukume — ずくめ means 'nothing but ~' and can be positive (黒ずくめ, いいことずくめ); まみれ is always a dirty substance clinging to a surface.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 万が一
materials.answer:
if by any chance; in the unlikely event; just in case

万が一 (literally 'one in ten thousand') introduces a remote, usually undesirable possibility — 'if by some chance / in the unlikely event'. As an adverb it pairs with a conditional (たら/ば/なら) and often prepares for the worst. It can also work as a noun: 万が一に備える ('prepare for any eventuality').
materials.reading: まんがいち
materials.notes:
It flags a low-probability, usually bad case; it is not the neutral 'if' of もし, which covers ordinary conditions.

It is commonly followed by a conditional clause (万が一失敗したら) or used as a noun (万が一に備える).

Synonyms: moshi — もし marks any hypothetical; 万が一 adds that the case is remote and usually unwelcome.

Related: tatoe-temo — たとえ〜ても concedes 'even if'; 万が一 sets up a rare possibility to prepare for, not to concede.

Source references: bunpro

万が一 ＋ に備える／のこと
