materials.prompt: する
materials.answer:
to do (irregular verb)

する means "to do" and is one of Japanese's two irregular verbs. Besides standing alone, it turns many nouns into verbs (勉強する, 電話する), so it appears constantly.
materials.reading: する
materials.notes:
する is irregular: it becomes し- in most forms (します, しない, して), not the regular verb patterns.

Many action nouns become verbs simply by adding する (勉強する, 電話する, 掃除する).

Related: kuru — くる is the other irregular verb learned together with する.

Source references: bunpro

する ＋ ［past: した］／［て form: して］

materials.prompt: すると
materials.answer:
and just then; thereupon; whereupon

すると links two events: right after the first, the second happened — often something the speaker observed, sometimes unexpected. ドアを開けた。すると、猫が飛び出してきた = I opened the door, whereupon a cat jumped out. It can also mean "if that's so, then…" in reaction to what was just said.
materials.reading: すると
materials.notes:
The second clause is usually something that happened on its own, often unexpected — not an action the speaker then chose to take.

Keep it apart from そうすると, which means "if you do it that way / in that case."

Related: sou-suru-to — そうすると supposes doing "that" and gives the result; すると reports what actually followed.

Related: to-conditional — The conditional と states a general "whenever A, then B"; すると connects two specific past events.

Related: soko-de — そこで is "and so" leading to a chosen next action; すると is "and just then" for what happened on its own.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Sentence。＋ すると、＋ Sentence（and just then / thereupon）

examples.english: I pressed the button, and just then the light went out.
examples.reading: ボタンをおした。すると、でんきがきえた。

examples.japanese: 窓を開けた。すると、冷たい風が入ってきた。
examples.english: I opened the window, and in came a cold wind.
examples.reading: まどをあけた。すると、つめたいかぜがはいってきた。

materials.prompt: 数字＋も
materials.answer:
as many as ~; (with negative) not even one

After a number plus counter, も signals that the speaker finds the amount remarkably large: 五杯も飲んだ = 'drank as many as five cups'. With 一＋counter and a negative verb it flips to total absence: 一つもない = 'not even one'.
materials.reading: すうじも
materials.notes:
も after a number comments on size — it does not mean 'also'. コーヒーを五杯も飲んだ says the speaker feels five is a lot.

For 'not even one', the counter must be the 一 form and the verb negative: 一つも食べませんでした.

Antonyms: suuryou-shika-nai — 数量＋しか〜ない paints the amount as too small; 数字＋も paints it as strikingly large.

Related: mo — Plain も means 'also, too'; after numbers it becomes an amount-emphasizer.

Related: sukoshi-mo-nai — 少しも〜ない denies even a small degree, much as 一つも〜ない denies even one item.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 数量＋しか～ない
materials.answer:
only ~ (an amount felt to be too little)

しか〜ない after a quantity says you have no more than that amount, and that it feels insufficient: 五百円しかない = 'I've only got five hundred yen'. The verb must be negative even though the English comes out affirmative.
materials.notes:
The negative is grammatical, not semantic: 三時間しか寝ませんでした means you DID sleep — just only three hours.

だけ with the same number is a neutral report; しか〜ない adds the complaint that it isn't enough.

Synonyms: dake — 三時間だけ寝た reports the same amount without the 'not enough' feeling.

Antonyms: suuji-mo — 数字＋も stresses that the amount is impressively large — the opposite framing.

Related: shika-nai — The parent pattern with plain nouns: 卵しかない.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Number ＋ Counter ＋ しか ＋ Verb［ない form］

examples.japanese: 昨日は三時間しか寝ませんでした。
examples.english: I slept only three hours last night.
examples.reading: きのうはさんじかんしかねませんでした。

materials.prompt: 数量＋は
materials.answer:
at least ~ (a minimum estimate)

は after a quantity marks it as a floor — 'at least that much': 二十分はかかる = 'it takes at least twenty minutes'. The speaker guesses the real figure is that big or bigger.
materials.reading: すうりょうは
materials.notes:
This is not the topic は: 五十人は来る doesn't topicalize 'fifty people', it estimates 'fifty at minimum'.

は doesn't work for 'at most' — for an upper limit use 数量＋しか〜ない or 多くても.

jlptsensei lists N3

Related: wa-topic — The everyday topic marker は; after quantities は shifts to 'at least'.

Related: suuji-mo — 数字＋も says the amount IS large; 数量＋は only sets a lower bound.

Related: kurai — くらい gives a rough 'about'; 数量＋は commits to a minimum.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たばかり
materials.answer:
just did; only just happened

Verb［た form］＋ ばかり says an action happened only a short while ago. The 'short while' is how the speaker feels — it can be minutes or, loosely, even longer, as long as it seems recent. Use it to explain that you're still new to or fresh from something.
materials.reading: たばかり
materials.notes:
〜たばかり is subjective 'not long ago,' while 〜たところ marks the exact moment right after finishing.

Don't confuse it with 〜てばかり, which means 'do nothing but ~.'

Synonyms: ta-tokoro — 〜たところ marks the exact moment of finishing; 〜たばかり feels 'not long ago,' even loosely.

Related: bakari — ばかり on its own means 'only / nothing but'; 〜たばかり means 'just did.'

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 赤ちゃんは生まれたばかりだ。

materials.prompt: 〜た弾みに・〜た拍子に
materials.answer:
in the instant of doing ~; and just then (accidentally)

弾み (はずみ) and 拍子 (ひょうし) both mean 'the momentary instant of' an action, after which an unintended, reflexive result follows — 転んだ拍子に手をついた = the moment I fell, I threw out my hand. Built on the た-form, the pattern stresses that the second event was accidental and triggered in that instant. It can also follow a noun as 〜の拍子に (何かの拍子に = by some chance).
materials.reading: たはずみに・たひょうしに
materials.notes:
弾み is read はずみ and 拍子 is read ひょうし here.

The following event is usually unintended or reflexive — a spontaneous reaction, not a planned action.

Synonyms: ta-totan — たとたん marks 'the moment ~, then ~' for any following event; 弾みに／拍子に stresses that the result was accidental and reflexive.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［た form］＋弾み（はずみ）に／拍子（ひょうし）に

examples.english: The instant I turned around, I bumped my head on the shelf.

examples.english: As I stood up, I knocked over the cup on the desk without meaning to.
examples.reading: たちあがったはずみに、つくえのうえのコップをたおしてしまった。

materials.prompt: たことがある
materials.answer:
have done ~ before

Talks about past experience: attach ことがある to a verb's た form to say "I have done ~ (at least once) before". Use it to share what you have or haven't tried, or to ask someone whether they have ever done something.
materials.reading: たことがある
materials.notes:
Use the た form for experience. The dictionary form plus ことがある (koto-ga-aru) means "there are times when I do ~", a recurring possibility — not a past experience.

The negative swaps ある for ない／ありません after the same た form: 一度もしたことがありません ("have never ~, not even once").

Related: koto-ga-aru — Dictionary form + ことがある means "there are times I do ~"; the た form means "have done before".

Related: koto-ga-dekiru — ことができる expresses ability ("can do"); たことがある expresses experience.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［た form］＋ ことがある

examples.english: I have never been late, not even once.
examples.reading: いちどもちこくしたことがありません。

materials.prompt: 〜たことにする・〜たことになる
materials.answer:
to pretend/treat as if ~ happened; to be regarded as if ~ happened

〜たことにする means someone decides to treat something as if it happened (or, with なかった, as if it didn't), often contrary to fact — 聞かなかったことにする = pretend I didn't hear it. 〜たことになる is the passive counterpart: it ends up officially or effectively counting as having happened — サインすれば受け取ったことになる = signing counts as having received it. Both build on the た-form.
materials.reading: たことにする・たことになる
materials.notes:
ことにする = someone chooses to treat it that way (often against the facts); ことになる = it ends up counting that way as a result.

Distinct from plain ことにする ('decide to do'), which follows the dictionary form.

Synonyms: furi-o-suru — ふりをする is to put on an act in the moment; たことにする sets up a fact to be treated as settled afterward.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.reading: さっきのはなしは、きかなかったことにするよ。

materials.prompt: たものだ
materials.answer:
used to do; would often do (nostalgic)

たものだ looks back fondly on something you used to do again and again — "used to ...; would often ...". It carries a nostalgic, reminiscing tone about a past habit, not a one-time event. It attaches to the た form.
materials.reading: たものだ
materials.notes:
It describes a repeated past habit with a nostalgic feel; for a single past action, just use the plain past.

Keep it apart from other ものだ uses (general truths, strong feeling); the nostalgic 'used to' sense needs the た form.

Related: mono-da — ものだ covers general truths and strong feeling; the た-form たものだ is specifically the nostalgic 'used to.'

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たところ
materials.answer:
have just finished doing (this very moment)

Verb［た form］＋ ところ marks an action that finished a moment ago — you are right at the point just after it. It pins the event to the immediate present on a timeline, so it fits sentences like 'I just this second arrived.'
materials.reading: たところ
materials.notes:
〜たところ is the moment just after finishing; 〜ているところ is the middle of doing, and 〜るところ is about to start.

Compared with 〜たばかり, 〜たところ points to the exact moment, while 〜たばかり just feels 'not long ago.'

Synonyms: ta-bakari — 〜たばかり also means 'just did,' but stresses little time has passed rather than the exact moment.

Related: teiru-tokoro — 〜ているところ is in the middle of doing; 〜たところ is the moment just after finishing.

Related: ru-tokoro-da — 〜るところ is about to do; 〜たところ has just done.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［た form］＋ ところ（だ／です）

examples.english: I've just arrived at the station right now.
examples.reading: いま、えきについたところです。

materials.prompt: 〜たところで
materials.answer:
even if (one does/did) ~, it would be no use

〜たところで sets up a hypothetical and dismisses it as futile: even if you do X, the result won't help. The main clause is negative or pointless — 急いだところで間に合わない = even if I hurry, I won't make it. Though it uses the た-form, it refers to a hypothetical or future action, and often follows いくら or 今さら.
materials.reading: たところで
materials.notes:
The main clause is negative or futile: 'even if ~, it won't help' — not a neutral 'even if'.

It takes the た-form but points to a hypothetical/future action, not a past one.

Synonyms: tatte — たって is a casual 'even if'; たところで adds the specific nuance that the effort would be pointless.

Synonyms: temo — ても is a neutral 'even if'; たところで strongly implies the outcome would be futile.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: No matter how much you regret it, what's done can't be undone.
examples.reading: いくらくやんだところで、すぎたことはもうもどらない。

materials.prompt: たとたん(に)
materials.answer:
the moment ...; just as ...; as soon as ...

たとたん(に) marks the instant one thing happened and something else immediately followed — "the moment ...; as soon as ...". The second event is usually unexpected or beyond the speaker's control, and both clauses are in the past. The に is optional.
materials.reading: たとたんに
materials.notes:
The second clause reports something that just happened, not a plan or request: no volitional, command, or invitation after とたん.

Both events are past and sudden; for a habitual 'every time,' use たびに instead.

Related: tara — たら is a broad trigger 'when/if'; とたん pins down one sudden, unexpected instant that just passed.

Related: tabi-ni — たびに is a repeated 'every time'; とたん is a single sudden moment.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜たつもりはない
materials.answer:
have no sense of having done ~; didn't mean to have done ~

Built on the た-form, 〜たつもりはない denies, from the speaker's own standpoint, that they did or intended a certain thing — 嘘をついたつもりはない = I don't believe I lied / I didn't mean to lie. It defends against an accusation or impression by asserting one had no such intent or awareness. Contrast with dictionary-form 〜つもりはない, which denies a future intention.
materials.reading: たつもりはない
materials.notes:
た-form つもりはない denies having done/intended something ('I didn't mean to have ~'); dictionary-form 〜つもりはない denies future intention ('I don't intend to ~').

It expresses the speaker's own view, so it often reads as a defense against how one is being perceived.

Synonyms: tsumori — つもり on its own states an intention; たつもりはない denies having had a given intention or awareness after the fact.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜たはいいが
materials.answer:
it's all well and good that ~, but; ~ turned out fine, only then

〜たはいいが presents a completed action as a positive, decisive step, then reveals an unforeseen problem it led to — 買ったはいいが使い方が分からない = buying it was fine, but I can't figure out how to use it. It builds on the た-form and often appears as はいいけれど. The pattern always pivots on that 'but', where trouble follows the good first move.
materials.reading: たはいいが
materials.notes:
The first clause is viewed positively as done; the twist is that it produced an unexpected difficulty.

The problem in the second clause is essential — without it the pattern makes no sense.

Synonyms: monono — ものの means 'although' generally; たはいいが specifically frames 'did the thing, but then hit trouble'.

Synonyms: towa-ie — とはいえ concedes a point before qualifying it; たはいいが centers on a completed action followed by an unforeseen snag.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: たびに
materials.answer:
every time; whenever

たびに says that each time one thing happens, another regularly follows — "every time; whenever." It attaches to a dictionary-form verb or to a noun with の, and points to something that repeats on each occasion.
materials.reading: たびに
materials.notes:
Use the dictionary form, not the past: 会うたびに, not 会ったたびに.

たびに is about repeated occasions; for one sudden moment ('as soon as'), use とたん.

Synonyms: mai-no-you-ni — 毎〜のように means 'nearly every time'; たびに means literally each and every time, without exception.

Related: ta-totan — とたん marks one sudden instant; たびに marks a recurring pattern across many occasions.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たちまち
materials.answer:
instantly; in no time; in a flash

たちまち is an adverb meaning that something happens with great speed, almost at once — a change completes 'in no time'. It often describes a sudden, sometimes striking shift affecting a whole situation, and feels more vivid and literary than すぐ.
materials.reading: たちまち
materials.notes:
It describes how fast a change unfolds; it does not mark the point in time 'the moment that ~' — for that, use とたん(に).

Related: ta-totan — たとたん(に) marks the exact moment one thing triggers another; たちまち describes the rapid speed of a change.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: ただ〜のみだ
materials.answer:
nothing but; merely; all that remains is

ただ〜のみだ frames something as 'nothing but ~' or 'all that is left is ~'. のみ is the literary equivalent of だけ, and ただ reinforces it with the sense of 'merely / simply'. あとはただ待つのみだ = all that remains now is to wait. It attaches to a dictionary-form verb or a noun and belongs to formal, written-style Japanese.
materials.notes:
のみ is formal and written; in ordinary conversation だけ is the natural choice.

ただ here means 'merely / nothing but', not the unrelated ただ meaning 'free of charge'.

Synonyms: nomi — のみ alone already means 'only' in a literary register; ただ〜のみだ frames it emphatically as 'nothing but'.

Synonyms: dake — だけ is the everyday word for 'only'; ただ〜のみだ is its formal, emphatic counterpart.

Related: bakari — ばかり also limits to 'only / just', but colloquially and often with a nuance of excess; ただ〜のみだ is formal and clean.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 他動詞・自動詞
materials.answer:
transitive and intransitive verb pairs

Japanese has many verb pairs: a 他動詞 (transitive), where someone acts on a thing marked with を, and a matching 自動詞 (intransitive), where the thing changes by itself and is marked with が. 開ける/開く, 閉める/閉まる, and 消す/消える are classic pairs you learn together.
materials.reading: たどうし・じどうし
materials.notes:
The transitive verb takes を and needs a doer; the intransitive takes が and describes the thing changing on its own.

The pairs must be memorized: 始める/始まる, 出す/出る, 入れる/入る don't follow one fixed rule.

For a resulting state, use intransitive ＋ ている (ドアが開いている) or transitive ＋ てある (ドアが開けてある).

Related: te-aru — 〜てある pairs with a transitive verb to show a state someone set up on purpose.

Related: te-iru — 〜ている with an intransitive verb shows the state that resulted.

Related: rareru-passive — The passive also drops the doer, but reshapes を→が differently from an intransitive pair.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 急に電気が消えた。
examples.english: The light suddenly went out.

materials.prompt: たがる
materials.answer:
to want to (of a third person, shown outwardly)

たがる reports that someone else looks like they want to do something, judged from outside signs. It's built from the 〜たい stem plus がる, and conjugates like an u-verb. Use it for other people's desires; for your own, plain 〜たい is correct.
materials.reading: たがる
materials.notes:
Use たがる for others' wants observed from outside; for your own desire say 〜たい (食べたい), not 食べたがる.

For a want happening right now, the ongoing 〜たがっている is usually more natural than plain 〜たがる.

たがる tends to take を for its object (お菓子を食べたがる), where 〜たい can also use が.

Synonyms: garu-gatteiru — 〜がる makes an adjective of feeling into a third-person 'shows signs of'; たがる does the same for 〜たい.

Related: tai — 〜たい states your own desire; たがる reports someone else's, seen from outside.

Related: ga-hoshii — 〜が欲しい wants a thing; 〜たがる wants to do an action.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たい
materials.answer:
want to do ~

Expresses the speaker's own desire to do something: attach たい to a verb's stem to say "I want to ~". The result conjugates like an い-adjective (たい → たくない → たかった). Use it for your own wishes, or in a question to ask what the listener wants to do.
materials.reading: たい
materials.notes:
たい describes the first person's desire (or asks "you"). To report that a third person wants something, switch to たがる.

The object can take が or を — 水が飲みたい and 水を飲みたい are both fine, with が feeling a touch stronger on the wanting.

Synonyms: ga-hoshii — がほしい wants a thing (a noun); たい wants to do an action (a verb).

Related: tagaru — たがる reports a third person's desire; たい is for your own.

Related: te-hoshii — てほしい wants someone else to do something; たい is wanting to do it yourself.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たくさん
materials.answer:
a lot; many; plenty

A quantity word meaning "a lot" or "many". It works as an adverb before a verb (eat a lot) and as a quantity with nouns (there are many). Learners use it whenever they want to say there is a large amount or number of something.
materials.reading: たくさん
materials.notes:
When placing たくさん directly before a noun, add の: たくさんの人 ("many people"). After a noun plus particle it stands alone: 人がたくさんいる.

たくさん is about amount or number; use とても for degree ("very"), not quantity.

Antonyms: amari-nai — あまり〜ない means "not much/not many"; たくさん means "a lot".

Related: totemo — とても is degree ("very"); たくさん is amount ("a lot").

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: たまえ
materials.answer:
do ~ (mild command from a superior to a subordinate)

たまえ attaches to the ます-stem to give a gentle order from someone of higher standing to someone below — a boss to a subordinate, a teacher to a student. It sounds masculine, somewhat old-fashioned and literary, and softer than a blunt imperative. It is rare in everyday modern speech.
materials.reading: たまえ
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 座りたまえ, not 座るたまえ.

It presumes the speaker outranks the listener and has a dated, masculine flavor; it is not a neutral polite request.

Synonyms: nasai — なさい is a firm command often used parent-to-child; たまえ is masculine, superior-to-subordinate, and more dated.

Related: meirei-kei — 命令形 is the blunt imperative like しろ/来い; たまえ is a gentler, more refined order.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ために
materials.answer:
because of; as a result of (cause)

In this use ために gives the reason or cause for what follows — "because of; as a result of." It often introduces a circumstance that led to a notable or unwanted outcome. It attaches to a plain-form clause, or to a noun with の.
materials.reading: ために
materials.notes:
This 'because of' ために tends to explain a notable or negative result and is more formal than から／ので.

The same shape ために also means 'in order to' (purpose); tell them apart by whether the second clause is a goal or an outcome.

Synonyms: node — ので states a cause neutrally in everyday speech; ために sounds more formal and often flags a significant result.

Synonyms: kara — から gives the speaker's reasoning; ために more often reports an objective cause and effect.

Related: tame-ni-purpose — Same shape, other sense: ため(に) as 'in order to' states a goal; this ために states a cause.

Related: sono-tame-ni — そのため(に) packages a whole prior sentence as 'that reason'; ために attaches directly to the cause clause.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ため(に)
materials.answer:
in order to; for the sake of (purpose)

In this use ため(に) states the goal you act toward — "in order to; for the sake of." With a dictionary-form verb it gives the purpose of a deliberate action; with a noun and の it means "for the benefit of." The subject controls the action aimed at the goal.
materials.reading: ために
materials.notes:
The goal ために takes a controllable, volitional verb and usually the same subject in both clauses; for aims you can't directly control (できる, 分かる, なる), use ように.

Say 合格するために ('in order to pass'), not 合格できるために — potential and uncontrollable verbs go with ように.

Synonyms: you-ni-so-that — ように states a goal reached through change or ability you can't fully control; ため(に) is for a deliberate, controllable aim.

Related: tame-ni — Same shape, other sense: this ため(に) is 'in order to' (purpose); the cause ために means 'because of.'

Source references: bunpro

examples.reading: にほんごをじょうずにはなすために、まいにちれんしゅうしている。

materials.prompt: 〜ためしがない
materials.answer:
there has never once been a case of ~; has never happened

ためし (例) means 'a precedent or instance'. 〜ためしがない, built on the た-form, says that a certain thing has never once occurred, usually with a note of reproach or disappointment — 約束を守ったためしがない = has never once kept a promise. It stresses that despite expectation, the event simply never happens.
materials.reading: ためしがない
materials.notes:
It normally attaches to the た-form and carries a critical tone: 'never once, despite expectations'.

ためし here is 例 ('instance'), not the verb 試す ('to try').

Synonyms: ta-koto-ga-aru — たことがない states plainly 'have never done'; ためしがない adds that it never happens despite being expected to, with a reproachful tone.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: たら
materials.answer:
if; when; after

〜たら is the everyday conditional: take the plain past (た form) and add ら. Depending on context it means 'if ~,' 'when ~,' or 'after ~.' Its big strength is that the main clause can be a request, command, or wish, which many other conditionals block.
materials.reading: たら
materials.notes:
〜たら covers both 'if' (hypothetical) and 'when/after' (sure to happen); context decides which.

Unlike 〜と, the main clause may be a request or command: 家に着いたら、電話してください.

Past ＋ 〜たら ＋ past can report a discovery: 窓を開けたら、雨が降っていた ('when I opened the window, it was raining').

Synonyms: ba — 〜ば is a more formal 'if'; 〜たら is the everyday conditional and also means 'when/after.'

Synonyms: to-conditional — 〜と is for automatic, always-true results; 〜たら allows requests and one-off cases.

Synonyms: nara — 〜なら responds to a supposition someone raised; 〜たら sets up your own condition.

Related: tara-dou — 〜たらどう suggests 'why don't you,' built on the 〜たら conditional.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たらどう
materials.answer:
why don't you ~?; how about ~ing?

〜たらどう offers a suggestion to the listener: 'why don't you ~?' The どう is short for どうですか ('how would it be?'), attached to the 〜たら conditional. Use it to gently recommend that the other person try something.
materials.reading: たらどう
materials.notes:
It advises the other person, not yourself; you can't use it about your own actions.

Said bluntly it can sound pushy or critical, so soften it with どうですか or a caring tone.

Synonyms: hou-ga-ii — 〜ほうがいい recommends one choice over another; 〜たらどう floats a suggestion more gently.

Related: tara-ii-desu-ka — 〜たらどう offers advice; 〜たらいいですか asks for it.

Related: tara — The conditional 〜たら is the base of this suggestion pattern.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［た form］＋ ら ＋ どう（ですか）

examples.japanese: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか。
examples.english: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?
examples.reading: つかれているなら、すこしやすんだらどうですか。

examples.japanese: 一度、医者に相談してみたらどう。
examples.english: How about consulting a doctor once?
examples.reading: いちど、いしゃにそうだんしてみたらどう。

materials.prompt: たらいいですか
materials.answer:
what/how/where should I ~? (asking for guidance)

〜たらいいですか asks someone for instructions: 'what should I do?' It pairs a question word (何・どこ・どう…) with the 〜たら conditional plus いいですか, literally 'would it be good if I ~?' Use it to politely request guidance on the right course of action.
materials.reading: たらいいですか
materials.notes:
It needs a question word to work: 何をしたらいいですか, どこに行けば… — without one it just states a condition.

For a softer, more tentative feel, 〜たらいいでしょうか is common; the casual form is 〜たらいい？

Synonyms: ba-ii — 〜ばいいですか asks the same 'what should I,' using 〜ば instead of 〜たら.

Related: tara — The conditional 〜たら underlies this fixed question pattern.

Related: tara-dou — 〜たらどう gives a suggestion; 〜たらいいですか asks for one.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: 疑問詞（何／どこ／どう…）＋ Verb［た form］＋ ら ＋ いいですか

examples.japanese: この書類はどこに出したらいいですか。
examples.english: Where should I submit these documents?
examples.reading: このしょるいはどこにだしたらいいですか。

examples.japanese: 旅行の前に何を準備したらいいですか。
examples.english: What should I prepare before the trip?
examples.reading: りょこうのまえになにをじゅんびしたらいいですか。

materials.prompt: 〜たら最後・〜たが最後
materials.answer:
once you do ~, that's the end of it; there's no going back

〜たら最後 (or the more emphatic 〜たが最後) says that once a certain action occurs, an inevitable and usually undesirable consequence follows, with no way back — 一度引き受けたら最後、途中でやめられない = once you take it on, there's no quitting halfway. Built on the た-form, it stresses a point of no return.
materials.reading: たらさいご・たがさいご
materials.notes:
最後 is read さいご; the consequence that follows is inevitable and usually undesirable.

が最後 is a slightly more emphatic and literary variant of ら最後.

Synonyms: ba-sore-made-da — ばそれまでだ means 'if ~, then it's all over'; たら最後 stresses that the action itself sets off an unstoppable chain.

Synonyms: you-mono-nara — ようものなら warns of dire consequences if one merely tried something; たら最後 says the deed, once done, cannot be undone.

Related: mono-nara — ものなら sets up a hypothetical with serious consequences; たら最後 fixes on the irreversible point after the action.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: あの人は話し出したら最後、延々としゃべり続ける。
examples.english: Once that person starts talking, they go on and on without end.
examples.reading: あのひとははなしだしたらさいご、えんえんとしゃべりつづける。

examples.japanese: この魚は、一度水から出したが最後、すぐに弱ってしまう。
examples.english: Once you take this fish out of the water, it weakens right away.
examples.reading: このさかなは、いちどみずからだしたがさいご、すぐによわってしまう。

materials.prompt: 〜たら〜たで
materials.answer:
even if/when ~ does turn out so, that brings its own issues

Aたら Aたで repeats the same predicate to say that even when a situation does come about, it carries its own downside — or works out somehow either way. お金があったらあったで悩みがある = even having money brings its own worries. The nuance is that neither outcome is clean: whichever way it goes, there is something to deal with.
materials.notes:
The same predicate is repeated on both sides; it is not two different actions.

The sense is 'even if it does happen, that has its own downside / it's fine either way', not a purely positive result.

Synonyms: nara-de — なら〜で carries the same 'if it is ~, that's its own matter' sense but attaches via なら to nouns/adjectives; たら〜たで uses the た-conditional.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Once the exam is over, then you start fretting about the results instead.

materials.prompt: 〜たら〜ところだ
materials.answer:
if (counterfactually) ~ had been so, ~ would have happened

This pattern pairs a counterfactual condition (〜たら) with a would-be result (〜ところだ, usually ところだった) — もう少し遅かったら、乗り遅れるところだった = if I'd been a little later, I would have missed it. The condition did not actually hold, and the ところだ clause describes what would have been on the verge of happening. It often appears with 危うく or あと少しで.
materials.notes:
It usually ends in ところだった for a past counterfactual: the condition did not actually occur.

The result clause describes what almost happened, so it often pairs with 危うく or あと少しで.

Synonyms: tokoro-datta — ところだった alone already means 'was about to / nearly happened'; たら〜ところだ supplies the explicit counterfactual condition.

Synonyms: ba-noni — ば〜のに expresses 'would have, if only' with regret; たら〜ところだ pairs the condition with a would-be event, often a narrow escape.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［た form］＋ら＋Verb［dictionary form］＋ところだった／ところだ

materials.prompt: 〜たり〜たりする
materials.answer:
do things like A and B

Lists a few representative actions without claiming they are the only ones: take the た form of each verb, add り, and finish with する. It says "I do things like A and B (among others)", which makes it handy for describing what you do on your day off or on a trip.
materials.reading: たりたりする
materials.notes:
The final する carries the tense and politeness — for the past, only the last verb changes: 〜たり〜たりしました.

Unlike the て form (which lists actions in strict order), 〜たり implies a non-exhaustive sample of activities.

Related: te-form — The て form lists actions in sequence; 〜たり gives a non-ordered sample of activities.

Related: shi — し lists reasons or facts side by side; 〜たり lists example actions.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［た form］＋ り ＋ Verb［た form］＋ り ＋ する

examples.japanese: 週末は本を読んだり音楽を聞いたりします。
examples.english: On weekends I do things like read books and listen to music.
examples.reading: しゅうまつはほんをよんだりおんがくをきいたりします。

materials.prompt: 〜たりとも
materials.answer:
not even a single ~; not so much as one ~

たりとも follows '一 + counter' and pairs with a negative to mean 'not even one' — 一日たりとも忘れない = I won't forget for even a single day, 一円たりとも無駄にできない = can't waste even one yen. It is emphatic and literary. The separate idiom 何人（なんぴと）たりとも means 'no one whosoever'.
materials.reading: たりとも
materials.notes:
It is fixed with 一 + a counter and requires a negative: it means 'not even one'.

何人（なんぴと）たりとも is a separate set idiom meaning 'no one whosoever', not the counting use.

Synonyms: mo — も with a minimal amount and a negative also gives 'not even ~'; たりとも is more emphatic and literary, and locks onto 一 + counter.

Related: dani — だに also gives an emphatic 'not even', but attaches to nouns/verbs in set phrases; たりとも counts with 一 + a counter.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: この計画では、一日たりとも無駄にはできない。
examples.english: In this plan, we cannot afford to waste even a single day.
examples.reading: このけいかくでは、いちにちたりともむだにはできない。

examples.japanese: 敵を前に、兵士たちは一瞬たりとも気を緩めなかった。
examples.english: Facing the enemy, the soldiers did not let their guard down for even an instant.
examples.reading: てきをまえに、へいしたちはいっしゅんたりともきをゆるめなかった。

materials.prompt: 〜たる・〜たるもの
materials.answer:
one who is (in the position of) ~ should; befitting one who is ~

たる is a literary copula (equivalent to である) used attributively. 〜たるもの(は) names someone in a certain role and states how a person in that position ought to behave — 指導者たるもの、模範を示すべきだ = one who is a leader should set an example. It is formal and written, and the following clause typically expresses duty or expectation. たる can also directly modify a noun (堂々たる態度).
materials.reading: たる・たるもの
materials.notes:
たる is a literary copula (= である); the whole pattern is formal and written.

たるもの typically leads to a statement of what befits or is required of someone in that role.

Synonyms: tomo-arou-mono-ga — ともあろうものが reproaches someone in a high position for a lapse; たるもの prescribes how such a person should act.

Synonyms: toshite — として states a role or capacity neutrally ('as a ~'); たるもの is formal and adds the weight of expected conduct.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 指導者たるもの、常に部下の模範を示さねばならない。
examples.english: One who is a leader must always set an example for those under them.
examples.reading: しどうしゃたるもの、つねにぶかのもはんをしめさねばならない。

examples.japanese: 医師たるもの、患者の前で弱音を吐くべきではない。
examples.english: A person in the position of a doctor should not show weakness in front of patients.
examples.reading: いしたるもの、かんじゃのまえでよわねをはくべきではない。

materials.prompt: 確かに
materials.answer:
certainly; it's true that ... (often conceding a point)

確かに expresses that something is certainly true — "surely; certainly." Very often it concedes a point before a pushback: 確かに〜が means "it's true that ..., but ...". On its own it simply confirms that you're sure of something.
materials.reading: たしかに
materials.notes:
Don't mix up the adverb 確かに ('certainly') with the な-adjective 確か ('sure, reliable') or 確か used to mean 'if I remember right.'

bunpro lists N2

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: たて
materials.answer:
freshly done; just done (and still fresh)

たて attaches to a verb stem to say the action was done just moments ago and the result is still fresh — 焼きたてのパン = freshly baked bread, できたて = just made. It forms a noun-like word and pairs with a limited set of verbs, especially about food and freshness.
materials.reading: たて
materials.notes:
たて works with only a handful of verbs (焼く, できる, 炊く, 塗る …); it isn't a free 'just did' marker — for that, use 〜たばかり.

Before a noun it links with の: 焼きたてのパン, not 焼きたてパン.

Related: ta-bakari — 〜たばかり works with any verb to say an action just happened; たて emphasizes the still-fresh result and forms a noun.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 焼きたてのパンはとてもいい匂いがする。
examples.english: Freshly baked bread smells wonderful.
examples.reading: やきたてのパンはとてもいいにおいがする。

examples.japanese: このお米は炊きたてだから、本当においしい。
examples.english: This rice was just cooked, so it's really delicious.
examples.reading: このおこめはたきたてだから、ほんとうにおいしい。

materials.prompt: たとえ〜ても
materials.answer:
even if (hypothetically) ...

たとえ〜ても sets up a hypothetical and says the result holds no matter what — "even if." The たとえ at the front signals early that a supposition is coming, and it pairs with a following ても. It stresses that the outcome won't change.
materials.notes:
たとえ needs a matching ても／でも later in the sentence; don't leave it hanging.

たとえ ('even if') is a different word from 例えば ('for example') — don't swap them.

Synonyms: temo — ても alone can mean 'even if'; たとえ〜ても adds an explicit, emphatic 'suppose that ...' at the front.

Related: tatte — たって is a casual spoken 'even if'; たとえ〜ても is the standard, emphatic hypothetical.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: たとえ ＋ Verb［て form］＋ も

examples.japanese: たとえ雨が降っても、試合は行われます。
examples.english: Even if it rains, the match will be held.
examples.reading: たとえあめがふっても、しあいはおこなわれます。

examples.japanese: たとえ失敗しても、挑戦したことに意味がある。
examples.english: Even if I fail, there's meaning in having taken on the challenge.
examples.reading: たとえしっぱいしても、ちょうせんしたことにいみがある。

materials.prompt: 例えば
materials.answer:
for example

例えば introduces a concrete example of a general statement, usually followed by a pause. After stating something broad, you use 例えば to name a specific case that illustrates it. It often teams up with listing words like 〜や, 〜とか, or 〜など.
materials.reading: たとえば
materials.notes:
例えば announces that an example is coming; it usually takes a comma-length pause after it.

It pairs naturally with 〜など／〜とか, which follow the examples themselves.

jlptsensei lists N3

Related: nado — など follows the examples that 例えば introduces.

Related: toka-toka — 〜とか lists casual examples; 例えば announces that one is coming.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 果物が好きです。例えば、りんごやみかんです。
examples.english: I like fruit. For example, apples and oranges.
examples.reading: くだものがすきです。たとえば、りんごやみかんです。

examples.japanese: 例えば、朝早く起きて散歩するのはどうですか。
examples.english: For example, how about getting up early and taking a walk?
examples.reading: たとえば、あさはやくおきてさんぽするのはどうですか。

materials.prompt: たった(の)
materials.answer:
only; just; a mere

たった emphasizes that a quantity is surprisingly small — 'only this much, a mere ~'. The optional の comes before the number (たったの千円). It stresses that the amount falls short of expectation, often with disappointment or to underline how little there is.
materials.reading: たったの
materials.notes:
たった attaches to a specific amount or number to stress its smallness; it is not a general 'only' like だけ that can follow any noun.

Synonyms: dake — だけ is a neutral 'only'; たった adds emphatic surprise at how small the amount is.

Synonyms: nomi — のみ is a formal 'only' without the emotional stress; たった dramatizes the smallness.

Related: bakari — ばかり with a number gives an approximate amount ('about'); たった pins down an exact, strikingly small figure.

Source references: bunpro

examples.japanese: この会社はたった二年で全国に店を広げた。
examples.english: This company expanded its stores nationwide in a mere two years.
examples.reading: このかいしゃはたったにねんでぜんこくにみせをひろげた。

examples.japanese: 財布にはたったの五百円しか残っていなかった。
examples.english: I had a mere 500 yen left in my wallet.
examples.reading: さいふにはたったのごひゃくえんしかのこっていなかった。

materials.prompt: たって
materials.answer:
even if; even though (casual)

たって is the casual, spoken version of ても — "even if; even though." You hear it in conversation where ても would sound a bit stiff. It attaches differently to each word type, and for nouns and な-adjectives it surfaces as だって.
materials.reading: たって
materials.notes:
たって is colloquial; in writing or polite speech, use ても instead: 急いでも rather than 急いだって.

For nouns and な-adjectives the form becomes だって (子供だって, 静かだって), not たって.

bunpro lists N2

Synonyms: temo — ても is the standard 'even if'; たって is its casual, spoken counterpart.

Related: tatoe-temo — たとえ〜ても spells out the hypothesis up front and is more emphatic; たって is a plain casual 'even if.'

Related: datte — だって is the form たって takes after a noun or な-adjective (子供だって = even a child).

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 今から走ったって、もう間に合わないよ。
examples.english: Even if you run now, you won't make it in time.
examples.reading: いまからはしったって、もうまにあわないよ。

examples.japanese: どんなに高くたって、これはどうしても欲しい。
examples.english: No matter how expensive it is, I really want this.
examples.reading: どんなにたかくたって、これはどうしてもほしい。

materials.prompt: てあげる
materials.answer:
to do something (as a favor) for someone

Verb［て form］＋ あげる does an action as a kindness for someone else, with the favor flowing away from the doer toward the receiver. It parallels あげる ('give'), but what's handed over is an action rather than an object. Use it when you help someone out.
materials.reading: てあげる
materials.notes:
The favor goes outward, from the doer to someone else; a favor done toward you takes 〜てくれる.

Said straight to a superior it can sound condescending ('I'll kindly do this for you'), so use it humbly or reword.

Synonyms: te-yaru — 〜てやる does a favor for someone below you, a pet, or a plant; 〜てあげる is the neutral-polite version.

Antonyms: te-kureru — 〜てあげる sends a favor away; 〜てくれる is a favor done toward you.

Related: te-morau — 〜てもらう receives a favor; 〜てあげる gives one.

Related: ageru-giving — あげる hands over an object; 〜てあげる does an action as the favor.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 友だちに本を貸してあげた。
examples.english: I lent my friend a book (as a favor).
examples.reading: ともだちにほんをかしてあげた。

examples.japanese: 母のかばんを持ってあげた。
examples.english: I carried my mother's bag for her.
examples.reading: ははのかばんをもってあげた。

materials.prompt: てある
materials.answer:
has been done (state)

Describes a state that remains because someone did something on purpose: attach ある to the て form of a transitive verb to say "~ has been done (and is still that way)". It implies deliberate preparation, so you'll meet it when talking about things set up in advance.
materials.reading: てある
materials.notes:
てある takes a transitive verb and usually が, implying a person did it on purpose (窓が開けてある = someone opened it and left it).

Compare 〜ている with an intransitive verb for a plain state (ドアが開いている = the door is open) versus てある for a deliberately made state.

bunpro lists N4

Related: te-iru — ている covers ongoing actions and natural states; てある is a state left on purpose by someone.

Related: te-oku — ておく is doing something in advance; てある is the resulting state after it's done.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: テーブルに花が飾ってあります。
examples.english: Flowers have been arranged on the table.
examples.reading: テーブルにはながかざってあります。

examples.japanese: 黒板に名前が書いてあります。
examples.english: The names are written on the blackboard.
examples.reading: こくばんになまえがかいてあります。

materials.prompt: てばかりいる
materials.answer:
to do nothing but ~; to always be ~ing (often critical)

〜てばかりいる attaches to the て form and says someone does one action over and over and little else — 遊んでばかりいる = does nothing but play around. It usually carries a critical or exasperated tone, painting the behavior as excessive and unbalanced. The いる can conjugate (ばかりいた, ばかりいて).
materials.reading: てばかりいる
materials.notes:
It usually sounds critical — that the person does this to the exclusion of what they should be doing.

Attach ばかり after the て form here: 泣いてばかりいる, not 泣くばかりいる.

Keep it apart from Verb［た form］＋ばかり ('just did'); てばかりいる is a repeated habit, not a one-off that just happened.

Synonyms: bakari — ばかり is the base 'only' particle; 〜てばかりいる is its ongoing-habit form with a verb and a critical edge.

Related: dake — だけ neutrally limits to 'only'; 〜てばかりいる adds the sense of an excessive, unbalanced habit.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［て form］＋ ばかりいる

examples.japanese: 弟は遊んでばかりいて、宿題を全然やらない。
examples.english: My little brother does nothing but play around and never does his homework.
examples.reading: おとうとはあそんでばかりいて、しゅくだいをぜんぜんやらない。

examples.japanese: 最近、姉はスマホを見てばかりいる。
examples.english: Lately my older sister does nothing but look at her phone.
examples.reading: さいきん、あねはスマホをみてばかりいる。

materials.prompt: てばかりはいられない
materials.answer:
can't just keep ~ing (something else needs doing)

てばかりはいられない combines て + ばかり ('only') + はいられない to say one cannot go on doing just this one thing — 落ち込んでばかりはいられない = 'I can't just keep moping'. It acknowledges the action but insists it can't continue as the only thing, because other responsibilities call. The tone is one of pulling oneself together to move on.
materials.reading: てばかりはいられない
materials.notes:
The ばかり ('only') is key: it says you can't do just this and nothing else, implying you must also do something more constructive.

It usually signals a resolve to stop dwelling and take action, so a positive next step often follows.

Synonyms: tewa-irarenai — てはいられない simply says you can't stay as you are; てばかりはいられない stresses you can't do only that one thing.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［て form］＋ばかりはいられない

materials.prompt: てちょうだい
materials.answer:
please do ~ (soft, casual request)

てちょうだい follows the て-form to make a gentle, casual request — 取ってちょうだい = 'pass it to me, would you'. It is softer and more familiar than てください, and is used mainly among family and close acquaintances, often by women or when speaking to children. It carries a warm, coaxing tone rather than a formal one.
materials.reading: てちょうだい
materials.notes:
It is casual and familiar; use てください with people you must be polite to.

It sounds gentle and is associated with women's speech and talking to children, so it can feel out of place from a man in a neutral setting.

Synonyms: te-kudasai — てください is the standard polite request; てちょうだい is softer, casual, and more intimate.

Related: te-hoshii — てほしい states a wish for someone to act ('I want you to ~'); てちょうだい directly makes the request.

Source references: bunpro

examples.reading: しゅくだいがおわったら、すぐにおしえてちょうだい。

materials.prompt: て・で
materials.answer:
て-form linking clauses: and (then); because

The verb て-form links clauses together: it can list actions in order ('do A, and then B') or give a light reason ('B because A'). The voiced で appears with certain verbs (読んで, 遊んで). The final verb carries the tense — the て-form itself stays tense-neutral.
materials.reading: て・で
materials.notes:
The て-form has no tense of its own; the last verb decides past or non-past for the whole sentence.

For a strong 'because,' use から／ので; the て-cause fits best when the result is an emotion or natural outcome (聞いて驚いた).

Some verbs voice the ending to で: 読んで, 飲んで, 遊んで — never 読んて.

Synonyms: te-kara — 〜てから marks a clear 'after doing'; the plain て-form just says 'and then.'

Synonyms: kara — から states an explicit reason; the て-form gives a softer, often emotional cause.

Related: kute-de — い-adjectives and nouns link with 〜くて／〜で; verbs use the verb て-form.

Related: to-and — 〜と joins nouns ('A and B'); the て-form joins verbs and clauses.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てでも
materials.answer:
even if one has to ~ (extreme means)

てでも follows the て-form to name an extreme measure one is willing to take to reach a goal — 借金してでも = 'even if I have to borrow money'. It highlights a drastic action offered as the means, and the main clause states a strong wish or determination to achieve the goal despite that cost.
materials.reading: てでも
materials.notes:
It names the extreme means one will resort to; the main clause expresses firm will or a strong desire.

Don't confuse it with plain ても ('even if'): てでも specifically presents an action as the drastic method used to accomplish something.

Synonyms: te-made — てまで also marks going to extremes, but often to criticize the excess; てでも stresses one's willingness and resolve.

Related: temo — ても is plain 'even if ~'; てでも adds でも to frame an extreme action as the means to an end.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I'll finish this work by tomorrow even if I have to stay up all night.
examples.reading: てつやしてでも、あしたまでにこのしごとをおわらせる。

materials.prompt: 〜て
materials.answer:
and; and then (verb linking)

The connective て form of a verb links it to what follows: "do A and (then) B". It joins actions in sequence within one sentence and is also the base for many other patterns (ている, てください, and more). Mastering how each verb group forms て is a core N5 skill.
materials.reading: て
materials.notes:
The final verb carries the tense: 起きて…洗いました means both actions were in the past.

How て forms depends on the verb group, with sound changes for u-verbs (書く→書いて, 飲む→飲んで, 待つ→待って).

Related: te-kara — てから stresses "after doing A, then B"; plain て just links the actions.

Related: tari-tari — 〜たり lists sample actions without order; て links them in sequence.

Related: te-kudasai — てください uses the て form to make a request; here て just connects clauses.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: てごらん
materials.answer:
go on, try doing; (please) look

〜てごらん is a soft, encouraging way to tell someone to try doing something — warmer than a plain command, and typically used by adults toward children or by a senior toward a junior. It comes from ご覧なさい (look/see). 食べてごらん = go on, try eating it.
materials.reading: てごらん
materials.notes:
It's used downward — to children, students, or close juniors — not toward superiors.

It's gentler than なさい but still a command; for a polite request to equals or superiors use 〜てみてください.

Synonyms: te-miru — てみる is the neutral 'try doing'; てごらん turns it into a gentle 'go ahead and try' command.

Related: nasai — なさい is a firm command; てごらん is softer and more encouraging.

Related: te-kudasai — てください is a polite request usable with anyone; てごらん is casual and aimed at juniors or children.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: て初めて
materials.answer:
not until ~; only after doing ~ (did I realize/come to)

〜てはじめて joins the て form to say that only after experiencing X does something Y become true — usually a realization. ひとりで暮らしてはじめて = only after living alone (did I understand...). The 初めて here means 'only at that point', not literally 'for the first time counting occasions'.
materials.reading: てはじめて
materials.notes:
初めて here means 'not until then / only at that point', so it is often followed by realization verbs like 分かる, 気づく.

The X part is a real experience that triggers the realization, not a hypothetical.

Related: kara-koso — からこそ stresses 'precisely because'; てはじめて stresses that the realization came only after the experience.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てほしい
materials.answer:
to want someone (else) to do ~

てほしい expresses wanting another person to do something. The person you want to act is marked with に, and ほしい inflects like an い-adjective. The negative 'want you NOT to' is 〜ないでほしい.
materials.reading: てほしい
materials.notes:
The subject differs from 〜たい: 〜たい = I want to do it myself; てほしい = I want another person to do it.

Mark the person you want to act with に: 君に来てほしい.

'Want you not to' is 〜ないでほしい (来ないでほしい = I want you not to come).

Related: ga-hoshii — がほしい wants an object; てほしい wants an action from someone.

Related: tai — 〜たい is wanting to do something yourself; てほしい is wanting someone else to do it.

Related: you-ni-te-hoshii — ように〜てほしい softens the request, often for outcomes not fully in the person's control.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun［person］＋ に ＋ Verb［て form］＋ ほしい
Verb［ない form］＋ でほしい［negative］

materials.prompt: ていく
materials.answer:
to go on doing; to do and then go; to continue from now

Verb［て form］＋ いく carries an action or change away from the present into the future — 'keep on ~ing from here.' It can also mean 'do something, then head off.' Its mirror image is 〜てくる, which brings change up to now. Write the auxiliary いく in kana.
materials.reading: ていく
materials.notes:
〜ていく moves change away into the future (増えていく); 〜てくる traces it up to the present.

When いく is the 'continue' auxiliary, write it in kana (〜ていく) rather than as the full verb 行く.

Antonyms: te-kuru — 〜ていく moves change away into the future; 〜てくる brings it up to the present.

Related: dandan — だんだん often pairs with 〜ていく to describe gradual change ahead.

Related: you-ni-naru — 〜ようになる marks reaching a new state; 〜ていく traces the ongoing change toward it.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: これからもにほんごをべんきょうしていきます。

materials.prompt: 〜て以来
materials.answer:
ever since ~; since (a past event)

以来 marks a point in the past after which a situation has continued unchanged up to now. It follows either the て-form of a verb (卒業して以来 = 'ever since graduating') or a noun (入社以来 = 'ever since joining the company'). The event is a single past change, and the clause that follows describes a state that has held ever since.
materials.reading: ていらい
materials.notes:
以来 marks a one-time past event as a starting point; it does not work for repeated or ongoing actions.

The following clause describes a lasting state or tendency that continues to the present, not a single later event.

For close, recent time frames (yesterday, this morning) 以来 sounds odd; it implies a stretch of time has passed.

Synonyms: te-kara — てから simply means 'after doing ~'; 以来 adds that the resulting state has lasted continuously up to now.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 大学を卒業して以来、彼とは一度も会っていない。
examples.english: I haven't seen him even once since I graduated from university.
examples.reading: だいがくをそつぎょうしていらい、かれとはいちどもあっていない。

examples.japanese: この製品は、発売以来ずっと人気が続いている。
examples.english: This product has stayed popular ever since it went on sale.
examples.reading: このせいひんは、はつばいいらいずっとにんきがつづいている。

materials.prompt: ている
materials.answer:
is doing; is in a state of ~

Attaches いる to a verb's て form to express either an action in progress ("is doing") or a continuing state that resulted from an action ("has done and remains so"). Which reading applies depends on the verb, making this one of the most important — and most versatile — N5 patterns.
materials.reading: ている
materials.notes:
With some verbs ている means the resulting state, not an action in progress: 結婚している ("is married"), 知っている ("know"), 住んでいる ("live").

In casual speech the い drops: 食べてる, 見てる.

Related: te-aru — てある is a state deliberately left by someone using a transitive verb; ている can be a natural state or ongoing action.

Related: mada-te-imasen — まだ〜ていません says "haven't done yet", the negative counterpart of a ている state.

Related: te-form — ている is built on the て form, the same base used to link verbs.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 今、音楽を聞いています。
examples.english: I'm listening to music right now.
examples.reading: いま、おんがくをきいています。

examples.japanese: 田中さんは結婚しています。
examples.english: Tanaka is married.
examples.reading: たなかさんはけっこんしています。

materials.prompt: ていた
materials.answer:
was doing; had been doing (past progressive/state)

ていた is simply the past of ている. It describes an action that was going on at some moment in the past (was ~ing), or a state that had come about and was still holding then. Casual ～ていた, polite ～ていました. Which reading applies depends on the verb, exactly as with ている.
materials.reading: ていた
materials.notes:
ていた is not the same as plain past: 食べていた = 'was eating' (in progress), while 食べた = 'ate' (simply happened).

With change-of-state verbs it reads as a lasting state, not an action: 住んでいた = 'lived / was living', 結婚していた = 'was married'.

Related: te-iru — ている places the ongoing action/state at the present; ていた places the same at a past reference point.

Related: te-kuru — てきた traces a change continuing up to now; ていた just situates an action in the past.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ いた／いました

examples.japanese: 電話したとき、姉はテレビを見ていました。
examples.english: When I called, my older sister was watching TV.
examples.reading: でんわしたとき、あねはテレビをみていました。

examples.japanese: 子どものころ、東京に住んでいました。
examples.english: When I was a child, I lived in Tokyo.
examples.reading: こどものころ、とうきょうにすんでいました。

materials.prompt: ていただけませんか
materials.answer:
could you please ~? (very polite request)

A very polite, softened way to ask someone to do something for you. It is built on the humble いただく (to receive) in its negative-potential-question shape, literally 'couldn't I receive the favor of your ~ing?' — which lands as a respectful 'could you please ~?'. Reach for it with superiors, customers, and strangers.
materials.reading: ていただけませんか
materials.notes:
This is softer and more polite than てください or てくれませんか; the affirmative ～ていただけますか is fine too but a touch more direct.

The subject is you (the one receiving the favor). てくださいませんか instead frames the other person as the doer; both are polite, but the viewpoint differs.

Synonyms: te-kurenai-te-moraenai — ～てもらえない／～てくれない are the plain, casual versions of this same request.

Related: te-morau — ていただく is the humble equivalent of てもらう (receiving the favor of an action).

Related: te-kudasai — てください is a plainer, more direct 'please do'; ていただけませんか is far more deferential.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ いただけませんか

examples.japanese: すみません、少し待っていただけませんか。
examples.english: Excuse me, could you please wait a moment?
examples.reading: すみません、すこしまっていただけませんか。

examples.japanese: この漢字の読み方を教えていただけませんか。
examples.english: Could you please tell me how to read this kanji?
examples.reading: このかんじのよみかたをおしえていただけませんか。

materials.prompt: ていては
materials.answer:
if one keeps doing ~ (a bad result will follow)

ていては takes the ている form and adds は to say that continuing an action will lead to an undesirable outcome — 遊んでいては = 'if you keep playing (you'll fail)'. It frames an ongoing habit or state as the cause of a coming problem, so the second clause is almost always negative. In casual speech ていては often contracts to てちゃ.
materials.reading: ていては
materials.notes:
The clause that follows is normally a bad consequence (won't make it, can't succeed), not a neutral result.

In casual speech ていては shrinks to てちゃ (飲んでちゃ); the meaning stays the same.

It criticizes a continuing action or state; for a one-off condition, plain たら or ば is more natural.

Related: tewa — ては is the base pattern for 'if ~, then a bad result'; ていては applies it specifically to a continuing action or state.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: If you keep drinking every day like that, you'll ruin your health.

materials.prompt: 〜てかなわない・〜てはかなわない
materials.answer:
unbearably ~; can't stand it that ~; too ~ to put up with

〜てかなわない says a condition is more than the speaker can bear — it is unbearably or intolerably so. 暑くてかなわない = unbearably hot, this heat is too much. It typically follows adjectives or verbs describing a sensation or feeling and expresses the speaker's own discomfort. The variant 〜てはかなわない frames it as 'it would be unbearable if ~', pushing back against a possibility.
materials.reading: てかなわない・てはかなわない
materials.notes:
Expresses the speaker's own unbearable discomfort; it isn't used to report someone else's feelings objectively.

Here かなわない means 'cannot endure', not the other 敵わない ('be no match for').

Synonyms: te-tamaranai — 〜てたまらない ('unbearably ~') is close and a touch more neutral in feeling; てかなわない stresses annoyance and exasperation at having to put up with it.

Synonyms: te-naranai — 〜てならない marks a feeling that wells up uncontrollably; てかなわない specifically marks something as too much to endure.

Synonyms: te-shou-ga-nai — 〜てしょうがない ('can't help feeling ~') is the casual all-purpose version; てかなわない leans toward an intolerable nuisance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 隣の工事の音がうるさくてかなわない。
examples.english: The noise from the construction next door is unbearably loud.
examples.reading: となりのこうじのおとがうるさくてかなわない。

examples.japanese: 毎日こう残業続きではかなわない。
examples.english: If overtime keeps piling up like this every day, I just can't take it.
examples.reading: まいにちこうざんぎょうつづきではかなわない。

materials.prompt: てから
materials.answer:
after doing ~; once ~ is done

Chains two actions in strict order: attach から to the て form of a verb to say the second action happens only after the first is finished. It stresses that the first action comes first and is fully done before the next one begins.
materials.reading: てから
materials.notes:
てから is about time order, not reason — for 'because', use から attached to a plain sentence instead.

Only the final verb carries the tense; the てから clause stays in the て form no matter when the events happen.

Synonyms: ato-de — あとで just means 'afterwards'; てから stresses that the first action must finish before the second.

Antonyms: mae-ni — まえに puts the main action before the other one; てから puts it after.

Related: te-form — てから is built on the same て form used to connect verbs.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 手を洗ってから昼ご飯を食べます。
examples.english: I eat lunch after washing my hands.
examples.reading: てをあらってからひるごはんをたべます。

examples.japanese: 仕事が終わってから、映画を見に行きました。
examples.english: After work finished, I went to see a movie.
examples.reading: しごとがおわってから、えいがをみにいきました。

materials.prompt: てからでないと
materials.answer:
not until you first do; can't unless you do first

〜てからでないと sets a required first step — nothing further can happen until it's done. It's usually followed by a negative outcome: 予約してからでないと入れない = you can't get in unless you book first. Literally 'if it isn't after doing ~.'
materials.reading: てからでないと
materials.notes:
The second clause is normally negative (〜ない／〜できない): 確認してからでないと答えられない.

It stresses order — X must come first before Y is possible; plain てから just says 'after,' without the 'can't otherwise' nuance.

bunpro lists N2

Related: te-kara — てから simply means 'after doing'; てからでないと adds that nothing else is possible until then.

Related: nakereba-naranai — なければならない states that an action is necessary; てからでないと makes that action a prerequisite for something else.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ からでないと／からでなければ ＋ （negative）

examples.japanese: 手を洗ってからでないと、食べてはいけません。
examples.english: You mustn't eat until you've washed your hands first.
examples.reading: てをあらってからでないと、たべてはいけません。

examples.japanese: 上司に確認してからでないと、返事ができません。
examples.english: I can't give an answer until I've checked with my boss first.
examples.reading: じょうしにかくにんしてからでないと、へんじができません。

materials.prompt: 〜てからというもの
materials.answer:
ever since ~; from the time ~, and continuing ever after

〜てからというもの marks a past event as the turning point after which a state has held continuously ever since. 引っ越してからというもの、一度も会っていない = ever since I moved, I haven't seen them even once. It is more emphatic and emotive than plain てから, stressing that a lasting change set in from that moment and persists. The following clause describes the ongoing situation.
materials.reading: てからというもの
materials.notes:
Points to a lasting change that has continued ever since a single past event, not a one-time result.

More emphatic and emotional than plain 〜てから; reserve it for a genuine before-and-after shift.

Synonyms: te-irai — 〜て以来 also means 'ever since ~' and is more neutral and objective; てからというもの adds emotional emphasis on the sustained change.

Related: te-kara — plain 〜てから just orders one action after another; てからというもの stresses a lasting change that has held ever since.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てこそ
materials.answer:
only by doing ~; it is precisely because one does ~

てこそ combines the て-form with the emphatic particle こそ to single out an action as the essential condition for a valued result — 努力してこそ成功する = 'it is only through effort that one succeeds'. The clause after it is normally positive and desirable: the point is that the good outcome is possible only because of the highlighted action.
materials.reading: てこそ
materials.notes:
The following clause is usually a positive or worthwhile result, since てこそ praises the condition that makes it possible.

It presents the action as the one indispensable condition; a plain から just gives a reason without that emphasis.

Synonyms: te-hajimete — て初めて means 'not until ~ did ...', stressing a first realization; てこそ stresses the essential condition for a good result.

Related: koso — こそ is the underlying emphatic particle ('precisely'); てこそ applies it to a verb as the key condition.

Related: ba-koso — ばこそ ('precisely because') is a more formal, literary way to stress a reason; てこそ focuses on an enabling action.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てください
materials.answer:
please do ~ (polite request)

Makes a polite request or instruction: attach ください to the て form of a verb to ask someone to do something. It is the standard courteous way to tell or ask a person to perform an action, common in classrooms, signs, and everyday service situations.
materials.reading: てください
materials.notes:
It is polite but still a request, so to a superior a softer form such as てくださいませんか sounds more respectful.

To ask someone NOT to do something, switch to the ない form: 〜ないでください.

Synonyms: te-request — Dropping ください leaves just 〜て, a casual version for friends and family.

Antonyms: naide-kudasai — 〜ないでください asks someone not to do something; てください asks them to do it.

Related: nasai — なさい is a firmer command used by parents and teachers; てください is a neutral polite request.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てくれない・てもらえない
materials.answer:
won't you ~?; could you ~? (casual request)

Two casual ways to ask a favor. 〜てくれない? = 'won't you do ~ for me?'; 〜てもらえない? = 'could I get you to ~?'. Both are the negative-question forms of てくれる and the potential もらえる, which softens the request. Say them with rising intonation.
materials.reading: てくれない・てもらえない
materials.notes:
These are casual. For polite speech use 〜てくれませんか／〜てもらえませんか, or the humble 〜ていただけませんか.

てもらえない builds on the potential もらえる ('can receive'), while てくれない uses plain くれる — both function as requests.

Synonyms: te-itadakemasen-ka — ていただけませんか is the polite, humble version of this same request.

Related: te-kureru — てくれる states 'does me a favor'; its negative question turns that into a request.

Related: te-morau — てもらう underlies てもらえない — 'could I receive the favor of your ~ing?'.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: てくれる
materials.answer:
to do (a favor) for me/us

てくれる marks that someone does an action as a favor for the speaker or the speaker's in-group. The doer is the subject (が/は); the beneficiary is you, often left unstated. The direction of the favor points toward the speaker's side.
materials.reading: てくれる
materials.notes:
The direction is fixed toward the speaker: 友だちが手伝ってくれる (my friend helps me). If you do the favor for someone else, switch to てあげる.

Contrast てもらう: with てくれる the giver is the subject (友だちが〜くれた); with てもらう the receiver is (私が友だちに〜もらった). Same event, different viewpoint.

The honorific version is てくださる: 先生が教えてくださった.

Related: kureru — plain くれる gives an object toward the speaker; てくれる gives an action as a favor.

Related: te-ageru — てあげる does a favor moving away from the speaker; てくれる, toward the speaker.

Related: te-morau — てもらう describes the same favor from the receiver's viewpoint (receiver = subject).

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てくれてありがとう
materials.answer:
thank you for ~ing

Thanks someone for doing something for you. It joins てくれる (someone does a favor for me) with ありがとう. Because it rests on てくれる, the action being thanked benefits the speaker. Polite: 〜てくれてありがとうございます, or with the honorific 〜てくださってありがとうございます.
materials.reading: てくれてありがとう
materials.notes:
Because it uses てくれる, the thanked action must be a favor toward you: 手伝ってくれてありがとう.

For politeness, swap くれて for くださって and add ございます: 来てくださってありがとうございます.

Related: te-kureru — てくれる (does a favor for me) is exactly what this phrase thanks the other person for.

Related: te-sumimasen — てすみません apologizes for an action; てくれてありがとう thanks for one — parallel structures.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: てくる
materials.answer:
to do and come back; to come to ~; to have been ~ing (up to now)

てくる attaches the motion verb 来る and carries several linked senses: (1) do something and come back (買ってくる = go buy and return); (2) a change moving toward the present or the speaker (寒くなってくる = it's getting cold); (3) an action or state continuing up until now (ずっと勉強してきた). It is the mirror of ていく.
materials.reading: てくる
materials.notes:
Direction is the key: てくる moves toward the speaker or up to the present, ていく moves away or into the future.

Don't read every てくる as literal 'come'. With change verbs it means 'come to / begin to': 慣れてくる = 'get used to it (gradually)'.

Related: te-iku — ていく moves away from the speaker or into the future; てくる moves toward the speaker or up to now.

Related: kuru — plain 来る is literal coming; てくる uses it as a helper attached to another verb.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てまで
materials.answer:
going so far as to ~; to the extreme of ~

てまで follows the て-form to describe going to an extreme length to achieve something — 借金してまで = 'going so far as to borrow money'. It is frequently used to question or criticize whether such an extreme is worth it, as in 〜てまでする必要はない = 'there's no need to go that far'. The nuance often leans skeptical or disapproving.
materials.reading: てまで
materials.notes:
It often carries a critical or doubtful tone — the speaker questions whether going to that extreme is justified.

Compare てでも, which frames the same extreme as one's own firm resolve; てまで more often evaluates the extreme from the outside.

Synonyms: te-demo — てでも frames an extreme means as one's own determination; てまで often questions or criticizes the extreme.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: てみる
materials.answer:
to try doing (and see how it goes)

From 見る, てみる means doing something to see how it turns out — 'try ~ing' / 'give it a go'. The focus is on the attempt and finding out the result, not on whether you succeed. It is usually written in kana, since 見る here is a helper, not literal 'look'.
materials.reading: てみる
materials.notes:
てみる is 'try and see the outcome'. For 'try hard to / attempt', use 〜ようとする instead.

Write it in kana (〜てみる); the auxiliary 見る has lost its literal 'look' meaning here.

Related: you-to-omou — ようと思う intends or plans to do; てみる just gives it a try to see the result.

Related: te-oku — both attach a helper verb to the て form; てみる = try and see, ておく = do in advance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜てみせる
materials.answer:
I'll do ~ (and show them); to demonstrate by actually doing ~

〜てみせる has two related senses. Literally it means performing an action to show someone how — お手本を書いてみせる = write it out to demonstrate. More pointedly, with volitional force it declares firm determination to accomplish something, often to prove others wrong: 必ず成功してみせる = I'll succeed, just you watch. The determination reading is emphatic and self-assertive, common in resolutions and challenges.
materials.reading: てみせる
materials.notes:
Distinguish the two readings: neutral 'demonstrate by doing' vs. emphatic 'I'll definitely do it (and prove it)' — context and often 必ず/きっと signal the latter.

The determination sense is about the speaker's own resolve; it isn't used to describe a third person's plans neutrally.

Synonyms: te-yaru — 〜てやる can also express defiant determination ('I'll show them / just you wait'); てみせる adds the nuance of proving it before others' eyes.

Related: te-miru — 〜てみる is 'try doing ~ (to see how it goes)'; てみせる is 'do ~ to show someone' or 'vow to pull it off' — resolve, not tentative trying.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てもらう
materials.answer:
to have/get someone to do ~ (for one's benefit)

てもらう describes receiving the favor of someone's action — you get someone to do something for you. The receiver (you or your in-group) is the subject; the doer is marked with に. The viewpoint is the receiver's.
materials.reading: てもらう
materials.notes:
Mark the doer with に: 友だちに手伝ってもらった (I had my friend help me).

Viewpoint flips vs てくれる: てもらう makes the receiver the subject (私が〜もらう); てくれる makes the giver the subject (友だちが〜くれる). Same event.

The humble/polite version is 〜ていただく (先生に教えていただいた).

Related: morau — plain もらう receives an object; てもらう receives an action as a favor.

Related: te-kureru — てくれる frames the same favor with the doer as subject; てもらう, with the receiver as subject.

Related: te-ageru — てあげる is doing a favor for someone else; てもらう is getting one done for you.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun［receiver］＋ が ＋ Noun［doer］＋ に ＋ Verb［て form］＋ もらう

materials.prompt: てならない
materials.answer:
can't help feeling ~; ~ terribly

てならない follows the て-form to say a feeling or impression wells up beyond the speaker's control — 気になってならない = 'I can't help worrying', 思えてならない = 'I can't help feeling that ...'. It often attaches to verbs of spontaneous thought and emotion. Similar to てたまらない, it leans somewhat formal and is especially common with 気がする, 思える, and the like.
materials.reading: てならない
materials.notes:
It works best with spontaneous feelings and impressions (思えてならない, 気になってならない), not deliberate actions.

It is a touch more formal and written than てたまらない, which sounds more everyday.

Synonyms: te-tamaranai — てたまらない stresses a feeling almost too strong to bear; てならない stresses a feeling that arises on its own and won't stop.

Synonyms: te-shou-ga-nai — てしょうがない is the more casual 'can't help ~'; てならない is somewhat more formal and literary.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ておく
materials.answer:
to do in advance; to do (and leave it that way) on purpose

From 置く (to place), ておく means doing something ahead of time as preparation, or deliberately leaving something in a certain state. In casual speech it contracts: 〜ておく → 〜とく, 〜でおく → 〜どく.
materials.reading: ておく
materials.notes:
Two senses share the form: preparing beforehand (予約しておく) and leaving something as-is on purpose (窓を開けておく).

The casual contraction drops いてお/んでお: 買っておく → 買っとく, 読んでおく → 読んどく.

Related: te-miru — both attach a helper verb to the て form; てみる means 'try and see', ておく means 'do in advance'.

Related: te-shimau-chau — another て + helper; てしまう marks completion or regret, ておく marks doing ahead of time.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ おく／おきます

materials.prompt: ～て
materials.answer:
casual request: please do ~

A bare て-form at the end of a sentence is a casual request — 'do this for me'. It is 〜てください with ください dropped, so 待って = wait (please), 見て = look. It sounds friendly but informal, so keep it for people you're close to.
materials.notes:
This is casual: to a boss, teacher, or stranger, use 〜てください rather than a bare 〜て.

Don't confuse this sentence-final request 〜て with the connective て that links clauses (待って、電話します = wait and then call).

Synonyms: te-kudasai — 〜てください is the polite full form; a bare 〜て is its casual short version.

Antonyms: naide-request — 〜ないで is the casual negative request 'please don't'; 〜て is the positive 'please do'.

Related: te-form — The same て-form links clauses mid-sentence; here it stands at the end as a request.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜てしかるべきだ
materials.answer:
ought to be ~; it is only natural/proper that ~; deserves to be ~

〜てしかるべきだ says something is proper and to be expected — it ought to be so as a matter of course. 努力は評価されてしかるべきだ = such effort ought to be, and deserves to be, recognized. しかるべき means 'appropriate / as it should be', so the phrase asserts that the state described by the て-form is the natural, reasonable thing. It is formal and often argues that something rightly should happen.
materials.reading: てしかるべきだ
materials.notes:
Formal, written or argumentative register; not for everyday conversation.

It often attaches to a passive て-form (評価されて, 認められて) to say 'ought rightly to be ~ed'.

Synonyms: beki-da — plain 〜べきだ states a direct 'should / ought to'; てしかるべきだ frames it as what is only natural and proper, often more measured and formal.

Synonyms: te-touzen-da — 〜て当然だ ('naturally ~; no wonder ~') also says something is to be expected; てしかるべきだ adds the sense that it is the proper, deserved thing.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: てしまう・ちゃう
materials.answer:
to do completely; to do (unfortunately, by accident)

てしまう adds one of two nuances: (1) completion — doing something fully, all the way through — or (2) regret — an action that turned out badly or happened by mistake. Context decides which. Casual contractions: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう, 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう.
materials.reading: てしまう・ちゃう
materials.notes:
The two nuances overlap: 全部食べてしまった can mean 'ate it all up' (completion) or 'ate it, oops' (regret).

Watch the voiced contraction: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう (食べちゃう), but 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう (飲んじゃう, 死んじゃう).

The regret sense very often appears in the past: 〜てしまった／〜ちゃった.

Related: te-oku — both are て + helper verb; てしまう marks completion or regret, ておく marks doing in advance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ しまう／しまいます

materials.prompt: てしょうがない・てしかたがない
materials.answer:
can't help feeling; unbearably; extremely

〜てしょうがない (and its twin 〜てしかたがない) says a feeling or sensation is so strong you can't do anything about it — you're overwhelmed by it. 眠くてしょうがない = unbearably sleepy; 気になってしょうがない = I can't stop worrying about it. It's mostly used about one's own feelings.
materials.reading: てしょうがない・てしかたがない
materials.notes:
しょうがない and しかたがない are interchangeable here; しょうがない is a bit more casual.

It's for spontaneous feelings and sensations (sleepy, hungry, worried), not for deliberate actions.

bunpro lists N2

Synonyms: te-tamaranai — てたまらない is a very close 'unbearably ~'; てしょうがない is slightly softer and more everyday.

Synonyms: te-naranai — てならない carries the same 'can't help feeling,' but sounds more written or literary.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］／い-adjective［て form］＋ しょうがない／しかたがない
な-adjective ＋ で ＋ しょうがない／しかたがない

materials.prompt: てすみません
materials.answer:
sorry for ~ing

Apologizes for an action you did or are doing: 〜てすみません = 'sorry for ~ing'. For a finished action, use the past 〜てすみませんでした. More casual is 〜てごめん(なさい). It mirrors てくれてありがとう, but as an apology rather than thanks.
materials.reading: てすみません
materials.notes:
For a completed action, apologize in the past: 遅れてすみませんでした.

To apologize for NOT doing something, use the negative 〜なくてすみません (返事できなくてすみません = sorry for not replying).

Related: te-kurete-arigatou — てくれてありがとう thanks for an action; てすみません apologizes for one.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ すみません／すみませんでした

examples.japanese: 遅くなってすみません。
examples.english: Sorry for being late.
examples.reading: おそくなってすみません。

examples.japanese: 何度も電話してすみませんでした。
examples.english: I'm sorry for calling so many times.
examples.reading: なんどもでんわしてすみませんでした。

materials.prompt: て済む
materials.answer:
can get by with just; be settled by (only)

〜て済む means a situation can be settled or gotten through with only that much — often less trouble than you'd feared. 電話で済む = it can be handled with just a phone call. 済む means 'to be finished / settled,' so the pattern says 'doing that much is all it takes.'
materials.reading: てすむ
materials.notes:
It often implies 'that's all it takes / you get off with just ~,' a lighter outcome than expected.

Distinct from 〜ずに済む / 〜ないで済む, which mean 'get by without having to do ~.'

Related: zu-ni-sumu — ずに済む means getting by WITHOUT doing something; て済む means getting by with just doing that much.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［て form］／い-adjective［て form］＋ 済む

materials.prompt: 〜て済むことではない
materials.answer:
not something that ~ will settle; ~ing is not enough to resolve it

〜て済むことではない declares that merely doing the stated action is not enough to put a matter to rest — the problem is too serious for that. 謝って済むことではない = this isn't something an apology will make right. 済む here means 'be settled / get by', so the negative says the issue won't be closed off just by that action, implying graver consequences or responsibility. It carries a reproachful, weighty tone.
materials.reading: てすむことではない
materials.notes:
済む here means 'be settled / suffice', so 〜て済むことではない says the action falls short of resolving the matter — it is not about literally 'finishing'.

Carries a reproachful, serious tone; reserve it for genuinely grave matters.

Synonyms: dewa-sumanai — 〜では済まない says a situation won't end with just ~ (and worse will follow); て済むことではない specifically denies that a given action can settle the matter.

Synonyms: zu-niwa-sumanai — 〜ずには済まない means one can't avoid doing ~ (it's unavoidable); て済むことではない means doing ~ isn't enough to resolve things — the opposite angle on 済む.

Related: te-sumu — 〜て済む affirms that something can be gotten through or settled by ~; て済むことではない negates exactly that.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［て form］＋済むことではない

examples.reading: これはたんとうしゃがやめてすむことではない、そしきぜんたいのもんだいだ。
