materials.prompt: てたまらない
materials.answer:
unbearably ~; can't stand how ~; dying to ~

てたまらない expresses a feeling or desire so strong the speaker can hardly bear it — 暑くてたまらない = 'unbearably hot', 会いたくてたまらない = 'dying to see someone'. It attaches to the て-form of adjectives and verbs of emotion or sensation. たまらない literally means 'cannot be endured', so the whole phrase conveys an overwhelming, uncontrollable state.
materials.reading: てたまらない
materials.notes:
It describes the speaker's own uncontrollable feeling or sensation, so it pairs with emotion and sensation words, not neutral statements.

For a desire, it attaches to the 〜たい form (見たくてたまらない), not the plain verb.

Synonyms: te-naranai — てならない conveys the same overwhelming feeling but leans formal and favors spontaneous thoughts (思えてならない).

Synonyms: te-shou-ga-nai — てしょうがない・てしかたがない is the more casual 'can't help feeling'; てたまらない stresses that the feeling is barely bearable.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: て当然だ
materials.answer:
it's only natural that ~; no wonder ~

て当然だ follows the て-form to say that a result is entirely natural or deserved given the circumstances — 怒られて当然だ = 'no wonder you got scolded / you deserved it'. It presents an outcome as the obvious, reasonable consequence of what came before, and can carry a 'that's what you get' nuance. It also appears as 〜のも当然だ.
materials.reading: てとうぜんだ
materials.notes:
It judges a result as natural and deserved, so it often carries a 'serves you right' or 'of course' tone.

It comments on why an outcome makes sense; it does not predict that something should happen the way はずだ does.

Related: hazu-da — はずだ predicts what should logically be the case; て当然だ judges an actual result as natural and deserved.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Since he practices every day, no wonder he's gotten good.

materials.prompt: てはいけない
materials.answer:
must not ~; may not ~

States that an action is not allowed: attach はいけない to the て form of a verb to prohibit it. It is the standard way to express rules and forbidden things, and it pairs naturally with the permission form てもいい.
materials.reading: てはいけない
materials.notes:
In casual speech ては often contracts to ちゃ (食べてはいけない → 食べちゃいけない).

Do not confuse it with なくてはいけない, which means the opposite — that you MUST do something.

Synonyms: cha-ikenai — ちゃいけない is the casual contraction of てはいけない.

Antonyms: temo-ii — てもいい grants permission ('may'); てはいけない withholds it ('must not').

Related: na-prohibitive — The particle な is a blunt 'don't'; てはいけない is the fuller, more explanatory prohibition.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ は ＋ いけない／いけません

materials.prompt: てはいけないから
materials.answer:
because you mustn't ~ (so...); so as not to

〜てはいけないから gives a prohibition itself as a reason — 'because you mustn't ~, ...' You state that some action is forbidden or undesirable, and that's why you take (or avoid) another action. 遅れてはいけないから、早く出た = I left early because I mustn't be late.
materials.reading: てはいけないから
materials.notes:
It's simply 〜てはいけない (must not) plus から (because); the から-clause gives the reason for the main clause.

The main clause is usually a precaution taken to avoid the forbidden outcome.

Related: te-wa-ikenai — てはいけない states the prohibition itself; てはいけないから uses that prohibition as the reason for another action.

Related: you-ni-so-that — ように expresses 'so that (a bad thing) won't happen'; てはいけないから frames the same idea as 'because it mustn't happen.'

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［て form］＋ はいけないから ＋ Sentence

materials.prompt: 〜てやまない
materials.answer:
to never cease to (wish, hope, love); to ~ from the bottom of one's heart

〜てやまない attaches to the て-form of a verb of emotion or desire and says the speaker holds that feeling ceaselessly, straight from the heart. It pairs only with a small set of feeling verbs — 願う, 祈る, 期待する, 愛する, 尊敬する — so 願ってやまない = never cease to wish, 尊敬してやまない = hold in unending respect. It is formal, literary language at home in speeches, tributes, and written prose.
materials.reading: てやまない
materials.notes:
Only a small set of emotion/desire verbs fit: 願う, 祈る, 期待する, 愛する, 尊敬する. It does not attach to ordinary action verbs (×食べてやまない).

Formal, written or ceremonial language; it sounds out of place in casual conversation.

Synonyms: te-tamaranai — てたまらない voices an emotion the speaker can hardly bear right now; てやまない is a lasting, heartfelt wish or feeling in formal prose.

Related: te-naranai — てならない marks a feeling that wells up spontaneously and won't be suppressed; てやまない stresses a devoted feeling held without end.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I wish you all continued and ever-greater success in the days ahead.

examples.english: All his life, he never ceased to love the sea and mountains of his hometown.
examples.reading: かれはしょうがい、こきょうのうみとやまをあいしてやまなかった。

materials.prompt: てやる
materials.answer:
to do (a favor) for someone lower in status; to do (defiantly)

てやる is like てあげる (do a favor) but directed at those lower in status — juniors, children, animals, plants — and in a blunter, more casual register. It can also carry a defiant 'just you watch' determination when the speaker is talking about themselves.
materials.reading: てやる
materials.notes:
The register is blunt. Toward equals or superiors use てあげる, not てやる.

It's common with juniors and pets/plants: 弟に教えてやる, 犬にえさをやる.

A second nuance is defiance/determination: 絶対に勝ってやる = 'I'll definitely win — just watch me'.

bunpro lists N1

Synonyms: te-ageru — てあげる is the neutral, politer form; てやる is blunter and aimed at those below the speaker.

Related: te-kureru — てくれる is a favor done toward the speaker; てやる is a favor the speaker does downward.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: My little brother was in trouble, so I helped him out.
examples.reading: おとうとがこまっていたので、てつだってやった。

examples.japanese: 子どもにえほんを読んでやった。
examples.english: I read a picture book to my child.
examples.reading: こどもにえほんをよんでやった。

materials.prompt: てよかった
materials.answer:
I'm glad that ~; it was good that ~

The て form plus よかった looks back on something and says you're glad or relieved it turned out that way: 来てよかった = I'm glad I came. Even though よかった is past, the feeling of relief is right now. For 'glad I didn't ~', switch the verb to the なくて form.
materials.reading: てよかった
materials.notes:
For 'I'm glad I didn't ~', use the なくて form: 行かなくてよかった (glad I didn't go), not the plain negative plus よかった.

Don't mix it up with 〜ばよかった／〜たらよかった, which express regret ('I should have ~'). てよかった is a positive, relieved feeling about what did happen.

Antonyms: ba-yokatta — 〜ばよかった regrets something you didn't do; 〜てよかった is glad about what you did.

Related: te-form — The pattern attaches よかった to the plain て form of the verb.

Related: nakute — The negative version 〜なくてよかった uses this なくて form.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 早めに家を出てよかったです。電車に間に合いました。
examples.english: I'm glad I left home early. I made the train.
examples.reading: はやめにいえをでてよかったです。でんしゃにまにあいました。

examples.japanese: あなたに相談してよかったです。気持ちが楽になりました。
examples.english: I'm glad I talked it over with you. I feel much better now.
examples.reading: あなたにそうだんしてよかったです。きもちがらくになりました。

materials.prompt: ている場合じゃない
materials.answer:
this is no time to be doing (something)

〜ている場合じゃない says the situation is too urgent or serious to be doing something — 'this is no time to be ~.' You point out that the current activity is inappropriate given more pressing matters. 笑っている場合じゃない = this is no time to be laughing.
materials.reading: ているばあいじゃない
materials.notes:
場合 here means 'situation,' so the phrase judges that the ongoing action doesn't fit the circumstances.

The fuller, more polite form is 〜ている場合ではない; 〜じゃない is the casual version.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: This is no time to be taking it easy. Let's get ready quickly.
examples.reading: のんびりしているばあいじゃない。はやくじゅんびしよう。

materials.prompt: ているところ
materials.answer:
in the middle of doing; right now doing

ところ literally means 'place', but here it points to a stage in time. Verb＋ているところだ pins the action to exactly the stage of being in progress — 'I'm right in the middle of ~ing'. It is more pointed than plain ている, zooming in on this very moment.
materials.reading: ているところ
materials.notes:
There are three matching stages: 〜るところ (about to), 〜ているところ (in the middle), 〜たところ (just finished). Match the verb form to the stage you mean.

It describes a moment, so it pairs with 今 or ちょうど, not with a duration like 三時間.

Related: te-iru — plain ている says an action is ongoing; ているところ zooms in on the exact in-progress moment.

Related: ta-tokoro — たところ marks an action just finished; ているところ marks one still in progress.

Related: ru-tokoro-da — るところだ is about to start; ているところ is mid-action.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［て form］＋ いるところ（だ／です）

examples.japanese: 今、晩ご飯を作っているところです。
examples.english: I'm right in the middle of making dinner.
examples.reading: いま、ばんごはんをつくっているところです。

examples.japanese: ちょうどレポートを書いているところに、友だちが来た。
examples.english: Right as I was writing my report, a friend showed up.
examples.reading: ちょうどレポートをかいているところに、ともだちがきた。

materials.prompt: 的
materials.answer:
-al; -ic; relating to; turns a noun into a な-adjective or adverb

的 attaches to a noun to make an adjective-like word meaning 'relating to / -al / -ic' — 一般的 = general, 科学的 = scientific, 積極的 = proactive. Add な before a noun (的な考え) and に to use it adverbially (的に説明する). It's extremely common in both writing and speech.
materials.reading: てき
materials.notes:
Use 的な before a noun and 的に as an adverb: 具体的な例, 具体的に説明する.

It attaches mainly to kanji compound nouns (社会的, 経済的), not usually to everyday native words.

Related: ppoi — っぽい is a casual '-ish' added to everyday words; 的 forms categorical '-al/-ic' adjectives from kanji compounds.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Please explain it more concretely.
examples.reading: もっとぐたいてきにせつめいしてください。

examples.english: He has a proactive personality and makes friends quickly.

materials.prompt: 手前
materials.answer:
seeing as ~; given one's position before others

手前 as a grammar pattern means 'because of one's standing or appearance in front of others, one has to ~'. Following a noun + の or a plain-form verb, it gives a reason rooted in pride, face, or obligation toward the people watching — 約束した手前 = 'having promised (and with others aware), I can't back out'. The following clause states what one must or cannot do to save face.
materials.reading: てまえ
materials.notes:
This 手前 gives a reason based on one's face or position before others; it is not the literal 手前 meaning 'in front of / this side'.

The main clause states an obligation or restraint one accepts to keep up appearances (can't refuse, can't complain).

jlptsensei lists N1

Synonyms: ijou-wa — 以上は gives a logical 'now that ~, naturally ~'; 手前 grounds the obligation specifically in appearances before others.

Synonyms: kara-niwa — からには means 'now that / so long as ~', stressing resolve; 手前 stresses saving face in front of people.

Related: ue-wa — 上は means 'now that ~ (I've done it), I must ~'; 手前 adds the specific motive of pride or appearances.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: With my juniors watching, I can't let myself complain.
examples.reading: こうはいたちのてまえ、よわねをはくわけにはいかない。

examples.english: Having said I'd take it on, I can't very well refuse now.

materials.prompt: ても
materials.answer:
even if; even though

ても sets up 'even if / even though' — the second clause holds regardless of the first. It attaches to the て form: 食べても, 高くても, 学生でも. It covers both the hypothetical ('even if it rains') and the actual ('even though I studied').
materials.reading: ても
materials.notes:
い-adjectives become 〜くても (高くても); nouns and な-adjectives take でも (雨でも, 便利でも).

With a question word it means 'no matter ~': だれが来ても (no matter who comes), いくら〜ても (no matter how much).

Don't confuse it with 〜てもいい ('may / it's okay'); ても on its own means 'even if'.

Related: temo-ii — 〜てもいい grants permission ('may'); ても alone means 'even if'.

Related: demo-even — でも is the particle 'even'; in the ても pattern, nouns and な-adjectives likewise take でも.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Even if it rains, we'll hold the match.
examples.reading: あめがふっても、しあいをします。

examples.japanese: たくさん食べても、太りません。
examples.english: Even though I eat a lot, I don't gain weight.
examples.reading: たくさんたべても、ふとりません。

materials.prompt: 〜てもどうにもならない
materials.answer:
it's no use even if ~; ~ won't help; nothing can be done even if ~

〜てもどうにもならない says that even doing the stated thing changes nothing — the situation is beyond remedy. 今さら後悔してもどうにもならない = there's no use regretting it now. どうにもならない means 'nothing can be done about it', so the pattern declares the action futile against an unfixable situation. It is often used to dismiss pointless worry, regret, or effort.
materials.reading: てもどうにもならない
materials.notes:
Declares the action pointless because the situation can't be changed — stronger than merely 'it's not very useful'.

Often paired with 今さら ('at this late stage') to stress that acting now would be futile.

Synonyms: temo-hajimaranai — 〜ても始まらない says there's no point setting out on ~ because it leads nowhere; てもどうにもならない says even doing ~ can't fix the situation.

Synonyms: temo-shou-ga-nai — 〜てもしょうがない ('no use ~ing') is the casual all-purpose version; てもどうにもならない stresses that the situation itself is beyond remedy.

Related: dou-nimo-nai — どうにも〜ない means '(cannot) ~ in any way at all'; てもどうにもならない is the fixed 'even if ~, nothing can be done'.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: ても始まらない
materials.answer:
it's no use even if you ~; nothing will come of ~ing

〜ても始まらない says that even if you do X, nothing will change or come of it, so there's no point. ひとりで悩んでも始まらない = it won't get you anywhere to worry alone. 始まらない is idiomatic here — 'nothing will get started', i.e. no progress.
materials.reading: てもはじまらない
materials.notes:
始まらない is figurative ('nothing will come of it'), not literally about something starting.

It is often used to talk someone out of pointless worry, complaint, or hesitation.

Synonyms: temo-shou-ga-nai — てもしょうがない frames the action as simply useless; ても始まらない frames it as producing no progress.

Related: temo — ても is the plain 'even if'; ても始まらない fixes the outcome as 'and it changes nothing'.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜てもいい
materials.answer:
may ~; it's okay to ~

Grants or asks permission: attach もいい to the て form of a verb to say an action is allowed. As a question it politely asks whether something is okay to do; as a statement it gives the go-ahead.
materials.reading: てもいい
materials.notes:
As a request for permission it usually takes ですか — 入ってもいいですか ('may I come in?').

For nouns and な-adjectives, use でもいい instead of てもいい.

Synonyms: temo-kamawanai — てもかまわない ('I don't mind if') is a more indifferent-sounding permission than てもいい.

Antonyms: te-wa-ikenai — てはいけない forbids the action; てもいい permits it.

Related: nakute-mo-ii — なくてもいい says you don't HAVE to do it; てもいい says you MAY do it.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ても構わない
materials.answer:
it's fine even if ~; I don't mind if ~

〜てもかまわない says that even if X happens, it doesn't bother the speaker — so it grants permission or shows willingness. 高くてもかまわない = I don't mind if it's expensive. 構わない literally means 'don't mind', giving it a softer feel than the blunter てもいい.
materials.reading: てもかまわない
materials.notes:
構わない means 'don't mind', so it reads as gentle permission; てもいい is a more direct 'may / it's okay to'.

The negative なくてもかまわない means 'it's fine even if you don't'.

Synonyms: temo-ii — てもいい is a plainer 'may / it's okay to'; てもかまわない softens it to 'I don't mind if'.

Antonyms: te-wa-ikenai — てはいけない forbids the action; てもかまわない allows it.

Related: temo — ても is the bare 'even if'; てもかまわない adds the judgment that the case is acceptable.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ても〜なくても
materials.answer:
whether ~ or not (the result is the same)

Pairing a positive 〜ても with the matching negative 〜なくても for the same word says the outcome holds either way — 降っても降らなくても = whether it rains or not. You state the two opposite cases and then a result that does not depend on which one is true.
materials.notes:
Both halves use the same predicate in opposite polarity: 行っても行かなくても, not two unrelated verbs.

For nouns and な-adjectives the pattern becomes 〜でも〜でなくても.

Related: temo — ても covers a single 'even if' case; 〜ても〜なくても lines up both cases to say it makes no difference.

Related: temo-kamawanai — てもかまわない grants permission for one case; 〜ても〜なくても says the result is fixed across both cases.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ても差し支えない
materials.answer:
it's fine even if ~; there is no problem with ~; may ~

〜ても差し支えない grants that doing something causes no problem or inconvenience — it is permissible. 写真を撮っても差し支えありません = you may take photos; there's no problem. 差し支え means 'hindrance / obstacle', so the phrase says 'even if ~, there is no hindrance'. It is a formal, polite way of giving permission, more measured than the everyday てもいい.
materials.reading: てもさしつかえない
materials.notes:
Formal, polite permission; in casual situations 〜てもいい is the natural choice.

差し支え means 'hindrance', so 差し支えない = 'poses no problem' — the whole says permission is granted, not that something is required.

Synonyms: temo-ii — 〜てもいい is the everyday 'may / it's okay to ~'; ても差し支えない is a formal, polite equivalent for granting permission.

Synonyms: temo-kamawanai — 〜ても構わない means 'I don't mind if ~'; ても差し支えない frames the same permission as 'causes no problem', slightly more formal.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ても知らない
materials.answer:
don't blame me if ~; I won't be responsible even if ~

〜ても知らない is a warning that the speaker washes their hands of the consequences: 'even if ~ happens, that's not my problem'. そんなに食べたら、お腹を壊しても知らないよ = if you eat that much and get a stomachache, don't blame me. 知らない here means 'I take no responsibility', not 'I don't know'. It typically follows a hypothetical the speaker has advised against, and is casual and admonishing.
materials.reading: てもしらない
materials.notes:
知らない here means 'I won't be responsible', not literally 'I don't know'.

Conversational and admonishing; usually aimed at behavior the speaker has warned against, often ending in 〜よ.

Related: tara-saigo — 〜たら最後 warns that once ~ happens an unavoidable bad result follows; ても知らない warns that the speaker won't take responsibility for such a result.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: てもしょうがない・てもしかたがない
materials.answer:
there's no use ~ing; no point even if you ~

〜てもしょうがない (also てもしかたがない) says that even if you do X, it won't help — expressing resignation or futility. 悔やんでもしょうがない = there's no use regretting it. The も is essential: it frames X as a pointless action.
materials.reading: てもしょうがない・てもしかたがない
materials.notes:
Don't drop the も: てしょうがない (no も) means 'can't help feeling; unbearably', a completely different point.

しょうがない and しかたがない are interchangeable here; しょうがない is the more casual spelling.

Synonyms: temo-hajimaranai — ても始まらない stresses that the action produces no progress; てもしょうがない stresses that it simply can't be helped.

Related: te-shou-ga-nai — Without も, てしょうがない means 'can't help feeling / extremely', not futility — an easy pair to confuse.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜点
materials.answer:

〜点 uses 点 as an abstract 'point/respect' to name the angle from which something is judged — usually as 〜という点で ('in the respect that') or 〜点で(は) ('in terms of'). 値段が安いという点で = in terms of being cheap. It pins down which aspect you're evaluating.

materials.notes:
Common frames: 〜という点で ('in the respect that ~') and 〜点では ('in terms of ~').

Related: to-iu — という labels or names a clause; 〜という点で uses it to single out the specific aspect under discussion.

materials.prompt: ては
materials.answer:
if ~ (a bad result follows); whenever ~

ては joins the て-form with は to set up a condition whose consequence is usually undesirable — 急いでは失敗する = 'if you rush, you'll fail'. It presents the action as a recurring or ongoing cause and leads into a negative outcome. In casual speech it contracts to ちゃ (or じゃ after voiced sounds).
materials.reading: ては
materials.notes:
The result clause is normally negative — a problem, failure, or something the speaker wants to avoid.

In casual speech ては becomes ちゃ and では becomes じゃ (やっては → やっちゃ).

This conditional ては differs from the everyday たら/と: it specifically frames the condition as leading to a bad result.

Synonyms: tara — たら is a neutral 'if / when ~'; ては specifically frames the condition as leading to an unwanted result.

Synonyms: to-conditional — と states a natural or automatic consequence; ては highlights the condition as the cause of something bad.

Related: te-ite-wa — ていては is the ている version, stressing that a continuing action or state brings the bad result.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てはいられない
materials.answer:
can't afford to stay ~; can't just keep ~ing

てはいられない is the negative potential of ている plus は — 'cannot remain in this state'. It says the speaker cannot afford to keep doing something or stay as they are because circumstances demand action — のんびりしてはいられない = 'I can't afford to take it easy'. It conveys urgency or emotional pressure to stop and act.
materials.reading: てはいられない
materials.notes:
It means one cannot stay in the current action or state because something more pressing calls for action.

The driving force is often urgency or emotion — you feel you must not just sit still.

Synonyms: te-bakari-wa-irarenai — てばかりはいられない adds ばかり ('only'), stressing you can't do just that one thing forever; てはいられない is the plain 'can't stay as I am'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: てはならない
materials.answer:
must not ~; may not ~ (formal prohibition)

てはならない follows the て-form to state a firm, often official prohibition — してはならない = 'must not do'. It is more formal and weighty than てはいけない, and is common in rules, laws, morals, and written instructions where a norm applies to everyone rather than to one person in the moment.
materials.reading: てはならない
materials.notes:
It is formal and impersonal, fitting rules, laws, and moral principles more than casual one-to-one prohibitions.

Everyday spoken prohibitions usually take てはいけない or だめ; てはならない sounds official or literary.

Synonyms: te-wa-ikenai — てはいけない is the everyday 'must not'; てはならない is more formal and used for rules and moral norms.

Antonyms: nakereba-naranai — なければならない is the positive obligation 'must do'; てはならない is the prohibition 'must not do'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ては〜ては
materials.answer:
doing ~ and ~ over and over (repeated alternating actions)

Pairing two て-form verbs with は describes a set of actions repeated in alternation — 書いては消し、書いては消し = 'writing and erasing, over and over'. The two verbs are usually opposite or complementary, and the pattern paints a vivid picture of the same cycle happening again and again.
materials.notes:
The two verbs typically form a contrasting or paired cycle (write/erase, come/go), not two unrelated actions.

It emphasizes repetition; the sentence usually continues into a description of the ongoing scene or its effect.

Related: tewa — Single ては sets up a condition with a bad result; the doubled ては〜ては paints repeated, alternating actions.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜と相まって
materials.answer:
combined with; coupled with; in tandem with

〜と相まって marks that one factor works together with another to produce a heightened result — 'combined with ~, coupled with ~'. A が B と相まって means A, together with B, brings something about, and the two factors reinforce each other so the outcome is notably strong. It is formal, written-style language, common in commentary and description.
materials.reading: とあいまって
materials.notes:
The two factors combine to strengthen a single outcome; it is not a plain 'A and B' listing.

Formal written style; 相まって is the て-form of 相まつ and is rarely heard in casual talk.

Related: dake-ni — だけに gives a single reason all the more fitting for its nature; と相まって says two factors act together to amplify a result.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: と
materials.answer:
and (listing nouns)

Joins nouns into a complete list: place と between nouns to connect them, like 'and' in English. It presents the listed items as the full set, implying nothing else is included.
materials.reading: と
materials.notes:
と links nouns only — it cannot join verbs or whole sentences.

と implies a complete list; use や when you want to give just a few examples out of more.

Related: ya — や lists a few representative examples; と lists the items exhaustively.

Related: to-with — The same particle と in its other core use, 'together with' someone.

Related: nado — など ('etc.') marks an open-ended list; と marks a closed, complete one.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜とあれば
materials.answer:
if it is (a case of); if it's for the sake of ~

〜とあれば sets up a special condition and says that, given it, one will readily do something one otherwise might not — 'if it's for ~, then...'. 子供のためとあれば = if it's for the children's sake, 必要とあれば = if it should prove necessary. The main clause usually expresses willing resolve or an inevitable response to that particular circumstance. It is more formal and weighty than a plain なら.
materials.reading: とあれば
materials.notes:
The condition is a special, weighty one that justifies the (often unusual) action that follows; it is stronger and more formal than a plain なら.

The main clause states a willing response or a natural consequence, not a neutral hypothetical.

Synonyms: nara — なら is a general 'if / in that case'; とあれば adds that the condition is special enough to prompt a willing or inevitable response.

Related: to-atte — とあって treats the special situation as an actual fact behind a result; とあれば treats it as a supposed condition prompting resolve.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜とあって
materials.answer:
because (of the special circumstance); given that

〜とあって presents a special or noteworthy circumstance as the reason a fitting consequence follows naturally — 'because it's ~, given that ~'. 連休とあって = it being a long holiday (so naturally...), 人気店とあって = as it's a popular shop. The situation is unusual or newsworthy enough that the result comes as a matter of course. It is common in reportage and in describing others' situations objectively.
materials.reading: とあって
materials.notes:
The reason is a special or notable situation and the result follows naturally; it is not used for ordinary, everyday causes.

It describes others' or general situations objectively; avoid it for stating a personal reason about yourself.

Synonyms: dake-atte — だけあって praises a result as living up to what a quality would lead you to expect; とあって simply gives a special situation as the reason a natural result follows.

Synonyms: koto-tote — こととて offers a reason in a soft, apologetic, literary tone; とあって states a notable circumstance behind an unremarkable-to-expect result.

Related: dake-ni — だけに stresses 'precisely because ~, all the more'; とあって leans on the situation being special or newsworthy.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜とばかりに
materials.answer:
as if to say ~; with a manner that all but says ~

〜とばかりに attaches a quoted thought to someone's behavior: they don't actually speak the words, but their manner or action conveys them — 'as if to say ~'. 帰れとばかりに、彼はドアを指さした = he pointed at the door as if to say 'get out'. It often accompanies a vivid gesture or a decisive move, and captures the attitude the person is broadcasting without words.
materials.reading: とばかりに
materials.notes:
The quoted words are not actually spoken — they render the attitude the person's manner conveys.

Do not confuse it with とばかり思っていた ('I was firmly convinced that ~'), which is unrelated.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: と
materials.answer:
whenever/if A, then B (natural result)

と joins two clauses to say that whenever A happens, B follows automatically. It's for predictable, natural consequences — how machines work, directions, habits, and cause-and-effect that always plays out the same way.
materials.reading: と
materials.notes:
The B clause usually can't be a request, invitation, or your own decision: avoid 〜と、〜てください. Use たら for those.

The part before と stays non-past plain, even about the past or the future: 春になると花が咲く.

This conditional と is separate from the quotative と ('that') and the noun-linking と ('and').

Synonyms: tara — たら is the most flexible 'if/when' and allows requests in the result; と is limited to automatic results.

Synonyms: ba — ば is a general conditional; と stresses that B always follows A.

Related: nara — なら reacts to a topic just raised; と states a repeatable, automatic consequence.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: と同時に
materials.answer:
at the same time as; the moment that; while also being

と同時に joins two things that happen or hold at the same time. With events it means 'the instant one happens, so does the other' — ベルが鳴ると同時に、みんな立ち上がった = the moment the bell rang, everyone stood up. With states it means 'while also being' — 彼は歌手であると同時に俳優でもある = he is a singer and at the same time an actor. It is fairly formal and common in writing.
materials.reading: とどうじに
materials.notes:
It ties two things to the very same moment or holds two qualities at once; it is not a casual 'while' for background action — for that use ながら.

With a noun, insert である: 教師であると同時に, not 教師と同時に.

jlptsensei lists N2

Synonyms: to-tomo-ni — と共に can mean 'together with' as well as 'at the same time'; と同時に focuses squarely on simultaneity.

Related: nagara — ながら is one person doing two things at once as background and foreground; と同時に ties two separate events or states to the same instant.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun ＋ である ＋ と同時に

examples.english: This job is demanding and at the same time very rewarding.

materials.prompt: と言えば
materials.answer:
speaking of ~; if you mention ~

〜といえば takes up a word or topic just raised and offers the association or comment it evokes — 夏といえば花火 = speaking of summer, fireworks. It's the go-to way to say 'now that you mention ~' and bring up a representative example or a related remark.
materials.reading: といえば
materials.notes:
Very close to というと; といえば slightly emphasizes the speaker's own strong association or a typical example.

Keep it apart from から言えば ('from the standpoint of ~'), a different frame.

Synonyms: to-iu-to — というと leans toward asking for clarification; といえば leans toward volunteering an association or example.

Related: sou-ieba — そういえば means 'come to think of it' with no set topic word; といえば hooks onto a specific word just said.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜といえども
materials.answer:
even; even though; although one may say ~

〜といえども concedes a point and then states something that holds despite it — 'even ~, even though it is ~'. プロといえども = even a professional, 子供といえども = even though they're just a child. It grants that the subject is X, yet the following clause runs against the expectation X would create. It is formal, somewhat literary, and often pairs with a sweeping generalization.
materials.reading: といえども
materials.notes:
It concedes 'even (granting that it's) ~' and then states a contrary point; it is more formal and emphatic than ても or とはいえ.

The following clause goes against what the conceded point would lead you to expect.

Synonyms: temo — ても is the everyday 'even if / even though'; といえども says the same with a formal, literary, concessive weight.

Related: monono — ものの concedes an established fact then notes it fell short of expectation; といえども concedes a category ('even a ~') before a contrary rule.

Related: nagara-mo — ながらも marks 'although, despite ~' between two facts of one subject; といえども concedes a generalized case.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜と言えなくもない
materials.answer:
one could even say that; it's not impossible to say ~

〜と言えなくもない is a hedged, doubly-negative way of granting a point — 'you can't say it isn't ~, so in a sense it is'. It offers cautious, partial agreement: 成功と言えなくもない = you could, in a way, call it a success. The speaker admits the description has some validity while staying noncommittal, so it softens an assertion and usually implies reservations.
materials.reading: といえなくもない
materials.notes:
The double negative makes it a weak, reserved 'you could sort of say ~', not a confident assertion.

It concedes partial truth while leaving room for doubt; the speaker is not fully committing.

Synonyms: nai-demo-nai — ないでもない ('it's not that one doesn't ~') is the same reserved double negative applied to actions or feelings; と言えなくもない applies it to a description.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: と言える
materials.answer:
you can say that ~; it can be said that ~

〜と言える presents a conclusion as something reasonably assertible — 成功したと言える = you could say it succeeded. It marks a measured, justified judgment rather than a whim, and is common in analysis. The negative 〜とは言えない means 'you can't really say that'.
materials.reading: といえる
materials.notes:
It frames a reasoned, defensible conclusion, so it fits essays and analysis, not casual venting.

The negative 〜とは言えない ('you can't really say that') is a very common counterpart.

Synonyms: to-ittemo-ii — と言ってもいい permits a slightly bold way of putting it ('you could even say'); と言える states a straightforwardly justified conclusion.

Related: to-kangaerareru — と考えられる frames it as 'is thought/considered'; と言える frames it as 'can be stated'.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: といい・たらいい
materials.answer:
I hope ~; it would be good if ~

〜といい and 〜たらいい express a hope, often about things you can't control: 晴れるといい = I hope it clears up. In advice contexts they also soften a suggestion into 'it would be good if you ~'.
materials.reading: といい・たらいい
materials.notes:
For a hope about someone else, it reads as 'I hope they ~'; the wish stays gentle rather than a demand.

といい／たらいい／ばいい all overlap for wishes; といい and たらいい are the most common for a plain 'I hope ~'.

jlptsensei lists N3

Synonyms: ba-ii — 〜ばいい also voices a wish or suggestion, built on the ば conditional.

Related: tara — たらいい is the たら conditional plus いい; たら on its own just means 'if/when'.

Related: te-hoshii — 〜てほしい directly wants someone to do something; 〜といい softly hopes it happens.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜といい〜といい
materials.answer:
both ~ and ~; whether you look at ~ or ~ (in every respect)

〜といい〜といい picks out two representative aspects of something and comments that, judging by both, an overall evaluation holds — 'both ~ and ~'. 色といいデザインといい = in both color and design, 味といい香りといい = both in taste and aroma. The speaker cites two examples to back a subjective judgment about the whole, and the closing clause is that evaluation, often admiration or criticism.
materials.notes:
It takes two nouns naming aspects or examples and leads to a subjective evaluation of the whole; the final clause is a judgment, not a neutral fact.

Different from 〜も〜も (plain 'both'): といい〜といい frames the two as evidence for an overall impression.

Related: to-iwazu-to-iwazu — といわず〜といわず means 'not just these two but everywhere, without distinction'; といい〜といい lists two aspects to support an overall evaluation.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜といおうか
materials.answer:
how should I put it; or perhaps I should say ~

〜といおうか introduces a description offered tentatively as the speaker reaches for the fitting words — 'what should I call it, or perhaps ~'. It often comes in pairs (〜といおうか〜といおうか) or just before a rephrasing, marking that the chosen word is only approximate. It is a shade more literary and reflective than 〜というか, and conveys genuine hesitation over how to characterize something.
materials.reading: といおうか
materials.notes:
It flags that the word chosen is only an approximation the speaker is reaching for; it is more formal and literary than というか.

It comments on how to describe something, not on whether the thing is true.

Synonyms: to-iu-ka-to-iu-ka — というか〜というか does the same word-searching in an everyday, conversational tone; といおうか is more literary and reflective.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: The sight was solemn, or perhaps I should say mystical — something hard to put into words.
examples.reading: そのこうけいは、そうごんといおうか、しんぴてきといおうか、ことばにしがたいものだった。

examples.english: His decision was reckless, or should I say brave — even now I can't decide which.
examples.reading: かれのけつだんは、むぼうといおうか、それともゆうかんだったのか、いまもはんだんがつかない。

materials.prompt: といった
materials.answer:
(things) such as A and B; like

といった follows two or more representative items and leads into the category they belong to — '(things) such as A and B'. サッカーやテニスといったスポーツ = 'sports such as soccer and tennis'. It presents the listed items as examples of a broader group named right after.
materials.reading: といった
materials.notes:
といった is followed by a summarizing noun (the category); here it is not the past tense of と言う.

Unlike など, which can close a list on its own, といった normally requires the category noun that follows it.

Synonyms: nado — など also lists representative examples ('such as / etc.') but can end a list without a following category noun; といった needs one.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: ずつうやはつねつといったしょうじょうがでたら、すぐびょういんへいってください。

materials.prompt: 〜といったらない・〜ったらない
materials.answer:
extremely; indescribably; ~ beyond words

〜といったらない (casual 〜ったらない) marks a degree so extreme that words fail — 'you can't describe how ~ it is'. うれしいといったらない = indescribably happy, 悔しいったらない = frustrated beyond words. It attaches mainly to adjectives (and some nouns) naming a strong impression and pushes it to the utmost. It is emotive and colloquial, most often about negative feelings but usable for positive extremes too.
materials.reading: といったらない・ったらない
materials.notes:
It pushes a quality to its extreme ('~ beyond description'), not a middling degree.

ったらない is the more casual, spoken contraction; といったらない is the fuller form.

Synonyms: kono-ue-nai — この上ない states 'the utmost, none higher' rather formally; といったらない voices the same extremity with emotive, colloquial force.

Synonyms: kagiri-da — 限りだ intensifies an emotion adjective ('extremely ~'); といったらない adds the nuance that the degree defies description.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: いちにちじゅうならんで、けっきょくかえなかったのだから、なさけないといったらない。

examples.english: The loneliness of that hushed mountain path at night was beyond describing.
examples.reading: しずまりかえったよるのさんどうのこころぼそさといったらなかった。

materials.prompt: と言っても
materials.answer:
although I say ~; even though you'd say ~ (it's actually more modest)

〜と言っても concedes a statement and then immediately scales it back — 料理ができると言っても、卵を焼くくらいだ = although I say I can cook, it's only frying an egg. It heads off an overblown reading of the first part by admitting the reality is more modest.
materials.reading: といっても
materials.notes:
The follow-up tones down whatever expectation the first part raised.

Don't confuse it with fixed phrases like 何といっても ('by all means / after all').

Related: kara-to-itte — からといって rejects a reason ('just because ~ doesn't mean...'); と言っても walks back a claim you just made.

Related: nan-to-itte-mo — 何といっても is a fixed 'after all, above all'; plain と言っても concedes and then qualifies.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Even though I call it close, it still takes a good thirty minutes on foot.
examples.reading: ちかいといっても、あるいてさんじゅうふんはかかる。

materials.prompt: と言ってもいい
materials.answer:
you could say ~; one might say ~

〜と言ってもいい means 'you could say that ~' or 'it's fair to say ~'. It lets you put forward a strong or bold characterization while framing it as one acceptable way to describe something, softening the claim.
materials.reading: といってもいい
materials.notes:
Literally 'even if you say ~, it's fine', so it presents a claim as justifiable rather than as flat fact.

Drop the いい and 〜と言っても becomes concessive ('even though I say ~'), a different meaning.

Related: to-ittemo — 〜と言っても alone is concessive ('even though you say'); adding いい makes it 'you may say'.

Related: to-iu — Both use 言う; と言ってもいい offers a description as acceptable, という attaches a name.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: という
materials.answer:
called ~; named ~

XというY means 'a Y called/named X'. Use it to introduce a name or label the listener may not know: 「はな」という店 = a shop called Hana. Literally it's 'a Y that is said (to be) X'.
materials.reading: という
materials.notes:
Reach for という when the name is new to the listener; a famous name usually doesn't need it.

The name before という takes the quotative と, so keep it: 「さくら」という, not 「さくら」の.

bunpro lists N3

Related: to-quotation — という is built from the quotative と plus 言う.

Related: to-iu-koto — 〜ということ nominalizes a whole statement; 〜という labels a noun.

Related: to-iu-nowa — 〜というのは introduces a term and then explains what it means.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: There was a call from a person named Tanaka.
examples.reading: たなかさんというひとからでんわがありました。

examples.english: My friend has a dog named Pochi.
examples.reading: ともだちは「ポチ」といういぬをかっています。

materials.prompt: というふうに
materials.answer:
in a way like; in such a manner (that)

というふうに describes the manner or way something is done or said — 'in a way like ~ / in such a manner'. It often follows a quoted content or a concrete example to characterize how an action proceeds: まず洗って、次に切る、というふうに… The related こういうふうに／そういうふうに mean 'like this / like that'.
materials.reading: というふうに
materials.notes:
というふうに characterizes the manner of an action; it is more colloquial than the ように of manner but works the same way.

It typically leads into a verb describing how something is done, not into a following noun.

Synonyms: you-ni-you-na — ように also expresses 'in the manner that'; というふうに is more conversational and often follows a quoted example.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: つかったものはもとのばしょにもどす、というふうにしゅうかんづけている。

materials.prompt: 〜というか〜というか
materials.answer:
or rather; I'd say ~, or maybe ~; how should I put it

〜というか〜というか lines up two ways of describing something when neither quite fits, letting the speaker grope toward the right characterization — '~, or should I say ~'. うれしいというか、ほっとしたというか = happy, or rather relieved. It conveys a mixed, hard-to-pin-down impression in a casual, thinking-aloud tone, and the two terms are often near-synonyms or two facets of one feeling.
materials.notes:
It signals that the speaker is searching for the right words and settling fully on neither; it is conversational in tone.

The two labels usually describe one thing from two angles, not two separate items.

Synonyms: to-iou-ka — といおうか searches for wording in a shade more literary, reflective tone; というか〜というか is the everyday, spoken pairing.

Synonyms: to-iu-yori — というより corrects one label to a better one ('rather than A, B'); というか〜というか leaves both labels standing as approximations.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: ［first phrase］＋というか＋［second phrase］＋というか

examples.english: His paintings are original, or maybe bizarre — either way, unforgettable.
examples.reading: かれのえは、どくそうてきというか、きばつというか、とにかくわすれられない。

examples.english: Passing left me happy, or rather in disbelief — a complicated feeling.
examples.reading: ごうかくして、うれしいというか、しんじられないというか、ふくざつなきもちだ。

materials.prompt: ということ
materials.answer:
the fact that ~; that ~ (nominalizer)

ということ turns a whole sentence into a noun meaning 'the fact/matter that ~'. It lets a full statement work as the subject or object of another clause — handy for talking about information, meaning, or what was said.
materials.reading: ということ
materials.notes:
Use ということ to package a whole statement or piece of information; plain こと or の nominalizes a single action instead.

Keep the と: it marks the preceding clause as a quoted idea, giving ということ, not just こと.

Synonyms: koto — plain こと nominalizes an action; ということ wraps a whole statement or fact.

Related: no-nominalizer — の also turns a clause into a noun, but for concrete events rather than reported statements.

Related: to-iu-koto-da — 〜ということだ ends a sentence with 'it means that' or reported 'I hear that'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 彼が来ないということを聞きました。
examples.english: I heard that he isn't coming.
examples.reading: かれがこないということをききました。

examples.japanese: 約束を守るということは大切です。
examples.english: Keeping your promises is important.
examples.reading: やくそくをまもるということはたいせつです。

materials.prompt: ということだ
materials.answer:
it means that ~; I hear that ~; in other words

〜ということだ has two everyday uses: reporting hearsay ('I hear that ~') and drawing or restating a conclusion ('which means that ~'). つまり〜ということだ sums something up; 部長は来ないということだ passes on news. Context tells the two apart.
materials.reading: ということだ
materials.notes:
The hearsay use relays information from a source; the conclusion use rephrases or infers, often after つまり.

Don't confuse it with というものだ, which asserts what something truly is.

Synonyms: souda-hearsay — そうだ only reports hearsay; ということだ also draws or restates conclusions.

Related: to-iu-wake-da — というわけだ presents a conclusion that follows naturally from what was said; ということだ can also just relay hearsay.

Related: to-iu-mono-da — というものだ asserts the true nature of something; ということだ reports or restates.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 部長はあした来られないということだ。
examples.english: I hear the manager can't come tomorrow.
examples.reading: ぶちょうはあしたこられないということだ。

examples.japanese: 返事がないということは、興味がないということだ。
examples.english: No reply means they're not interested.
examples.reading: へんじがないということは、きょうみがないということだ。

materials.prompt: ということは
materials.answer:
which means; that is to say; so that means

ということは takes a known fact or statement and draws the logical conclusion that follows from it — 'which means / so that means'. 電気がついているということは = 'the lights are on, which means...'. It often stands at the head of a sentence as a connector (ということは、〜) to walk the listener through an inference.
materials.reading: ということは
materials.notes:
Distinguish from ということだ, which reports hearsay or restates a definition; ということは draws your own inference from something already known.

The concluding clause usually states a deduction (〜のだろう・はずだ・わけだ), since ということは introduces the reasoning that leads to it.

Synonyms: tsumari — つまり restates the same content more simply ('in other words'); ということは derives a fresh consequence from it.

Related: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ reports what was heard or defines a term; ということは reasons out what a fact implies.

Related: to-iu-wake-da — というわけだ presents the resulting explanation ('that's why'); ということは explicitly walks through the inference to reach it.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Sentence［plain form］＋ ということは

examples.japanese: 電気がついているということは、彼はもう帰っているはずだ。
examples.english: The lights are on, which means he must already be home.
examples.reading: でんきがついているということは、かれはもうかえっているはずだ。

examples.japanese: 明日は祝日か。ということは、銀行は閉まっているね。
examples.english: Tomorrow's a holiday, huh. Which means the banks will be closed.
examples.reading: あしたはしゅくじつか。ということは、ぎんこうはしまっているね。

materials.prompt: 〜というもの
materials.answer:
for (a whole stretch of ~); over the entire period of

When 〜というもの follows a length of time, it stresses that throughout that whole span a state continued — 'for the entire ~, all through ~'. ここ一か月というもの = all through this past month, ここ十年というもの = for these ten years now. It emphasizes how long and unbroken the period felt, usually alongside a description of an ongoing state or feeling, and it attaches to time expressions, often with ここ or この.
materials.reading: というもの
materials.notes:
This use follows a span of time to emphasize its whole unbroken length; it differs from というものだ ('~ is really something' / the nature of ~).

It sets up a continuous state over that period, so the sentence usually describes something lasting, not a one-off event.

Related: to-iu-mono-da — というものだ passes an emphatic 'that's just how ~ is' judgment; というもの after a time span instead stresses the unbroken length of the period.

Related: aida — 間 neutrally marks 'during / while'; というもの adds emotional emphasis on how long that whole stretch dragged on.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: For this whole past month, he has barely spoken a word to me.
examples.reading: ここいちかげつというもの、かれはろくにくちをきいてくれない。

examples.japanese: 事故以来、この数年というもの、彼女は不安と闘い続けてきた。
examples.english: Ever since the accident, all through these past several years, she has kept battling anxiety.
examples.reading: じこいらい、このすうねんというもの、かのじょはふあんとたたかいつづけてきた。

materials.prompt: というものだ
materials.answer:
that really is ~; that's what you call ~ (emphatic assertion)

というものだ makes an emphatic, often evaluative assertion about the true nature of something — 'that really is ~ / that's what you call ~'. 助け合うのが友情というものだ = 'helping each other is what friendship truly is'. The speaker states a general truth or firm judgment, frequently with a reflective or critical tone.
materials.reading: というものだ
materials.notes:
Don't confuse it with the negative というものではない ('it's not necessarily so'); というものだ affirms strongly.

It voices conviction about how something essentially is, not a neutral description of a single event.

Synonyms: mono-da — ものだ states general truths or 'should' advice; というものだ frames a stronger, evaluative assertion about a thing's essential nature.

Antonyms: to-iu-mono-dewa-nai — というものではない is the direct counter — 'it's not necessarily the case that ~'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Helping each other in hard times — that's what true friendship really is.
examples.reading: こまったときにたすけあうのが、ほんとうのゆうじょうというものだ。

examples.japanese: 締め切りを守らないのは、社会人として無責任というものだ。
examples.english: Failing to meet deadlines is, for a working adult, truly irresponsible.
examples.reading: しめきりをまもらないのは、しゃかいじんとしてむせきにんというものだ。

materials.prompt: というものではない・というものでもない
materials.answer:
it's not necessarily the case that; it's not as simple as

というものではない denies that something is absolutely or universally true — 'it's not necessarily the case that ~ / it's not as simple as ~'. It pushes back on an over-generalized assumption, often that doing X automatically brings a good result: お金があれば幸せというものではない. The でもない variant is a slightly softer 'nor is it that'.
materials.reading: というものではない・というものでもない
materials.notes:
It rejects an over-generalization, not the claim entirely; it says 'not always', not 'never'.

Contrast というわけではない, which corrects a specific inferred conclusion; というものではない targets a sweeping 'if X then always Y' assumption.

Synonyms: towa-kagiranai — とは限らない also means 'not necessarily so'; というものではない specifically rejects an 'if X, then always Y' generalization.

Synonyms: kanarazushimo — 必ずしも is the adverb 'not always' that pairs with a negative; というものではない is the full clause-ending pattern expressing it.

Antonyms: to-iu-mono-da — というものだ asserts strongly that something truly is a certain way; というものではない denies it holds absolutely.

Related: to-iu-wake-dewa-nai — というわけではない softly denies a specific inferred conclusion; というものではない denies a general rule.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: あやまればすむというものでもない。

materials.prompt: というのは
materials.answer:
the thing called ~ is; that is to say; the reason is that ~

〜というのは raises a topic to explain it — either defining it ('~ is (defined as)...') or giving the reason behind it ('the reason is that...'). 「敷金」というのは…お金のことです defines a word; 疲れているというのは、忙しいからです explains a cause, often ending in からだ.
materials.reading: というのは
materials.notes:
In the definition use it often ends with 〜ことです／意味です.

In the explanatory use it usually ends with 〜からだ ('the reason is that...').

Synonyms: to-iu-to — というと reacts to a topic or asks for clarification; というのは stops to define or explain it.

Related: to-iu — という names or labels a word; というのは takes that named word as the topic to explain.

Related: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ restates a conclusion or relays hearsay; というのは sets up a definition or reason.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: 'Shikikin' refers to money you pay when renting a room.

examples.english: The reason I've been tired lately is that work is busy.
examples.reading: さいきんつかれているというのは、しごとがいそがしいからです。

materials.prompt: というのは事実だ
materials.answer:
it is a fact that ~; there's no denying that ~

〜というのは事実だ affirms that a stated thing — sometimes surprising or contested — really is true. 努力したというのは事実だ = it's a fact that he made an effort. It often concedes a point before a 'but', acknowledging the truth of X on the way to a qualification.
materials.reading: というのはじじつだ
materials.notes:
It commonly sets up a concession: 'it's a fact that X, but...'.

事実 asserts something as factually true, not as mere hearsay or opinion.

Related: to-iu-nowa — というのは opens a topic to define or explain; というのは事実だ closes by affirming that topic as true.

Related: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ restates or relays; というのは事実だ asserts the stated matter is factual.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: という理由で
materials.answer:
for the reason that ~; on the grounds that ~

〜という理由で presents the stated matter as the given or official reason for something — 体調が悪いという理由で欠席した = missed it on the grounds of feeling unwell. It's more explicit and formal than plain から, and can hint that the reason is merely the stated pretext.
materials.reading: というりゆうで
materials.notes:
It's more formal and explicit than から, naming the reason as 'the grounds'.

Depending on context it can carry a 'under the pretext of ~' undertone.

Related: kara-to-itte — からといって rejects a reason as insufficient ('just because ~ doesn't mean...'); という理由で presents the reason straight.

Related: ni-yotte — によって marks a cause or means broadly; という理由で names a specific stated reason or grounds.

Source references: bunpro

examples.reading: たいちょうがわるいというりゆうで、かれはかいぎをけっせきした。

materials.prompt: という点から考えると
materials.answer:
considering it from the standpoint of; in terms of the point that

という点から考えると frames a judgment from one particular angle or criterion — 'considering it from the standpoint of ~ / when you think about it in terms of ~'. It is formal, essay-style Japanese that names the perspective from which an evaluation is made before delivering it.
materials.reading: というてんからかんがえると
materials.notes:
This is written, formal register; in casual speech から見ると ('from the viewpoint of') sounds more natural.

The 点 names the specific aspect being weighed, so it pairs with a following judgment about that aspect.

Synonyms: kara-miru-to — から見ると is the concise, general 'from the viewpoint of'; という点から考えると explicitly names a stated criterion (点) and is more formal.

Related: ni-totte — にとって marks whose perspective something matters to ('for ~'); という点から考えると names the criterion used to evaluate it.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Noun ＋ という点から考えると
Sentence［plain form］＋ という点から考えると

examples.japanese: 安全という点から考えると、この設計にはまだ問題がある。
examples.english: Considering it from the standpoint of safety, this design still has problems.
examples.reading: あんぜんというてんからかんがえると、このせっけいにはまだもんだいがある。

examples.japanese: 費用がかかるという点から考えると、この計画は現実的ではない。
examples.english: In terms of the point that it is costly, this plan is not realistic.
examples.reading: ひようがかかるというてんからかんがえると、このけいかくはげんじつてきではない。

materials.prompt: と言うと
materials.answer:
speaking of ~; when you say ~ (do you mean...)

〜というと picks up a word or topic just mentioned and either expands on the association it brings to mind ('speaking of ~') or asks the other person to confirm what they meant ('when you say ~, do you mean...?'). 京都というと、古いお寺 = speaking of Kyoto, old temples come to mind.
materials.reading: というと
materials.notes:
It overlaps with と言えば, but というと leans toward an automatic association or a request to clarify.

The 言う here is idiomatic ('when it comes to ~'), not a literal 'say'.

Synonyms: to-ieba — といえば is nearly the same; というと leans toward an automatic link or asking the speaker to clarify.

Related: to-iu-nowa — というのは stops to define or explain the topic; というと reacts to it or seeks confirmation.

Related: sou-ieba — そういえば means 'come to think of it', a looser reminder; というと ties to a topic just named.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.japanese: 京都というと、古いお寺を思い出す。
examples.english: Speaking of Kyoto, old temples come to mind.
examples.reading: きょうとというと、ふるいおてらをおもいだす。

examples.japanese: 「あの人」というと、田中さんのことですか。
examples.english: When you say 'that person', do you mean Tanaka?
examples.reading: 「あのひと」というと、たなかさんのことですか。

materials.prompt: 〜というところだ・〜といったところだ
materials.answer:
at most; roughly; about (no more than)

〜というところだ・といったところだ gives an approximate figure or assessment, usually with the sense 'at most, no more than that' — 'I'd say about ~'. せいぜい五千円といったところだ = five thousand yen at the very most, まずまずといったところだ = so-so, about middling. It attaches to nouns, numbers, or short clauses to sum up a modest estimate or a middling evaluation; といったところ is a touch more idiomatic than というところ.
materials.reading: というところだ・といったところだ
materials.notes:
It typically caps an estimate at a modest upper limit ('at most ~'); it is not used for large or impressive figures.

Often paired with せいぜい or まずまず to underline 'no more than this'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun／Number＋というところだ／といったところだ
Sentence［plain form］＋というところだ／といったところだ

examples.japanese: 客の入りは、多くても三割といったところだろう。
examples.english: The turnout is thirty percent at most, I'd say.
examples.reading: きゃくのいりは、おおくてもさんわりといったところだろう。

examples.japanese: 準備はまずまず、あとは本番を待つだけというところだ。
examples.english: Preparations are so-so; at this point it's just a matter of waiting for the real thing.
examples.reading: じゅんびはまずまず、あとはほんばんをまつだけというところだ。

materials.prompt: 〜というわけだ
materials.answer:
that's why; so that means; it follows that

〜というわけだ presents the current statement as the natural conclusion or restatement that follows from what was just said — 'so that means ~, that's how it is'. It either draws a logical upshot (終電を逃した、というわけだ = so that's why...) or rephrases a situation more plainly, and the listener is expected to see it as the sensible conclusion of the preceding context.
materials.reading: というわけだ
materials.notes:
It marks a conclusion that follows naturally from context; don't confuse it with というわけではない ('it doesn't necessarily mean ~'), which denies such a conclusion.

Different from わけがない ('there's no way'); というわけだ affirms a reasonable upshot.

Synonyms: wake-da — わけだ draws the conclusion directly; というわけだ frames the whole preceding statement as the thing that leads to it, often when restating.

Synonyms: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ can report hearsay or sum up a meaning; というわけだ specifically presents a reasoned upshot of the context.

Related: tsumari — つまり cues a restatement or summary; というわけだ closes the sentence by presenting it as the logical conclusion.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.japanese: 終電を逃したので、歩いて帰るしかなかったというわけだ。
examples.english: I missed the last train, so that's why I had no choice but to walk home.
examples.reading: しゅうでんをのがしたので、あるいてかえるしかなかったというわけだ。

examples.japanese: つまり、この二つの部署が来月から一つになるというわけですね。
examples.english: In other words, these two departments will be merged into one starting next month — that's the idea, right?
examples.reading: つまり、このふたつのぶしょがらいげつからひとつになるというわけですね。

materials.prompt: というわけではない
materials.answer:
it's not that ~; it doesn't mean that ~ (partial denial)

というわけではない softly denies a conclusion the listener might draw — 'it's not that ~ / it doesn't mean that ~'. 嫌いというわけではない = 'it's not that I dislike it (I just...)'. It corrects a likely misunderstanding without denying everything, so it is a hedged, partial negation.
materials.reading: というわけではない
materials.notes:
It negates a specific inferred conclusion, not the whole situation; something else is usually true instead.

Compare というものではない, which denies an over-generalized rule; わけ targets the particular conclusion someone might jump to.

jlptsensei lists N1

Synonyms: wake-dewa-nai — わけではない is the same partial denial without という; adding という foregrounds a stated or implied claim being corrected.

Related: kara-to-itte — からといって ('just because ~') often sets up the assumption that というわけではない then denies.

Related: to-iu-mono-dewa-nai — というものではない denies a general 'X always leads to Y' rule; というわけではない denies one specific conclusion.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Sentence［plain form］＋ というわけではない

examples.japanese: 毎日料理をするが、料理が好きというわけではない。
examples.english: I cook every day, but it's not that I actually like cooking.
examples.reading: まいにちりょうりをするが、りょうりがすきというわけではない。

examples.japanese: 全部読んだが、内容を理解したというわけではない。
examples.english: I read all of it, but that doesn't mean I understood the content.
examples.reading: ぜんぶよんだが、ないようをりかいしたというわけではない。

materials.prompt: というより
materials.answer:
rather than ~; more like B than A

〜というより refines how you describe one thing, saying B is a more accurate label than A — 優しいというより気が弱い = not so much kind as timid. It compares two descriptions of the same thing and is often followed by むしろ ('rather').
materials.reading: というより
materials.notes:
It weighs two descriptions of one thing, not two separate options — that latter job belongs to plain より.

It's often reinforced by むしろ in the second half.

Synonyms: dewa-nakute — ではなくて flatly rejects A for B; というより softens it to 'B is the more fitting way to put it'.

Related: yori — より alone compares two separate things; というより compares two labels for the same thing.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 彼は優しいというより、ただ気が弱いだけだ。
examples.english: He's not so much kind as just timid.
examples.reading: かれはやさしいというより、ただきがよわいだけだ。

examples.japanese: これは趣味というより、もう仕事だね。
examples.english: At this point this is more like work than a hobby.
examples.reading: これはしゅみというより、もうしごとだね。

materials.prompt: と言われている
materials.answer:
it is said that ~

〜と言われている reports what people in general say or believe, with no named source: 'it is said that ~'. The passive 言われる ('is said') plus ている presents the statement as widely held.
materials.reading: といわれている
materials.notes:
It's deliberately source-less — for common knowledge or reputation, not something one person told you (there, use 〜と言っていた).

Its siblings とされている and と考えられている sound more formal or reasoned; 言われている is plain hearsay.

Synonyms: to-sarete-iru — 〜とされている is more official-sounding; 〜と言われている is everyday hearsay.

Related: to-kangaerarete-iru — 〜と考えられている implies a reasoned conclusion; 〜と言われている is just what people say.

Related: souda-hearsay — 〜そうだ also reports hearsay but usually from a specific recent source.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Sentence［plain form］＋ と言われている

examples.japanese: お茶は体にいいと言われている。
examples.english: Green tea is said to be good for your health.
examples.reading: おちゃはからだにいいといわれている。

examples.japanese: この橋は百年以上前に作られたと言われています。
examples.english: This bridge is said to have been built over a hundred years ago.
examples.reading: このはしはひゃくねんいじょうまえにつくられたといわれています。

materials.prompt: 〜といわず〜といわず
materials.answer:
not just ~ or ~; both ~ and ~ and everywhere in between

〜といわず〜といわず names two representative parts and says the statement applies not only to them but comprehensively, without distinction — 'not just ~ or ~ but all over'. 手といわず顔といわず = hands, face, everywhere, 昼といわず夜といわず = day and night alike. The two examples are chosen to imply 'and everything or everywhere else too', stressing that no part is exempt.
materials.notes:
The two nouns are just examples standing for 'and everywhere or everything else too'; it does not mean only those two.

Different from といい〜といい, which lists two aspects to support an evaluation; といわず stresses 'without distinction, all of it'.

Synonyms: nari-nari — なり〜なり offers 'either ~ or ~, whichever you pick'; といわず〜といわず instead sweeps in everything without exception.

Related: to-ii-to-ii — といい〜といい cites two aspects as evidence for an overall judgment; といわず〜といわず means 'all of it, everywhere, without distinction'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 子供たちは、手といわず服といわず、泥だらけになって帰ってきた。
examples.english: The children came home caked in mud — hands, clothes, everywhere.
examples.reading: こどもたちは、てといわずふくといわず、どろだらけになってかえってきた。

examples.japanese: 平日といわず休日といわず、その店の前には行列ができていた。
examples.english: Weekday or weekend, no matter which, there was always a line in front of that shop.
examples.reading: へいじつといわずきゅうじつといわず、そのみせのまえにはぎょうれつができていた。

materials.prompt: と考えられる
materials.answer:
it is thought that; it can be considered that

と考えられる is the passive of 考える, used to present a conclusion as an objective, reasoned inference rather than a personal opinion — 'it is thought / it can be considered that'. It is standard in academic and formal writing, where the passive deliberately avoids naming who holds the view.
materials.reading: とかんがえられる
materials.notes:
It states a reasoned, impersonal conclusion; it is more objective and formal than と思う ('I think').

The passive form intentionally leaves the thinker unnamed, presenting the view as generally accepted.

Synonyms: to-sareru — とされる presents something as an established or officially accepted view; と考えられる frames it as a reasoned inference.

Related: to-omou — と思う voices a personal opinion; と考えられる states an objective, impersonal conclusion via the passive.

materials.prompt: と考えられている
materials.answer:
is considered ~; is thought to be ~

〜と考えられている presents something as what people generally think or have reasoned to be true: 'it is considered / thought that ~'. Common in explanations, science, and news, it marks a conclusion rather than mere gossip.

materials.notes:
More analytical than 〜と言われている: 考えられている implies people reasoned their way to this view.

Formal, written register — you'll meet it in news and academic writing more than everyday chat.

materials.prompt: と聞いた
materials.answer:
I heard that ~

〜と聞いた reports information you got from someone: 'I heard that ~'. The plain statement before と is what you were told, and 聞いた marks it as something you personally heard secondhand.
materials.reading: ときいた
materials.notes:
This is firsthand hearsay — you heard it from a source, unlike source-less 〜と言われている ('people say').

〜と聞いています ('I understand / I've heard') presents the information as your current knowledge.

Synonyms: souda-hearsay — 〜そうだ also relays hearsay; 〜と聞いた stresses that you yourself heard it.

Related: to-iwarete-iru — 〜と言われている is what people in general say; 〜と聞いた is what you were told.

Related: to-omou — Both take a plain-form clause plus と; 聞いた reports hearing, 思う reports thinking.

materials.prompt: 〜ときている
materials.answer:
and on top of that; what's more, it's ~ (so naturally...)

〜ときている adds an emphatic supporting fact, usually one more reason piling onto a situation — 'and what's more it's ~, on top of that ~'. The added fact is presented as a given that clinches the point, often with an air of 'no wonder'. It typically comes after a run of listed merits or faults and sums up why some result is only to be expected. It is colloquial.
materials.reading: ときている
materials.notes:
It piles on an extra, clinching reason ('and on top of that ~'), reinforcing the conclusion; it is not a neutral 'and'.

Colloquial and emphatic; the added point usually explains why a result is only to be expected.

Related: tokitara — ときたら opens a familiar topic for complaint; ときている adds a final reinforcing reason to a build-up.

Related: dake-ni — だけに gives one reason 'all the more fitting'; ときている tacks on an extra reason that clinches an expected result.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: とみえる・とみえて
materials.answer:
it seems that ~ (deduction from evidence)

〜とみえる draws a conclusion from what you can observe: 'it seems that ~, judging by the evidence'. 〜とみえて connects that inference to a following clause that shows the evidence or result.
materials.reading: とみえる・とみえて
materials.notes:
It's deductive — you infer a cause from a visible result — so it feels more reasoned than 〜そうだ ('looks like').

Somewhat literary; in everyday speech 〜らしい or 〜みたいだ are more natural.

jlptsensei lists N3

Synonyms: rashii — 〜らしい also infers from evidence but is more colloquial; 〜とみえる is more deductive and literary.

Related: souda-appearance — 〜そうだ reads an appearance directly; 〜とみえる reasons back to a cause.

Related: you-da — 〜ようだ is a broad 'it seems'; 〜とみえる specifically infers from observed evidence.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜とみると
materials.answer:
upon seeing / judging that ~ (one then acts)

〜とみると marks that, on perceiving or judging a situation, someone promptly acts in response — 'seeing that ~, he ...'. 客が来ないとみると、店を閉めた = judging that no customers were coming, he closed the shop. The subject sizes up the situation and reacts to it. It is a touch calmer than と見るや, which stresses acting at the very instant of perceiving.
materials.reading: とみると
materials.notes:
The subject perceives or judges a situation and then acts on that assessment.

Less abrupt than と見るや, which emphasizes acting the very moment of perceiving.

Synonyms: to-miru-ya — と見るや carries the same core idea but is more literary and stresses the immediacy of the reaction.

Related: ya-ina-ya — や否や means 'the instant ~ happened'; とみると adds that the subject judged a situation and then acted on it.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜と見るや
materials.answer:
the instant one saw / judged that ~

〜と見るや is a literary, dramatic version of とみると: the very instant someone perceives or judges a situation, they immediately act — 'the moment he saw ~, he ...'. 隙ありと見るや、猫は飛びかかった = the instant it spotted an opening, the cat pounced. The や here marks that the action came without a beat's delay, not a question. It suits vivid narration.
materials.reading: とみるや
materials.notes:
Literary and emphatic; stresses that the action followed the very instant of perceiving.

The や marks immediacy here, not an interrogative.

Synonyms: to-miru-to — とみると shares the same core sense but is calmer and less dramatic than と見るや.

Synonyms: ya-ina-ya — や否や also means 'the instant ~'; と見るや specifically pivots on the subject seeing or judging something first.

Related: ga-hayai-ka — が早いか marks two actions almost overlapping in time; と見るや foregrounds the act of perceiving that triggers the response.

Related: nari — なり marks a second action right on the heels of the first; と見るや adds that a judgment of the situation set it off.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: と並んで
materials.answer:
along with; on a par with; ranking alongside; as ... as

Literally 'standing in a row with', Noun ＋ と並んで is mostly used figuratively to rank two things at the same level — この寺は京都と並んで有名だ = this temple is famous, on a par with Kyoto. It presents the two as comparable in standing or reputation. It has a formal, evaluative tone, common when praising or ranking things.
materials.reading: とならんで
materials.notes:
Figuratively it ranks two items as equals in level or fame, not just 'next to' in space.

The thing you rank alongside takes と: 京都と並んで, not 京都に並んで.

Synonyms: to-onaji-kurai — と同じくらい measures two things as roughly equal in a stated degree; と並んで ranks them at the same level of standing.

Related: to-tomo-ni — と共に is 'together with / at the same time'; と並んで places two things side by side as equals in rank.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜となると・〜となれば
materials.answer:
when it comes to ~; if it comes to the point that ~

〜となると・〜となれば marks that once a matter becomes a real or serious prospect, a fitting reaction or consequence follows — 'when it actually comes to ~'. 留学するとなると、費用がかかる = if it comes to studying abroad, it costs money. It attaches to a noun, a plain-form verb, or a whole clause. The nuance is that raising the matter to a concrete stage changes what is required or how one feels about it.
materials.reading: となると・となれば
materials.notes:
Signals that when a matter becomes a genuine prospect, a particular consequence naturally follows.

Distinguish from ともなると, which adds an 'even / as much as' emphasis on a high level or rank.

Synonyms: tomo-naru-to — ともなると・にもなると adds that the level or rank reached is notably high; となると is the neutral 'when it comes to'.

Related: to-ieba — と言えば raises a topic by association ('speaking of ~'); となると focuses on the consequences of a matter becoming real.

materials.prompt: 〜との
materials.answer:
~ that; to the effect that (quote modifying a noun)

〜との links a quoted statement, report, or thought to a following noun of communication — 連絡・報告・知らせ・指示・話・うわさ. It is the noun-modifying counterpart of と／という: 延期になったとの連絡 = word that it had been postponed. Common in news, business, and other formal writing. It packs a whole reported clause into a modifier of the noun that names how the information came.
materials.reading: との
materials.notes:
Used before nouns of communication or thought (連絡, 指示, うわさ...) to attach a reported clause; the formal counterpart of という in that position.

Do not confuse this quotative との with the plain possessive/comitative の.

Synonyms: to-iu — という is the general attributive quote; との is used specifically before nouns of communication in formal reports.

Related: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ reports hearsay as a full predicate ('it is said that'); との folds the same kind of report into a noun modifier.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: と思う
materials.answer:
I think that ~

〜と思う states your opinion, guess, or judgment: 'I think that ~'. The idea before と stays in plain form, and 思う holds your personal view. Add the volitional to get 〜ようと思う ('I intend to').
materials.reading: とおもう
materials.notes:
Keep the clause before と in plain form even when polite: 高いと思います, not 高いですと思います.

と思う is your own current opinion. To report what someone else thinks, use 〜と思っている.

Related: to-quotation — と思う is the quotative と plus 思う.

Related: darou — だろう states a guess directly; と思う frames it explicitly as your opinion.

Related: you-to-omou — 〜ようと思う uses 思う with the volitional to say you intend to do something.

materials.prompt: と同じで・と違って
materials.answer:
like, the same as (と同じで); unlike, different from (と違って)

This pair sets up a comparison as the background to a statement. Noun ＋ と同じで means 'just like ~, (so) ...' — 兄と同じで、私も甘いものが好きだ = like my brother, I love sweets too. Noun ＋ と違って means 'unlike ~, ...' — 去年と違って、今年は涼しい = unlike last year, this year is cool. The first half names what you compare with; the main point comes after.
materials.reading: とおなじで・とちがって
materials.notes:
The compared thing takes と: 兄と違って, not 兄に違って.

と同じで introduces a similarity that leads into your point; when you just want to state 'A and B are the same', use と同じだ at the end instead.

Synonyms: to-onaji-kurai — と同じくらい measures two things as roughly equal in degree; と同じで just flags a likeness to lead into a point.

Related: ni-kurabete — に比べて frames an explicit contrast of amounts; と違って simply says 'not like ~' as a setup for the main clause.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: Unlike last year, this summer is very cool.

materials.prompt: と同じくらい
materials.answer:
about the same as; roughly as ... as

Noun ＋ と同じくらい compares two things and says they are about equal in some quality or amount — 弟は父と同じくらい背が高い = my brother is about as tall as my father. くらい (＝ぐらい) softens it to 'roughly, about the same', not exactly equal. An adjective or amount usually follows to say what they match in.
materials.reading: とおなじくらい
materials.notes:
It means 'about the same', not 'exactly the same'; for a strict equality use と同じ without くらい.

The thing you compare against takes と, not より: 父と同じくらい, not 父より同じくらい.

Synonyms: to-narande — と並んで ranks two things as being on the same level or reputation; と同じくらい measures them as roughly equal in a stated quality.

Related: hodo — AほどBない compares by saying B falls short of A; と同じくらい says two things land at about the same point.

Related: ni-kurabete — に比べて sets up a contrast between two things; と同じくらい stresses that they come out about even.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: と
materials.answer:
quotation marker (~ that; ~ so)

と marks the content of speech or thought and hands it to a reporting verb like 言う (say), 思う (think), or 書く (write). The quoted part stays in plain form, and と links it to what someone said, thought, or wrote.
materials.reading: と
materials.notes:
The clause before と ends in plain form even in polite speech: 来ると言いました, not 来ますと言いました (a direct quote inside 「」 keeps its original politeness).

This quotative と is different from the conditional と ('when/if') and the と that joins nouns ('A and B').

Synonyms: tte — って is the casual spoken version of quotative と.

Related: to-omou — 〜と思う is this quotative と with 思う, marking your opinion.

Related: to-iu — 〜という uses the same と to attach a name or label to a noun.

Related: to-conditional — Conditional と means 'when/if'; don't confuse it with this quotative と.

materials.prompt: 〜とされる
materials.answer:
is regarded as; is held to be; is said to be

〜とされる presents something as what is generally held, established, or officially regarded to be the case — 'is considered ~, is deemed ~'. 健康に良いとされる = is held to be good for one's health, 最古とされる = regarded as the oldest. The judgment is attributed to society, authorities, or general consensus rather than the speaker's own view. It is common in explanatory, academic, and news writing; とされている stresses the ongoing established state.
materials.reading: とされる
materials.notes:
The view is attributed to general consensus, rules, or authority — not offered as the speaker's own fresh opinion.

とされる/とされている reports an established judgment; と言われる leans more toward general hearsay ('people say').

Synonyms: souda-hearsay — そうだ (hearsay) reports 'I hear that ~' from a specific source; とされる presents an established, widely-held judgment.

Related: rareru-passive — The passive れる/られる underlies とされる; on its own it marks who is affected, while とされる specifically frames a view as generally accepted.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: とされている
materials.answer:
is regarded as ~; is deemed ~

〜とされている says that something is officially or generally regarded and treated a certain way: 'is deemed / regarded as ~'. It's the most formal of the reporting siblings and fits rules, customs, and accepted facts.
materials.reading: とされている

After a noun, insert だ: マナー違反だとされている, not マナー違反とされている in most cases.
