materials.prompt: とすれば・としたら・とすると
materials.answer:
assuming that; supposing; if A (is the case), then B

These three attach to a plain-form clause to set up a supposition and draw a logical consequence — 彼の話が本当だとしたら、大変だ = supposing his story is true, that's a serious matter. You assume A for the sake of argument, then state what would follow. とすれば, としたら, and とすると are largely interchangeable; the second clause is usually a judgement, guess, or conclusion.
materials.reading: とすれば・としたら・とすると
materials.notes:
This is a hypothesis for reasoning, so the second clause is typically a judgement or inference, not a request or command.

Don't confuse it with plain たら for 'when': ついたら電話して is temporal, but 本当だとしたら大変だ is 'supposing it's true'.

Synonyms: nara — なら also picks up a supposition to comment on; とすれば・としたら leans more toward reasoning out a logical consequence.

Related: tara — たら often means 'when/after' in time; としたら is purely 'supposing that', for hypothetical reasoning.

Related: to-ieba — と言えば picks up a word to talk about it ('speaking of'); としたら assumes something is so and reasons from it.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: と～と、どちらが
materials.answer:
between A and B, which one?

This pattern asks someone to compare exactly two things and choose: AとBと、どちらが〜？ = 'Between A and B, which is more ~?' The reply typically comes back with 〜のほうが to name the winner.
materials.notes:
Use どちら (casual どっち) for a choice between two items; for three or more, ask with どれ or use 一番.

The second と is often dropped: AとB、どちらが〜 is equally natural.

Related: yori-hou-ga — より〜のほうが is the usual shape of the answer that names the chosen one.

Related: no-naka-de-ichiban — For picking the top of three or more, use 〜の中で一番 instead of a two-way どちら.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Noun［A］＋ と ＋ Noun［B］＋ と、どちらが ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective ＋ か

materials.prompt: と共に
materials.answer:
together with; along with; at the same time as

と共に has two related uses. With a noun it means 'together with' — 家族と共に新年を迎えた = I welcomed the new year together with my family. With a verb of change it means 'as ~ happens, so does ...' — 年を取ると共に体力が落ちる = as you age, your stamina declines. It is a formal, written-flavoured equivalent of 〜と一緒に and 〜につれて.
materials.reading: とともに
materials.notes:
It is stiff and written; in casual speech 〜と一緒に is more natural for 'together with'.

The 'as ~ changes' use needs a verb of change or development (増える, 進む), where two things shift in parallel.

Related: to-douji-ni — と同時に pins two things to the same instant; と共に can be broader 'together with' or a gradual parallel change.

Related: ni-tsurete — につれて is 'as A gradually changes, B changes too'; と共に covers that plus plain 'together with'.

Related: ni-shitagatte — にしたがって also means 'as ~ proceeds'; と共に adds the separate sense of accompaniment ('together with').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: As technology has advanced, our lives have changed along with it.
examples.reading: ぎじゅつがすすむとともに、わたしたちのせいかつもかわってきた。

materials.prompt: と
materials.answer:
with; together with

Marks the person or thing you do something together with: place と after a noun to show a companion or partner in the action. It answers 'with whom?' and often pairs with 一緒に for emphasis.
materials.reading: と
materials.notes:
This と marks a co-participant; it is a different use from the と that lists nouns ('A and B').

For a tool or means ('with a pen'), use で, not と.

Related: issho-ni — 一緒に ('together') often teams up with と to stress doing the action jointly.

Related: to-and — The same particle と in its listing use, 'A and B'.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 途中で・途中に
materials.answer:
on the way; partway; in the middle of (doing something)

途中で marks a point partway through a movement or an action, often where something interrupts it — 家に帰る途中で友達に会った = I met a friend on the way home; 会議の途中で電話が鳴った = the phone rang in the middle of the meeting. After a verb use the dictionary form; after a noun join with の. で is the usual particle, marking where the mid-point event occurs.
materials.reading: とちゅうで・とちゅうに
materials.notes:
After a noun you need の: 会議の途中で, not 会議途中で.

途中で points at a specific mid-point where something happens; うちに and あいだに frame a whole span of time during which you do something.

bunpro lists N2

Related: aida-ni — あいだに frames a whole stretch of time in which you do something; 途中で pinpoints a single moment partway through.

Related: uchi-ni — うちに is 'while a state still holds'; 途中で is 'at a point midway through an action or trip'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: He fell asleep partway through the movie.
examples.reading: えいがのとちゅうで、かれはねてしまった。

materials.prompt: とか(で)
materials.answer:
(I heard) something like ~; and reportedly because ~

とか, and especially とかで, reports something heard in a vague, non-committal way — '(I heard) something like ~'. とかで adds a reported reason: 熱があるとかで休んだ = 'he was off, apparently because he had a fever or something'. The speaker signals the information is secondhand and imprecise.
materials.reading: とかで
materials.notes:
This hearsay/vague とか differs from the listing とか (AとかB, 'things like A and B').

The で adds 'and for that (reported) reason', linking the vague hearsay to a result.

Synonyms: souda-hearsay — そうだ reports hearsay as heard; とかで is vaguer ('something like') and adds a reported reason with で.

Related: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ reports information as a clear conclusion or definition; とかで keeps it deliberately vague and secondhand.

Related: rashii — らしい draws a conjecture from what one has heard; とかで simply relays the vague report as a reason.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: とか～とか
materials.answer:
such as A and B; among other things

とか〜とか lists a couple of examples out of many: 'things like A and B'. It's a casual, non-exhaustive list — you name a few and imply there's more you're not listing.
materials.notes:
Casual in tone; in formal writing prefer や or など.

Non-exhaustive — it means 'among others'. Plain と, by contrast, lists a complete, exact set.

Synonyms: ya — や also lists examples but is more neutral; とか is more casual and can list actions.

Synonyms: nado — など rounds off an example list ('and so on') more formally than とか.

Related: tari-tari — 〜たり〜たり lists example actions with verbs; とか〜とか can list nouns or actions casually.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: とき
materials.answer:
when; at the time of ~

Marks the time or occasion when something happens: place とき after a verb, adjective, or noun phrase to mean 'when ~'. The form and tense of the word before とき shows whether the action is before, during, or after the main event.
materials.reading: とき
materials.notes:
The tense before とき matters: 食べるとき is 'when about to eat', 食べたとき is 'when I had eaten'.

It is often written in kana (とき) in this grammatical 'when' use, rather than as the plain noun 時.

bunpro lists N4

Related: mae-ni — まえに pins the action to just before an event; とき marks the general time it happens.

Related: ato-de — あとで marks 'after'; とき marks the moment 'when' something is the case.

Related: aida — あいだ covers a whole span 'while'; とき points to a particular time or occasion.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ときたら
materials.answer:
when it comes to ~ (with exasperation); as for ~

〜ときたら singles out a topic — usually a person or thing close to the speaker — and leads into a complaint or exasperated remark about it. うちの息子ときたら = as for my son (honestly...), この天気ときたら = this weather, of all things. It sets up the topic with a fed-up, critical attitude, so the following comment is typically negative. It is colloquial and emotive.
materials.reading: ときたら
materials.notes:
The comment that follows is almost always a complaint or criticism; it carries an exasperated tone, not a neutral 'as for'.

The topic is usually someone or something familiar to the speaker; don't use it for distant, respectful reference.

Synonyms: towa — とは reacts with surprise or evaluation to a fact ('to think that ~'); ときたら fixes a familiar topic and grumbles about it.

Related: to-kiteiru — ときている piles on an extra clinching reason; ときたら opens a topic to complain about.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: とっくに
materials.answer:
long ago; already (a long time back)

とっくに is a casual adverb meaning something happened well before now — 'long ago / already (ages ago)'. とっくに終わったよ = 'it finished ages ago'. It stresses that the event lies far in the past relative to the moment being discussed, often with mild surprise the listener didn't already know.
materials.reading: とっくに
materials.notes:
It emphasizes 'already, a long time ago' and is colloquial, so it goes with a completed or past state.

It is stronger and more casual than a plain すでに ('already').

Synonyms: sude-ni — すでに is the neutral, more formal 'already'; とっくに is casual and stresses that it was a long time ago.

Related: mou — もう marks 'already' at or by now; とっくに pushes the timing well back into the past.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: That book? I finished it ages ago.
examples.reading: そのほんならとっくによみおわったよ。

examples.english: She left home long ago and should be heading to the station by now.
examples.reading: かのじょはとっくにいえをでて、えきにむかっているはずだ。

materials.prompt: ところだった
materials.answer:
almost; nearly; was about to (but it didn't actually happen)

Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった describes something that very nearly happened but in the end did not — もう少しで転ぶところだった = I almost fell over. It often comes with もう少しで or 危うく ('nearly, narrowly'). The key point is that the event was avoided; you are relieved or startled that it didn't come to pass.
materials.reading: ところだった
materials.notes:
The action did not actually happen — it was a near miss, not a real event.

Use the dictionary form for 'was about to' (乗り遅れるところだった); the た form + ところ (乗り遅れたところ) means 'had just done it', which is the opposite outcome.

jlptsensei lists N2

Related: kakeru — 〜かける is an action started but left half-done; ところだった is one that nearly started but never actually happened.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった
もう少しで／危うく ＋ Verb［dictionary form］＋ ところだった

materials.prompt: ところで
materials.answer:
by the way; now then (changing the topic)

ところで begins a sentence to switch to a new, often unrelated topic — a spoken 'by the way'. It frequently leads into a question: そうですか。ところで、ご家族はお元気ですか = I see. By the way, is your family well? Use it to move the conversation somewhere new after finishing, or setting aside, the current subject.
materials.reading: ところで
materials.notes:
Don't mix it up with ところが: ところで changes the topic, ところが marks an unexpected result.

It introduces a break from the current topic, so it's usually followed by a fresh remark or a question, not a continuation of the same thread.

Synonyms: sate — さて shifts to the next stage of the same flow ('now then'); ところで jumps to a new, often unrelated topic.

Related: tokoro-ga — Look-alike: ところが means 'however' and reverses an expectation; ところで just changes the subject.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 今日は本当に暑いね。ところで、明日の予定は決まった。
examples.english: It's really hot today. By the way, have you decided on tomorrow's plans?
examples.reading: きょうはほんとうにあついね。ところで、あしたのよていはきまった。

examples.japanese: 報告は以上です。ところで、来週の会議は何時からでしょうか。
examples.english: That's the end of my report. By the way, what time does next week's meeting start?
examples.reading: ほうこくはいじょうです。ところで、らいしゅうのかいぎはなんじからでしょうか。

materials.prompt: ところが
materials.answer:
however; even so; but (contrary to what was expected)

ところが begins a new sentence to introduce a result that runs against what you expected. You set up an expectation, then ところが flips it: 楽しみにしていた。ところが、当日は雨で中止になった = I'd been looking forward to it. But then it rained that day and it got cancelled. The surprise is a fact that happened, not something you planned.
materials.reading: ところが
materials.notes:
What follows ところが is an unexpected fact, not your will or a request: you can't say ところが、行きましょう.

It marks a genuine reversal of expectation; for a plain neutral 'but' between clauses, しかし or が is enough.

Synonyms: shikashi — しかし is a neutral 'however'; ところが specifically marks a result that reverses what you expected.

Related: keredomo — けれども contrasts two clauses within a sentence; ところが starts a fresh sentence with a surprising turn.

Related: tokoro-de — Easy to confuse: ところで changes the topic ('by the way'); ところが marks an unexpected reversal ('however').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I'd thought it would be easy. But when I tried it, it was really hard.

examples.english: He promised he'd come. And yet on the day there wasn't even a word from him.
examples.reading: かれはくるとやくそくした。ところが、とうじつはれんらくさえなかった。

materials.prompt: ところに・ところへ
materials.answer:
just as ~; right when ~ (an event breaks in)

ところに / ところへ marks the precise moment one situation is unfolding when another event breaks in — 'just as ~ / right when ~'. 出かけようとしたところに電話が来た = 'just as I was about to leave, the phone rang'. The second event typically interrupts or coincides with the first.
materials.reading: ところに・ところへ
materials.notes:
It needs an intruding event or arrival, often with に／へ marking the point it comes in; this is not the plain 場所 'place'.

に and へ are largely interchangeable here.

Related: ta-tokoro — たところ marks the point an action has just finished; ところに／ところへ marks a moment interrupted by another event.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［dictionary／ている／た form］＋ ところに／ところへ
い-adjective ＋ ところに／ところへ

materials.prompt: 〜ところを
materials.answer:
although (it is a time/situation when ~); even though you are ~

〜ところを marks a situation or moment and then says that, despite it, something happens — most often in set courtesy phrases thanking or apologizing for imposing at an inconvenient time. お忙しいところを = though you are busy, お休みのところを = though you were resting. It concedes the other person's circumstances before the main action. It can also mark the very moment an action is caught or interrupted (勉強しているところを見られた).
materials.reading: ところを
materials.notes:
In polite formulas it concedes the listener's (often inconvenient) circumstances: お忙しいところを、恐れ入ります.

It also marks the moment an ongoing action is caught or interrupted, with を as the object of that catching (見つかる, 見られる).

Related: tokoro-ni — ところに marks 'right at the moment when ~' as the timing of an arrival or event; ところを concedes a situation ('though it is ~') or marks the object caught in the act.

Related: monono — ものの is a plain 'although ~'; ところを specifically concedes the listener's circumstances in courtesy phrases or frames the moment of an interruption.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ところを見ると
materials.answer:
judging from the fact that ~

ところを見ると draws an inference from an observed fact — 'judging from the fact that ~'. 笑っているところを見ると、うまくいったのだろう = 'judging from the fact that she's smiling, it must have gone well'. The speaker reasons from visible evidence to a likely conclusion, usually ending in a conjecture.
materials.reading: ところをみると
materials.notes:
The clause usually ends in a guess (〜のだろう・らしい・にちがいない), since ところを見ると supplies evidence for an inference rather than a fact.

The evidence is something actually observed, not merely assumed.

Synonyms: kara-miru-to — から見ると can mean 'judging from' too, but also 'from the viewpoint of'; ところを見ると specifically reasons from an observed fact.

Related: kara-shite — からして also reasons 'judging from' a single telling detail; ところを見ると points to an observed scene as the evidence.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Sentence［plain form］＋ ところを見ると

examples.japanese: あの二人がよく話しているところを見ると、仲がいいのだろう。
examples.english: Judging from how those two often talk, they must get along well.

examples.english: Judging from the fact that the lights are off, it seems he's already gone to bed.
examples.reading: でんきがきえているところをみると、かれはもうねたらしい。

materials.prompt: とも
materials.answer:
even if; no matter (how) ~ (formal concession)

In formal, literary Japanese 〜とも expresses concession — 'even if / no matter (how) ~'. It attaches to a verb's volitional form (何が起ころうとも = 'no matter what happens') or an い-adjective's 〜く form (いかに苦しくとも). The outcome holds regardless of the condition.
materials.reading: とも
materials.notes:
This concessive とも is formal and written; ordinary speech uses ても／たとえ〜ても instead.

Don't confuse it with sentence-final とも ('of course') or with 少なくとも／遅くとも ('at the least / at the latest').

Synonyms: temo — ても is the everyday 'even if / even though'; とも is its formal, literary equivalent, attached to the volitional or 〜く form.

Related: tatte — たって is the casual spoken 'even if'; とも sits at the opposite, most formal end of the register scale.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ともあろうものが
materials.answer:
of all people; someone who is supposed to be ~

〜ともあろうものが attaches to a person of standing or a respected role and voices criticism or disbelief that someone in that position acted unworthily — 'for someone who is supposed to be ~ to do that'. 教師ともあろう者が = a person who is supposedly a teacher, of all people. The clause that follows expresses disappointment that their reputation should have prevented the behavior. 者 may also appear as 者が or the ending as ものだ.
materials.reading: ともあろうものが
materials.notes:
Reserved for someone whose position or reputation should have kept them from the behavior.

The following clause voices criticism or disbelief, not neutral description.

Synonyms: toshita-koto-ga — としたことが notes an out-of-character blunder, often one's own; ともあろうものが judges someone by their lofty role.

Related: majiki — まじき labels conduct as unbefitting a role (〜にあるまじき); ともあろうものが names the person and expresses the disbelief directly.

Related: towa — とは voices the bare surprise; ともあろうものが frames that surprise around a person's status.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: いちりゅうきぎょうともあろうものが、こんなずさんなたいおうをするとはおどろきだ。

materials.prompt: 〜ともなく・〜ともなしに
materials.answer:
without particular intention; from no definite ~

〜ともなく・〜ともなしに has two uses. With an action verb it repeats the verb to mean doing it without conscious intent — 見るともなく見る = look without really meaning to, absent-mindedly. With a question word it means 'from/at no definite ~': どこからともなく = from somewhere or other, 誰からともなく = from no one in particular. Despite the ない-like なしに, it is not a plain negative form.
materials.reading: ともなく・ともなしに
materials.notes:
With an action verb the verb is repeated (聞くともなく聞く) to mean 'doing it without meaning to'.

With a question word it means 'from/at no definite ~'; it is not a negation despite the なしに ending.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ともなると・〜にもなると
materials.answer:
once it reaches (as much / as high as) ~

〜ともなると・〜にもなると marks that once a subject reaches a notably high level — rank, age, amount, or occasion — a matching special situation naturally follows. 社長ともなると、責任も大きい = once you're a company president, the responsibility is great too. The 'even / as much as' emphasis on that elevated level is what sets it apart from the plainer となると.
materials.reading: ともなると・にもなると
materials.notes:
Implies the subject has reached a notably high level (rank, age, amount, occasion) at which a fitting consequence follows.

Contrast plain となると, which lacks this 'even / as much as' emphasis on degree.

Synonyms: to-naru-to — となると・となれば is the neutral 'when it comes to', with no emphasis on a high level; ともなると adds that 'as much as' nuance.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: Once you're a professional shogi player, they say you read dozens of moves ahead.

materials.prompt: ともすれば
materials.answer:
apt to; prone to; liable to

ともすれば sets up a tendency to slip easily into a state — usually an undesirable one — under the right conditions. It pairs naturally with 〜がち, 〜やすい, or 〜かねない: ともすれば油断しがちだ = one is apt to grow careless. The variant ともすると has the same meaning. It flags a pull toward a certain (often negative) outcome, not a one-time event.
materials.reading: ともすれば
materials.notes:
Describes a tendency to fall into an often negative state, not a single occurrence.

Frequently paired with 〜がち, 〜やすい, or 〜かねない; the variant ともすると is equivalent.

Synonyms: gachi — がち is the suffix 'tends to ~' on a verb or noun; ともすれば is the adverb that sets up such a tendency, often with がち itself.

Synonyms: kirai-ga-aru — 嫌いがある states that something has a (negative) tendency as a trait; ともすれば frames a liability to slip that way under certain conditions.

Related: yasui — 〜やすい says an action is easy to do or happen; ともすれば adds the sense of a worrying pull toward it.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: ともすれば＋Sentence（〜がち／〜やすい／〜かねない）

examples.japanese: 気を抜くと、ともすれば食生活が乱れがちになる。

examples.reading: きをぬくと、ともすればしょくせいかつがみだれがちになる。

examples.english: The more earnest a person is, the more prone they are to backing themselves into a corner.
examples.reading: まじめなひとほど、ともすればじぶんをおいつめてしまう。

materials.prompt: 〜とも〜とも
materials.answer:
cannot say whether ~ or ~ (neither is affirmed)

〜とも〜とも pairs two opposite possibilities and then denies committing to either, closing with a negative — 言えない, 言わない, つかない, 分からない. 良いとも悪いとも言えない = I can't say whether it's good or bad. The two slots hold contrary options (yes/no, good/bad), and the point is that neither one is settled on.
materials.notes:
Nearly always closes with a negative (言えない・つかない・分からない): neither alternative is affirmed.

The two slots are usually opposite possibilities, not just any two items.

Related: ka-ka — か〜か lists alternatives, one of which holds; とも〜とも＋negative refuses to commit to either.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: とおり(に)
materials.answer:
in the same way as; just as; exactly as

とおり(に) says an action happens exactly the way something else describes or predicts. After a verb it uses the plain form — 私が言ったとおりになった = it turned out just as I said; 書いてあるとおりに作る = make it just as it is written. After a noun, join with の — 地図のとおりに行く = go exactly as the map shows. The に is often dropped with no change in meaning.
materials.reading: とおりに
materials.notes:
After a noun you need の: 地図のとおり, not 地図とおり.

Use the た form for something already done or said you are matching (言ったとおり), and the dictionary form for an instruction to follow now (言うとおり).

Related: mama — まま keeps a state unchanged while you do something else; とおり(に) matches an action to a model or instruction.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Please assemble it exactly as written in the instructions.
examples.reading: せつめいしょにかいてあるとおりに、くみたててください。

materials.prompt: 通す
materials.answer:
to do (an action) all the way through to the end; to carry on doing without stopping

As an auxiliary, Verb［stem］＋ 通す says you carry an action right through to the finish, often sticking with it despite difficulty — やり通す = see it through, 言い通す = keep insisting to the end. It conjugates like a normal う-verb (通した, 通して). The nuance is persistence: you hold to the action from start to finish.
materials.reading: とおす
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 守り通す, not 守る通す.

〜通す stresses keeping something up all the way through, often against resistance; 〜切る simply means finishing a set amount off (食べ切る = eat it all up).

Synonyms: nuku — 〜抜く also means carrying through to the end, but highlights getting there despite hardship; 〜通す highlights staying consistent the whole way.

Related: kiru — 〜切る is finishing a quantity off completely; 〜通す is keeping one action going right to the end.

Related: tsuzukeru — 〜続ける just keeps an action going; 〜通す adds the sense of sticking with it all the way to completion.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: It was tough, but I ran the whole way through to the end.
examples.reading: くるしかったが、さいごまではしりとおした。

examples.english: He kept insisting all along that he hadn't done it.

materials.prompt: とりわけ
materials.answer:
especially; above all; in particular

とりわけ singles out one item as exceptional among a group that already shares some quality — 'above all, in particular'. 今年の夏はとりわけ暑い = this summer is especially hot. It is a touch more emphatic and formal than 特に, and can attach to a whole clause or directly qualify an adjective. Use it to pull one case out of many as standing head and shoulders above the rest.
materials.reading: とりわけ
materials.notes:
Picks out one item as exceptional within a group that already shares the quality ('~ in particular').

A little more emphatic and formal in tone than 特に.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜としたことが
materials.answer:
of all people, ~ (an out-of-character blunder)

〜としたことが expresses dismay that a normally reliable person did something so unlike them. It attaches to a person (very often 私), and the clause that follows admits an uncharacteristic mistake or lapse: 私としたことが、うっかりしていた = of all people, I was being careless. The tone is self-reproach or gentle astonishment that someone who should have known better slipped up.
materials.reading: としたことが
materials.notes:
The following clause admits an out-of-character mistake, not a routine one; the point is that this person of all people slipped up.

Most natural about oneself with 私; the が marks the subject, and the blunder is stated in the clause that follows.

Synonyms: tomo-arou-mono-ga — ともあろうものが criticizes someone by their lofty role or title; としたことが centers on behavior that is out of character, often one's own.

Related: towa — とは voices bare surprise that a fact is even true; としたことが adds that the person responsible should have known better.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Noun［person, usually 私］＋としたことが

examples.japanese: 私としたことが、初歩的なミスを見逃してしまった。
examples.english: I of all people overlooked such an elementary mistake.
examples.reading: わたしとしたことが、しょほてきなミスをみのがしてしまった。

examples.english: For a veteran like him to trip over such a simple problem — how unlike him.
examples.reading: ベテランのかれとしたことが、こんなたんじゅんなもんだいでつまずくとは。

materials.prompt: として
materials.answer:
as; in the role of; in the capacity of

Noun ＋ として names the role, position, or capacity in which someone or something acts — 医者として働く = work as a doctor; お礼として渡す = give it as a token of thanks. It labels the standpoint from which the action is done, so the noun before it is a role, status, or purpose rather than a person's viewpoint.
materials.reading: として
materials.notes:
として marks the role something serves in (代表として = as a representative); にとって marks whose viewpoint you judge from (私にとって = for me) — don't swap them.

For 'as a rule / in principle' senses, として combines into set phrases like 原則として; the core idea is still 'in the capacity of'.

Related: ni-totte — にとって gives the standpoint from which you evaluate ('for ~'); として gives the role in which one acts ('as ~').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: として〜ない
materials.answer:
not even a single one; none at all

With a 'one + counter' phrase, 〜として〜ない expresses total negation — 'not even a single one'. 一人として反対しなかった = 'not a single person objected'. The として emphasizes that the negation covers every last member without exception.
materials.notes:
This として needs a 'one + counter' phrase before it and a negative predicate after; it is not the として meaning 'as / in the role of'.

The result is emphatic 'none at all', stronger than a plain negative.

Related: toshite — として on its own means 'as / in the role of'; in 〜として〜ない it instead intensifies a total negation after a 'one + counter' phrase.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: としては
materials.answer:
as (a) ~; for a ~; speaking as ~

としては sets a standpoint or standard for judgment — 'as (a) ~ / for a ~ / speaking as ~'. 新人としてはよくやっている = 'for a newcomer, she's doing well'; 私としては反対だ = 'as for me, I'm against it'. It frames a judgment against the norm for that role or from that person's position.
materials.reading: としては
materials.notes:
Compare にしては ('for ~, contrary to expectation'), which stresses a mismatch with the standard; としては just states the standard or standpoint without implying surprise.

With a person it often means 'speaking for ~ / from ~'s position', not a comparison.

Synonyms: toshite — として states a role or capacity plainly; としては adds は to foreground that role as the standard or standpoint for what follows.

Related: ni-shite-wa — にしては means 'for ~' with a note of surprise at not matching the norm; としては states the norm or standpoint without that mismatch.

Related: ni-totte — にとって marks whose interest something concerns ('for ~'); としては sets a standard or position from which a judgment is made.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: としても
materials.answer:
even if; even assuming that ~

としても supposes a case and concedes that it does not change the outcome — 'even if / even assuming that ~'. 本当だとしても驚かない = 'even if it's true, I won't be surprised'. It combines a hypothetical (とする) with the concessive も.
materials.reading: としても
materials.notes:
としても supposes something hypothetically ('even if we assume'), whereas ても can also concede an actual fact; としても leans clearly on a supposition.

After a noun or な-adjective, insert だ: 本当だとしても, not 本当としても.

Synonyms: temo — ても concedes 'even if / even though', including actual facts; としても adds the sense of supposing a hypothetical case.

Related: to-sureba-to-shitara — とすれば・としたら supposes a case and reasons forward from it; としても supposes a case but concedes it changes nothing.

Related: tatte — たって is the casual spoken 'even if'; としても is the more composed 'even assuming that ~'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: とっさに
materials.answer:
instantly; reflexively; on the spur of the moment

とっさに describes an instinctive reaction made in a split second, before there is time to think — typically in response to something sudden. とっさに身をかわす = dodge reflexively, とっさに手が出る = one's hand shoots out on reflex. The emphasis is that the action was unplanned and immediate. The noun form とっさの also appears, as in とっさの判断 (a split-second decision).
materials.reading: とっさに
materials.notes:
This is an instinctive, unplanned reaction to something sudden, not merely an action you chose to do quickly.

Often paired with emergencies or surprises; the noun-modifying form is とっさの＋Noun (とっさの判断).

Related: tsui — つい is doing something you shouldn't without thinking (often a habit); とっさに is reacting instantly to something sudden.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜とて
materials.answer:
even ~; even if ~ (literary)

〜とて is a literary particle with two related senses. After a noun it means 'even ~', singling out a case you might think exempt: 子供とて許されない = even a child is not excused. After a verb it means 'even if / even though', usually with a futile or negative outcome: 悔やんだとて、もう遅い = even if you regret it, it's too late now. It belongs to formal or written Japanese; in speech でも or ても does the same work.
materials.reading: とて
materials.notes:
Literary; in everyday speech use でも or ても instead.

In the 'even if' sense the result is typically negative or futile: 〜とて〜ない.

Synonyms: temo — ても is the everyday 'even if / even though'; とて is its literary, formal-writing equivalent.

Related: de-are — であれ・であろうと concedes across alternatives ('whatever it be'); とて concedes a single case as 'even ~ / even if ~'.

Related: tatte — たって is the casual spoken 'even if'; とて sits at the opposite, literary end of the register scale.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: とても
materials.answer:
very; extremely

Intensifies an adjective or adverb: put とても before it to say 'very'. It is a neutral, everyday booster that works in both polite and casual speech, and it is one of the first intensifiers a learner uses.
materials.reading: とても
materials.notes:
Place it before the word it strengthens, never after — とても おいしい, not おいしい とても.

With a negative verb, とても can mean 'cannot possibly', but the plain 'very' use is by far the most common at this level.

Related: amari — あまり pairs with a negative to mean 'not very'; とても boosts toward 'very'.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: とても〜ない
materials.answer:
cannot possibly; by no means; there's no way (one could)

When とても is followed by a negative — usually a potential negative — it stops meaning 'very' and instead means 'cannot possibly'. この量は一日ではとても終わらない = there's no way this amount finishes in a day; そんな高い車はとても買えない = I couldn't possibly buy such an expensive car. It stresses that something is far beyond one's ability or reach.
materials.notes:
Here とても means '(not) possibly', the opposite of its everyday 'very'; the clue is the negative predicate that follows.

It needs a negative ending — usually a potential negative like 買えない, 終わらない — not an affirmative one.

Synonyms: nakanaka — なかなか〜ない is 'just won't happen easily'; とても〜ない is a flat 'cannot possibly, it's out of reach'.

Related: doushitemo — どうしても〜ない is 'can't, however hard I try'; とても〜ない is 'can't possibly, it's beyond reach'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: とても ＋ Verb［ない form］［usually a potential negative］

examples.english: There's no way this much homework will get finished.
examples.reading: こんなにたくさんのしゅくだいは、とてもおわらない。

materials.prompt: 〜とは
materials.answer:
to think that ~!; the very idea that ~

In its emotive use, 〜とは reacts with surprise, shock, admiration, or dismay to a fact — 'to think that ~!'. まさか彼が犯人だったとは = to think he was the culprit. The sentence often trails off after とは, leaving the reaction (驚いた, 情けない...) unspoken. It is a little more formal or written than the colloquial なんて. Separately, とは also serves as a defining marker ('X とは Y' = X means Y).
materials.reading: とは
materials.notes:
In the emotive use the sentence often breaks off after とは (…とは！／…とは思わなかった), the reaction left unsaid.

Keep this surprise とは separate from the defining とは, which explains what a term means ('X means Y').

Synonyms: nanka-nante — なんて is the colloquial 'to think that ~!'; とは carries a slightly more formal, written tone.

Related: koto-ka — ことか exclaims over a degree ('how very ~!'); とは reacts with surprise that a fact is even the case.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: あのまじめなかれがかいしゃをやめるとは、おどろきだ。

materials.prompt: 〜とはいえ
materials.answer:
that said; even so; nonetheless

〜とはいえ concedes a point and then states something that runs contrary to what that point would lead you to expect — 'even though ~, still ...'. It is more formal and written than とはいうものの, and can either join clauses or open a sentence as 'Nonetheless, ...'. 便利とはいえ、頼りすぎは良くない = convenient though it is, relying on it too much is bad. The main clause qualifies or resists the conceded premise.
materials.reading: とはいえ
materials.notes:
More formal and written than とはいうものの; fine at the head of a sentence ('Nonetheless, ...').

The main clause presents something contrary to what the conceded part would suggest.

Synonyms: towa-iu-mono-no — とはいうものの is nearly identical in meaning, slightly softer and more conversational.

Related: monono — ものの concedes within a single sentence ('although'); とはいえ can stand alone as a sentence-opening 'nonetheless'.

Related: nagara-mo — ながらも concedes about one subject's own action or state ('even while ~ing'); とはいえ concedes a whole statement.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 規則とはいえ、これほど厳しいと従業員の不満も大きい。
examples.english: Rules or not, when they're this strict the employees' discontent runs high.

examples.english: I got a job offer. Even so, there's still a lot to prepare before I start.
examples.reading: ないていをもらった。とはいえ、にゅうしゃまでにはまだじゅんびすべきことがおおい。

materials.prompt: とは言うものの
materials.answer:
having said that; that said; nevertheless

とはいうものの concedes what was just stated and then presents a reality that runs against the expectation it creates — 'having said that, ...'. 春とはいうものの、まだ寒い = it may be spring, but it's still cold. It can join clauses within a sentence or open a new one after a full stop. The contrast clause describes an actual situation, not a hypothetical one.
materials.reading: とはいうものの
materials.notes:
Concedes the previous statement, then states a fact that cuts against the expectation it raises.

The contrasting clause is a real situation, not a supposition.

Synonyms: towa-ie — とはいえ carries the same 'that said' meaning in a more compact, formal shape.

Synonyms: monono — ものの joins a concession and its counter within one sentence ('although'); とはいうものの more often stands as its own connective clause.

Related: to-ittemo — と言っても downplays or qualifies a preceding claim; とはいうものの fully concedes it, then contrasts.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: I'm supposedly on a diet, but I can hardly resist the lure of sweets.
examples.reading: ダイエットちゅうだとはいうものの、あまいもののゆうわくにはなかなかかてない。

examples.reading: きゅうりょうはあがった。とはいうものの、ぶっかもあがったのでせいかつはらくにならない。

materials.prompt: とは限らない
materials.answer:
not necessarily; it isn't always the case that ~

Sentence［plain form］＋ とは限らない pushes back on a general assumption, saying it doesn't always hold — 高いものが必ずいいとは限らない = expensive things aren't necessarily good. It admits the idea is often true while denying that it's always true. It pairs naturally with 必ずしも ('not always') earlier in the sentence.
materials.reading: とはかぎらない
materials.notes:
It means 'not always', not 'never': it allows exceptions rather than denying the idea outright.

It often teams up with 必ずしも for emphasis: 必ずしも〜とは限らない.

Related: kanarazushimo — 必ずしも is the adverb 'not always' that often sets up this pattern; とは限らない is the ending that denies a blanket rule.

Related: wake-dewa-nai — わけではない denies a conclusion drawn from the situation; とは限らない denies that a general rule always holds.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Sentence［plain form］＋ とは限らない

examples.japanese: 高いものが、必ずしもいいとは限らない。
examples.english: Expensive things aren't necessarily good.
examples.reading: たかいものが、かならずしもいいとはかぎらない。

examples.japanese: たくさん練習したからといって、試合に勝てるとは限らない。
examples.english: Practicing a lot doesn't necessarily mean you'll win the match.
examples.reading: たくさんれんしゅうしたからといって、しあいにかてるとはかぎらない。

materials.prompt: 〜とは比べものにならない
materials.answer:
no comparison with ~; in a different league from ~

〜とは比べものにならない states that the gap between two things is so wide they cannot be measured on the same scale — 'no comparison with ~'. 昔のとは比べものにならないほど速い = incomparably faster than the old one. Context tells you which side comes out ahead. It often appears as 〜とは比べものにならないほど＋adjective to stress just how far apart they are.
materials.reading: とはくらべものにならない
materials.notes:
Says the gap is too great to compare, not merely that one is somewhat more than the other.

Context, not the phrase itself, tells you which side is superior; often 〜ほど＋adjective follows.

Related: ni-kurabete — に比べて makes a plain 'compared with ~'; とは比べものにならない says the two are too far apart to compare at all.

Related: niwa-oyobanai — には及ばない says one side clearly falls short of the other; 比べものにならない stresses that the gap itself is beyond comparison.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun＋とは比べものにならない

examples.japanese: 今の医療技術は、百年前とは比べものにならないほど進歩している。
examples.english: Today's medical technology has advanced beyond any comparison with a century ago.

examples.english: This camera's image quality is in a different league from a phone's.
examples.reading: このカメラのがしつは、スマホのものとはくらべものにならない。

materials.prompt: 〜とは打って変わって
materials.answer:
in total contrast to ~; utterly unlike ~

打って変わる means 'to change completely', so 〜とは打って変わって marks a striking, wholesale reversal from a previous state or from the thing named — 'in total contrast to ~'. 昨日とは打って変わって、今日は晴天だ = in complete contrast to yesterday, today is clear. It stresses that the change is dramatic and often surprising, usually within the same subject over time rather than a gradual shift.
materials.reading: とはうってかわって
materials.notes:
Highlights a complete, often surprising reversal from a prior state, not a gradual change.

Typically contrasts the same subject before and after, rather than two unrelated things.

Related: ni-hikikae — に引き換え contrasts two different things, often with a judgmental edge; とは打って変わって stresses one subject's dramatic change from a former state.

Related: ni-hanshite — に反して means 'contrary to (an expectation or standard)'; とは打って変わって points to a complete change from how things were before.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Noun［prior state, e.g. 昨日／普段］＋とは打って変わって

examples.japanese: 午前中の混雑とは打って変わって、午後の店内は閑散としていた。
examples.english: In total contrast to the morning crowds, the shop was deserted in the afternoon.
examples.reading: ごぜんちゅうのこんざつとはうってかわって、ごごのてんないはかんさんとしていた。

examples.japanese: 彼女は面接では、普段とは打って変わって、はきはきと話した。
examples.english: In the interview she spoke crisply, utterly unlike her usual self.
examples.reading: かのじょはめんせつでは、ふだんとはうってかわって、はきはきとはなした。

materials.prompt: 〜つ〜つ
materials.answer:
now ~ now ~; alternately doing one thing and its opposite

A literary pattern that joins two verb stems (連用形) each with つ, describing two actions that alternate or play off one another — typically a pair of opposites. 行きつ戻りつ = pacing back and forth, 追いつ追われつ = chasing and being chased by turns. It survives mainly in set expressions, often pairing one active verb with its passive form. The tone is descriptive and literary, not everyday speech.
materials.notes:
Mostly limited to fixed pairs (行きつ戻りつ, 浮きつ沈みつ, 追いつ追われつ); it is not freely productive with any two verbs.

The two verbs are usually opposites, and often one is the active and the other the passive form of the same verb.

Synonyms: tari-tari — 〜たり〜たり is the everyday way to list alternating or representative actions; つ〜つ is a frozen literary form confined to set opposite-verb pairs.

Related: tsutsu — つつ ('while / although') marks one action accompanying another and is fully productive; the doubled つ〜つ is a separate fixed pattern for two alternating actions.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: つい
materials.answer:
without meaning to; end up doing despite oneself

つい marks doing something you didn't really mean to do — you slip and do it despite knowing better, often out of habit or weak willpower. It very frequently pairs with 〜てしまう, which underlines the unintended result. Typical of everyday confessions like eating sweets or staying up too late.
materials.reading: つい
materials.notes:
つい is about slipping into an unintended action; don't confuse it with ついに (finally, at last).

It commonly teams up with 〜てしまう to stress that the result was unintended: つい食べてしまった.

Related: tsui-ni — Sounds close but ついに means 'finally, at last'; つい means 'without meaning to.'

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: ダイエット中なのに、つい甘いものを食べてしまった。
examples.english: Even though I'm on a diet, I ended up eating something sweet without meaning to.

examples.english: It was so interesting that I ended up reading late into the night before I knew it.
examples.reading: おもしろくて、ついよるおそくまでほんをよんでしまった。

materials.prompt: ついに
materials.answer:
finally; at last; in the end

ついに marks the arrival of something long awaited or long building — after much time or effort, it finally comes to pass. With a negative it means something never happened in the end (ついに来なかった = never showed up in the end). It often carries a note of emotion or significance.
materials.reading: ついに
materials.notes:
Don't confuse it with the similar-looking つい (without meaning to): ついに = finally, つい = accidentally.

With a negative it means 'never ~ in the end': ついに分からなかった = in the end I never figured it out.

Related: tsui — Sounds close but つい means 'without meaning to'; ついに means 'finally, at last.'

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: The new game I'd been waiting for has finally gone on sale.
examples.reading: まっていたあたらしいゲームが、ついにはつばいされた。

materials.prompt: ついでに
materials.answer:
while you're at it; on the same occasion; on the way

ついでに marks doing a second thing while you're already doing the first — you take advantage of one occasion to get another errand done at little extra effort. It attaches to a verb (dictionary or た form) or to a noun with の. The main action comes first; the ついでに action is the bonus.
materials.reading: ついでに
materials.notes:
The primary action is stated first; the ついでに part is the extra, secondary thing done 'while you're at it.'

Attach it to a noun with の: 散歩のついでに, not 散歩ついでに.

Related: nagara — ながら is doing two actions at the same moment; ついでに is one occasion used to also handle a secondary errand.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: さんぽのついでに、パンをかってかえった。

materials.prompt: 〜尽くす
materials.answer:
to do (something) thoroughly / to the very end; to exhaust; to use up completely

Verb stem + 尽くす says the action is carried out completely, to the limit, leaving nothing over — either using something up (使い尽くす = use up entirely, 食べ尽くす = eat it all) or doing something exhaustively (知り尽くす = know inside out, 語り尽くす = talk through completely). It stresses that the action has been taken as far as it can go. The intransitive counterpart 尽きる ('run out') is a separate verb.
materials.reading: つくす
materials.notes:
尽くす is transitive ('do fully / use up'); the paired intransitive 尽きる means '(something) runs out' — 力を出し尽くす vs 力が尽きる.

It stresses thoroughness and exhaustion, unlike 〜切る, which often stresses seeing an action decisively through to the end.

Synonyms: kiru — 〜切る marks carrying an action decisively through to completion (走り切る); 尽くす emphasizes doing it exhaustively or using it up to the last.

Synonyms: nuku — 〜抜く stresses pushing an action through to the end despite hardship; 尽くす stresses thoroughness and leaving nothing undone.

Related: toosu — 〜通す means keeping an action up all the way through; 尽くす means carrying it out to its fullest extent.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: When it comes to this town, I know every last corner of its back alleys.
examples.reading: このまちのことなら、ろじのすみずみまでしりつくしている。

materials.prompt: つまり
materials.answer:
in other words; that is to say; in short

つまり introduces a restatement or summary of what was just said — you rephrase it more simply or boil it down to its point. 'In other words / that is to say / in short.' It links a fuller explanation to a tighter conclusion drawn from it.
materials.reading: つまり
materials.notes:
つまり restates or sums up the same content; it doesn't introduce a new result the way だから or それで does.

Synonyms: sunawachi — すなわち is a more formal, precise 'namely'; つまり is the everyday 'in other words.'

Related: to-iu-koto — ということだ often closes a つまり restatement, summing up 'it means that ~.'

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: My father's older sister — in other words, my aunt — came to visit.

examples.english: He didn't reply. In other words, he isn't interested.
examples.reading: かれはへんじをくれなかった。つまり、きょうみがないということだ。

materials.prompt: つもりだ
materials.answer:
intend to; plan to ~

States a firm intention you have already decided on: attach つもりだ to a verb's dictionary form for "I intend to ~", or to the ない form for "I intend not to ~". It conveys a settled personal plan rather than a vague wish.
materials.reading: つもりだ
materials.notes:
つもりだ is stronger and more decided than 〜ようと思う ("I'm thinking of doing").

It describes your own intention, not a fixed schedule; for scheduled events use 予定だ.

Synonyms: you-to-omou — 〜ようと思う is a softer "I'm thinking of doing"; つもりだ is a firmer, settled intention.

Related: yotei-da — 予定だ states a fixed schedule or arrangement; つもりだ states your personal intention.

Related: tai — たい expresses desire ("want to"); つもりだ expresses a decided plan ("intend to").

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 夏休みに国へ帰るつもりです。
examples.english: I intend to go back to my home country during summer vacation.
examples.reading: なつやすみにくにへかえるつもりです。

examples.japanese: 今日は何も買わないつもりです。

examples.reading: きょうはなにもかわないつもりです。

materials.prompt: つもりだった
materials.answer:
had intended to (but didn't); thought I had done

つもりだった is つもり (intention) in the past — you had meant to do something, usually with the implication that it didn't turn out that way. In the 〜たつもりだった pattern it means you were under the impression you'd already done something when in fact you hadn't.
materials.reading: つもりだった
materials.notes:
It often implies the intention went unfulfilled: 早く帰るつもりだった = I meant to leave early (but didn't).

〜たつもりだった = 'I thought I had done it' — a mistaken belief: 送ったつもりだった = I was sure I'd sent it.

Related: tsumori — つもりだ states a present intention; つもりだった puts it in the past, often hinting it fell through.

Related: hazu-da — はずだ is an expectation based on reasoning; つもりだった is your own past intention or belief.

Source references: jlptsensei

Verb［た form］＋ つもりだった

materials.prompt: つもりで
materials.answer:
with the intention of; with the mindset that; as if

つもりで sets the mindset or assumption you act under — you carry out the main action 'with the intention of' or 'as if' something were the case. 手伝うつもりで来た = I came intending to help; 死んだつもりで頑張る = give it your all as if your life depended on it. It leads into a following action rather than ending the sentence.
materials.reading: つもりで
materials.notes:
つもりで colors the attitude behind the next action; it isn't a sentence-ender like つもりだ.

With 〜たつもりで it means 'acting as if you had ~': 貯金したつもりで = as though you'd saved that money.

bunpro lists N2

Related: tsumori — つもりだ ends a sentence stating an intention; つもりで leads into the action done under that intention.

Related: tsumori-datta — つもりだった is a past intention, often unfulfilled; つもりで is the mindset you act under right now.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜つつ・〜つつも
materials.answer:
while doing ~; even though ~ (concessive つつも)

つつ attaches to the ます-stem and has two uses. Plain つつ means 'while doing ~', marking two actions the same person does at once (a formal, written equivalent of ながら). つつも adds a concessive twist — 'even though / despite ~' — where the two clauses clash, as in 悪いと知りつつも = 'even though I know it's wrong'. Both belong to a literary, formal register.
materials.reading: つつ・つつも
materials.notes:
Attach it to the ます-stem: 考えつつ, not 考えるつつ.

Both clauses must share the same subject, just like ながら.

つつ is formal and mostly written; in everyday speech ながら is the natural choice.

Synonyms: nagara — ながら is the everyday word for doing two things at once; つつ is its formal, written counterpart.

Synonyms: nagara-mo — ながらも matches the concessive つつも ('even though'); ながらも is somewhat less literary.

Related: tsutsu-aru — つつある uses the same つつ but means 'in the process of ~', describing gradual change, not two simultaneous actions.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 資料を確認しつつ、会議の準備を進めた。
examples.english: I moved ahead with preparing for the meeting while checking the materials.
examples.reading: しりょうをかくにんしつつ、かいぎのじゅんびをすすめた。

examples.japanese: 体に悪いと知りつつも、つい甘い物を食べてしまう。
examples.english: Even though I know it's bad for my health, I can't help eating sweets.
examples.reading: からだにわるいとしりつつも、ついあまいものをたべてしまう。

materials.prompt: つつある
materials.answer:
to be in the process of ~; to be gradually ~ing

つつある attaches to the ます-stem to say a change is steadily under way and moving toward a certain state — 減りつつある = 'is gradually decreasing', 回復しつつある = 'is on the way to recovering'. It emphasizes a continuous progression in one direction and, like つつ, has a formal, written flavor. It pairs most naturally with verbs of change.
materials.reading: つつある
materials.notes:
Attach it to the ます-stem: 変わりつつある, not 変わるつつある.

Unlike a plain ている, つつある stresses a gradual, ongoing shift toward a new state, so it suits change verbs (増える, 減る, 治る) rather than momentary actions.

It is formal and largely written; in conversation ている is more usual.

Related: tsutsu — Plain つつ means 'while doing ~' (two simultaneous actions); つつある means a single change is ongoing.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: With advances in medical technology, that illness is gradually being cured.
examples.reading: いりょうぎじゅつのしんぽで、そのびょうきはなおりつつある。

materials.prompt: 〜続ける
materials.answer:
to continue doing; to keep doing

〜続ける attaches to the ます-stem to say an action keeps going without stopping — 走り続ける = keep running, 待ち続ける = keep waiting. It focuses on carrying one action on and on. The compound conjugates like a る-verb (続けた, 続けて).
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 読み続ける, not 読む続ける.

Keep 〜続ける (transitive, 'someone keeps doing') apart from 〜続く: use 続ける when a person keeps up the action, 続く when a situation goes on by itself.

Antonyms: owaru — 〜続ける keeps an action going; 〜終わる ends it once it's done.

Related: hajimeru — 〜始める marks the start of the action that 〜続ける then keeps going.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: って
materials.answer:
casual quotation: ~ (that)

A casual, conversational marker that reports what someone said or something you heard: "~ they say" or "I heard that ~". It is a spoken shortcut for と (with 言う/聞く) or という. You'll hear it constantly in everyday talk to pass along information.
materials.reading: って
materials.notes:
って is casual — in formal writing or speech, use と or という instead.

It often marks hearsay ("I heard ~") and can trail off without 言う: 明日は雨だって ("they say it'll rain").

jlptsensei lists N4

Synonyms: to-quotation — と is the standard, more formal quotation marker; って is its casual spoken form.

Related: to-iu — という introduces or names a quoted content; って is the casual contraction of it.

Related: to-omou — と思う reports what you think; って reports what was said or heard.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: They say it'll rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: あの店は安いって聞きました。
examples.english: I heard that shop is cheap.
examples.reading: あのみせはやすいってききました。

materials.prompt: って感じ
materials.answer:
the vibe of ~; kind of like ~

って感じ is casual speech for 'the feeling/vibe of ~.' The って is the colloquial quoting particle and 感じ means 'impression,' so together they wrap up a mood or a rough impression. It often trails off at the end of a thought or adds がする.
materials.reading: ってかんじ
materials.notes:
It's very casual — avoid it in polite speech or formal writing.

って here is the spoken quotative; 感じ is 'impression,' so the whole thing gives a loose 'sort of like ~' feel.

Synonyms: mitai-da — 〜みたい also gives an impression ('seems like'); って感じ is looser, spoken slang.

Related: tte — って is the casual quoting particle used inside って感じ.

Related: you-da — 〜ようだ states an impression formally; って感じ is its casual cousin.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ってば・〜ったら
materials.answer:
I said ~! ; come on, ~ (impatient insistence or exasperation)

Both are colloquial sentence-enders that add impatience or exasperation. ってば reasserts something the listener didn't heed — もう行くってば = I said I'm going! ったら similarly nags or scolds, and after a person's name expresses exasperated fondness or complaint — お父さんったら = oh, Dad, honestly… They belong to casual spoken Japanese and always carry clear emotion.
materials.reading: ってば・ったら
materials.notes:
Casual spoken style only; too emotional and informal for polite or written contexts.

This ったら is the exasperated ender; don't confuse it with conditional 〜たら ('if / when').

Synonyms: tte — casual って quotes or restates what was said; adding ば (ってば) turns it into impatient insistence that the point already stands.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: う動詞
materials.answer:
godan (う-verb) conjugation

う-verbs (godan verbs) are the verb group whose final -u kana shifts across a whole row of the kana chart when you conjugate. For the plain negative, change the final -u kana to its -a row form and add ない (書く→書かない); the past uses the sound-change た／だ endings (飲む→飲んだ); the negative-past ends in なかった. Recognising this group is the first big step to conjugating Japanese verbs.
materials.reading: うどうし
materials.notes:
A verb ending in -る can be either group: う-verbs like 分かる (分からない) shift the vowel, while る-verbs like 食べる (食べない) just drop る. The ending alone does not decide the group.

The plain past has sound changes (音便): 書く→書いた, 泳ぐ→泳いだ, 飲む→飲んだ, 待つ→待った. Learn them by ending.

Related: ru-verbs — る-verbs (ichidan) conjugate more simply — just drop る and add the ending.

Related: suru — する is irregular and follows neither the う- nor る-verb pattern.

Related: kuru — くる is irregular, changing its stem vowel (きます・こない) unlike regular groups.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Dictionary ＋ 書く・飲む・話す［ends in an う-row kana］
Negative: final kana → あ-row ＋ ない — 書く→書かない
Past: 書く→書いた／飲む→飲んだ／話す→話した
Negative-past: あ-row ＋ なかった — 書く→書かなかった

materials.prompt: うちに
materials.answer:
while (still) ~; before ~ changes

〜うちに picks out a window of time and says to act within it. After a plain state it means 'while ~ still holds' (熱いうちに = while it's still hot); after a ない-form it means 'before ~ happens' (忘れないうちに = before I forget). The nuance is that the window will close, so do it now.
materials.reading: うちに
materials.notes:
〜ないうちに means 'before ~ happens' (暗くならないうちに = before it gets dark); plain 〜うちに means 'while the state still lasts'.

It carries the sense that the window will end, so act during it — it is not a neutral 'while'.

Related: aida-ni — 〜間に marks a defined span and something happening within it; 〜うちに adds the sense that the state may change, so act now.

Related: nai-uchi-ni — 〜ないうちに is the negative pattern of this point — 'before ~ happens'; plain 〜うちに is 'while ~ still lasts'.

Related: mae-ni — 〜前に just says 'before' a point in time; 〜ないうちに adds 'while it hasn't yet happened, take the chance'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜うちに入らない
materials.answer:
doesn't count as; can hardly be called (a real ~)

〜うちに入らない says that something falls short of qualifying as a full or proper example of a category — 'that doesn't count as ~'. この程度の雨なら降ったうちに入らない = a little rain like this hardly counts as rain; 一度会っただけでは知り合いのうちに入らない = meeting once doesn't make you acquaintances. It dismisses the case as too slight to bear that label.
materials.reading: うちにはいらない
materials.notes:
This うちに入らない judges that something fails to qualify as a category; it is not the time expression 〜うちに ('while ~').

Related: ni-suginai — 〜にすぎない says something is 'no more than ~'; うちに入らない says it doesn't even qualify as ~.

materials.prompt: 上で
materials.answer:
after doing ~ and then; upon ~; in the course of ~

With the past form or a noun + の, 〜上で means 'after deliberately doing X, then do Y' — 相談した上で = after discussing it, then… . With the dictionary form it means 'in the course of / for the purpose of' (生きる上で = in living / in life). The 'after' use marks a considered step taken before the next action.
materials.reading: うえで
materials.notes:
With the past form (確認した上で) it means 'after taking step X, then do Y', and is more formal and deliberate than 〜てから.

With the dictionary form (働く上で) it shifts to 'in the course of / for the purpose of', not 'after'.

Related: te-kara — 〜てから is the everyday 'after doing'; 〜た上で is more formal and stresses X as a deliberate step taken before Y.

Related: ato-de — 〜後で just orders two events in time; 〜た上で implies you do X on purpose as a basis for doing Y.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 上に
materials.answer:
on top of that; besides; not only ~ but also

〜上に adds a second point in the same direction as the first — 'and on top of that'. 駅から近い上に = close to the station, and on top of that…. Both points lean the same way (both good, or both bad), so it stacks reasons rather than contrasting them.
materials.reading: うえに
materials.notes:
〜上に piles on a point in the same direction (good + good, or bad + bad); it does not contrast the way 一方で does.

Watch the attachment by word type: 近い上に (い-adj), 静かな上に (な-adj), 病気の上に (noun).

bunpro lists N2

Synonyms: dake-de-naku — 〜だけでなく ('not only ~ but also') adds a second item too; 〜上に leans more on 'and worse/better still, on top of that'.

Synonyms: nominarazu — 〜のみならず is the stiff, written 'not only ~ but also'; 〜上に is everyday and stresses stacking a further point.

Synonyms: bakari-ka — 〜ばかりか adds a surprising further point ('not only ~ but even ~'); 〜上に simply piles on more of the same tendency.

Related: shi — 〜し loosely lists reasons or points; 〜上に more tightly stacks a second point on top of the first.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 上は
materials.answer:
now that; since (one has done)

〜上は presents a decisive fact — usually a decision made or an action already taken — as grounds for the resolve or obligation that follows. 引き受けた上は = now that I've undertaken it. The second clause states determination or what must naturally be done. It is formal and somewhat literary; in everyday speech からには is more usual.
materials.reading: うえは
materials.notes:
上は is formal and follows a verb of decision or action already taken; the second clause expresses resolve or obligation.

In conversation, からには is the more natural choice.

Synonyms: ijou-wa — 以上は is very close in meaning; 上は is more literary and centers on a decision or action already taken.

Synonyms: kara-niwa — からには is the everyday, conversational equivalent; 上は is more formal and written.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 動詞（非過去）
materials.answer:
non-past verb form (present / future)

The non-past is the verb form that covers both the present and the future in Japanese — there is no separate future tense. Its plain shape is the dictionary form, and its polite shape ends in ます; context and time words tell you whether it means 'do' or 'will do'.
materials.reading: どうしひかこ
materials.notes:
Japanese has no dedicated future tense — the same non-past form covers 'do' and 'will do'.

The non-past also expresses habits and general truths, not only single upcoming actions.

Related: masu — ます is the polite ending that makes a non-past verb formal.

Related: verb-noun — A verb modifying a noun normally appears in this non-past plain form.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 動詞＋名詞
materials.answer:
verb modifying a noun (relative clause)

Lets a verb describe a noun directly, the way a relative clause does in English: put a plain-form verb right before the noun it modifies, with no の or extra word in between. This is how Japanese builds phrases like 'the book I read' or 'the person who came'.
materials.reading: どうしめいし
materials.notes:
Use the plain form before the noun, never the ます form — 食べる人, not 食べます人.

Do not insert の between the verb and the noun the way you would after another noun.

Related: verb-non-past — Modifying verbs usually take the plain non-past form.

Related: i-adjective-noun — い-adjectives modify nouns the same direct way, with no linking word.

Related: na-adjective-noun — な-adjectives need な before the noun; verbs attach with nothing in between.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: は別として
materials.answer:
setting ~ aside; apart from ~; leaving aside whether ~

は別として sets one matter aside as a separate issue so you can turn to the main point — 'putting X to one side, ...'. It attaches to a noun, and with a yes/no question it becomes 〜かどうかは別として ('leaving aside whether...'). It doesn't exclude members from a group; it just brackets off a topic for now.
materials.reading: はべつとして
materials.notes:
It brackets a topic off as a separate issue; it doesn't mean 'except for' in the sense of excluding items — that is 以外.

For a yes/no point, use 〜かどうかは別として to mean 'leaving aside whether...'.

bunpro lists N2

Synonyms: wa-tomokaku — はともかく is very close in meaning ('setting aside'); は別として leans a little more on treating the matter as a distinct, separate issue.

Related: igai — 以外 excludes items from a set ('other than X'); は別として brackets a topic off to focus elsewhere.

Related: nara-tomokaku — ならともかく means 'if it were X, fine, but...'; は別として simply sets X aside without that conditional contrast.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Sentence＋ かどうか ＋ は別として

examples.japanese: 味は別として、この店は値段が安くて助かる。
examples.english: Taste aside, this shop is cheap, which is a big help.

materials.prompt: は〜で有名
materials.answer:
X is famous for ~

〜は〜で有名です says what something is well known for — その町はお茶で有名です = that town is famous for its tea. The で marks the reason or feature it is famous for. To say 'famous for doing something', nominalize the verb with こと first: 早く走ることで有名だ.
materials.notes:
With で, the place is famous because of that feature; 〜が有名 instead means that feature itself is the famous thing.

For being famous for an action, turn the verb into a noun with こと: 作ることで有名, not 作るで有名.

Related: toshite — 〜として marks the role or capacity something is known in; 〜で有名 marks the feature it is famous for.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun ＋ は ＋ Noun ＋ で有名（だ）
Verb［plain form］＋ ことで有名（だ）

examples.english: This region is famous for its delicious tea.
examples.reading: このちほうはおいしいおちゃでゆうめいです。

examples.japanese: 彼は絵がうまいことで有名です。
examples.english: He's famous for being good at drawing.
examples.reading: かれはえがうまいことでゆうめいです。

materials.prompt: 〜はどうであれ
materials.answer:
whatever ~ may be; no matter what ~ is

〜はどうであれ concedes a point — 'whatever X may be, no matter what X is' — and then asserts that the main clause holds regardless. 理由はどうであれ = whatever the reason, 結果はどうであれ = whatever the outcome. であれ is the concessive form of である, and the pattern dismisses the named factor as irrelevant to the conclusion.
materials.reading: はどうであれ
materials.notes:
Formal in register; であれ is the concessive form of である, not a request.

The main clause states something that stands firm regardless of the factor set aside before はどうであれ.

Synonyms: de-are — であれ is the general 'whatever/no matter' form; はどうであれ is the fixed frame 'whatever the ~ may be' built on どう.

Related: you-ga-you-to — ようが・ようと concedes over a verb ('no matter how one does'); はどうであれ concedes over a noun.

Related: ni-seyo-ni-shiro — にせよ・にしろ means 'even if / whether ~ or'; はどうであれ specifically dismisses a noun as making no difference.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: Whatever the reason, violence can never be excused.

examples.reading: けっかはどうであれ、さいごまでぜんりょくをつくすつもりだ。

materials.prompt: はどうですか
materials.answer:
how about ~?

はどうですか offers something or asks for an opinion about it, like "how about ~?" or "how is ~?". You use it to suggest an option politely or to ask how something is going.
materials.reading: はどうですか
materials.notes:
いかがですか is a politer version for formal situations or when serving guests.

The same phrase both offers something (コーヒーはどうですか) and asks for an evaluation (仕事はどうですか); tone and context tell them apart.

Related: masen-ka — ませんか invites someone to do a verb; はどうですか offers or asks about a noun.

Related: wa-topic — The は here is the topic marker, setting up what you are asking about.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: How about some coffee?

examples.japanese: 新しい仕事はどうですか。
examples.english: How's the new job?
examples.reading: あたらしいしごとはどうですか。

materials.prompt: 〜わ
materials.answer:
sentence-final particle adding soft emphasis or feeling (stereotypically feminine)

Sentence-final わ attaches to the plain form and adds a gentle, emotive touch to a statement. Said with a rising intonation it is classic feminine 'role language' — the わ of fiction and older speech — and can sound affected in real modern conversation. A separate, flat or falling わ is gender-neutral and very common in casual and Kansai speech, where it marks a mild self-directed assertion (そろそろ行くわ = 'I'll head off now'). Teach it as expressive softening, and read the intonation to tell the two apart.
materials.reading: わ
materials.notes:
The rising, softly emphatic わ is stereotyped feminine role language and can sound theatrical in everyday modern speech.

A flat/falling わ (common in Kansai and casual male speech) simply marks mild assertion and is not gendered; intonation, not the syllable, distinguishes them.

Related: wa-wa-de — Same syllable, different construction: わ〜わで lists a pile-up of (usually bad) events, not a sentence-final softener.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.japanese: あら、きれいな花が咲いているわ。
examples.english: Oh, look — there are pretty flowers in bloom.
examples.reading: あら、きれいなはながさいているわ。

materials.prompt: は～が～は
materials.answer:
contrast: A is ~, but B is ~

This pattern sets two things against each other in one sentence. Both A and B take the contrastive は, and the middle が works as the conjunction 'but', joining the two clauses. The result spotlights how A and B differ: 肉は食べますが、魚は食べません = I eat meat, but I don't eat fish.
materials.notes:
Both は here are contrastive: they exist to highlight the A-versus-B difference, not merely to name topics.

The middle が is the conjunction 'but', not the subject-marking が.

Related: kedo — けど is the casual 'but'; this pattern pairs it with double は to make the contrast explicit on both sides.

Related: shikashi — しかし is a formal 'however' that starts a new sentence; は～が～は draws the contrast inside one sentence.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: は言うまでもない
materials.answer:
it goes without saying that ~; needless to say ~

〜は言うまでもない states that something is so obvious it need not be said — 健康の大切さは言うまでもない = the importance of health goes without saying. It marks the point as too self-evident to need explaining, often before adding a further point. The connective form 言うまでもなく means 'needless to say', at the head of a sentence.
materials.reading: はいうまでもない
materials.notes:
It presents something as obvious to everyone; do not use it for information that is actually new or surprising to the listener.

言うまでもなく at the head of a clause works as an adverb ('needless to say'); 〜は言うまでもない closes a statement.

Related: made-mo-nai — 〜までもない (N1) says an action isn't even worth doing; 言うまでもない is the set phrase 'it goes without saying'.

Source references: bunpro

Sentence［plain form］＋ のは言うまでもない

materials.prompt: は〜くらいです
materials.answer:
about the only ~ is; roughly the extent of it is ~

は〜くらいです presents something as the modest limit of what applies — the most you can say, or the only real example. 運動と言えば、犬の散歩くらいです = as for exercise, dog-walking is about the only one. くらい here downplays the amount or degree, framing it as small or the sole case.
materials.notes:
くらい (also ぐらい) here marks a modest limit or the sole example, not an approximate number like '10 people or so'.

The tone is downplaying — 'it's only about this much'; it does not emphasize a large amount.

Related: kurai — くらい・ぐらい broadly marks approximate amount or degree; は〜くらいです uses it to frame something as the modest limit.

Related: shika-nai — 〜しかない flatly limits things to 'nothing but'; は〜くらいです softly presents the modest extent instead.

Related: hodo — ほど also scales degree; くらい in this pattern downplays it to 'about the only / that little'.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: はもちろん
materials.answer:
~ of course, and also ~; not to mention ~; not only ~ but also ~

はもちろん presents X as the obvious, taken-for-granted case and then adds a further, more noteworthy item Y, usually marked with も — 'X goes without saying, and Y as well.' It attaches to a noun and often appears as はもちろんのこと. The point being added after it is the one that carries the real information.
materials.reading: はもちろん
materials.notes:
The item before はもちろん is the expected/obvious one; the item added afterward (often with も) is the more surprising or noteworthy point.

It attaches to a noun; for 'not only... but also' after verbs or full clauses, だけでなく is the more general pattern.

Synonyms: dake-de-naku — だけでなく ('not only') is more general and attaches to verbs and clauses; はもちろん takes a noun and frames it as the obvious case.

Related: wa-oroka — はおろか is stronger ('let alone') and usually pairs with a negative or extreme; はもちろん is neutral and simply adds a second item.

Related: mo-mata — もまた marks 'also, too' for one added item; はもちろん frames the first as obvious before adding the notable one.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun＋ はもちろん（のこと）、〜も

examples.english: This dish is hugely popular not only with kids but with adults too.

examples.english: He can speak French as well as English, of course.
examples.reading: かれはえいごはもちろん、フランスごもはなせる。

materials.prompt: はもとより
materials.answer:
not to mention ~; let alone ~; of course ~, and also

〜はもとより presents X as an obvious given ('X, of course') and then adds Y as a further, often more notable case — 'not only X but also Y'. It is formal and written. The Y that follows usually carries も or まで ('even Y').
materials.reading: はもとより
materials.notes:
X はもとより treats X as taken for granted and adds Y; the second item normally carries も/まで.

It is formal and written; in speech はもちろん gives the same 'not to mention' sense more casually.

Synonyms: wa-mochiron — はもちろん is the everyday equivalent; はもとより says the same thing in a more formal, written register.

Related: dake-de-naku — だけでなく plainly adds 'not only X but Y'; はもとより frames X as an obvious given first.

Related: bakari-ka — ばかりか adds a stronger, sometimes surprising Y; はもとより simply treats X as a matter of course.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun ＋ はもとより ＋ Noun ＋ も／まで

examples.english: He speaks not just English but even French and Spanish.

materials.prompt: ～は～の一つだ
materials.answer:
~ is one of (several / many) ~

〜は〜の一つだ presents one thing as a member of a larger group — 'X is one of the Y'. 京都は人気のある町の一つだ = Kyoto is one of the popular cities. It's a simple, natural way to place something among many of its kind rather than singling it out as the only one.
materials.notes:
The group noun before 一つ is plural in sense, so a describing phrase usually comes first: 世界で一番大きい国の一つ = one of the biggest countries in the world.

一つ counts things; for people, use 〜の一人 (ひとり) instead — 優秀な学生の一人だ = one of the excellent students.

Related: ichiban — 一番 singles out the one top item; 〜の一つだ instead places something among several of its kind.

Related: no-naka-de — の中で marks the group; 〜の一つだ picks out one member of that group.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜はおろか
materials.answer:
let alone; not to mention; to say nothing of

〜はおろか says that not only the greater or more obvious thing but even a more basic one is (typically) not the case. 漢字はおろか、ひらがなも書けない = can't write even hiragana, let alone kanji. It attaches to a noun, and the second, more basic item is usually marked with も, さえ, or すら, in a generally negative sentence. This is formal, written Japanese.
materials.reading: はおろか
materials.notes:
The second item (marked も／さえ／すら) is the more basic case, and the whole sentence is usually negative.

It attaches to nouns; the emphasis is 'even the obvious thing doesn't hold, never mind the harder one'.

Synonyms: dokoro-ka — どころか can also reverse an expectation ('far from ~'); はおろか strictly builds a 'not even the basic thing' scale.

Synonyms: nominarazu — のみならず adds 'not only ~ but also' in positive statements; はおろか works in negatives ('let alone').

Related: sae — さえ ('even') often marks the second, basic item in a はおろか sentence.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜はさておき
materials.answer:
setting ~ aside; leaving ~ aside for now

〜はさておき sets one topic aside in order to move on to a more pressing or important one — 'leaving ~ aside, let's get to ~'. 冗談はさておき = joking aside, 建前はさておき = setting the official line aside. It attaches to a noun and is a common way to pivot from a lesser matter to the real point at hand.
materials.reading: はさておき
materials.notes:
It attaches directly to a noun (冗談はさておき), signalling a deliberate pivot to the main issue.

The item set aside is simply postponed as less urgent, not judged; it does not carry the critical 'neglecting' tone of 〜はそっちのけで.

Synonyms: wa-tomokaku — はともかく also brackets a matter off; はさておき leans more on 'setting it aside to move on to the main point'.

Related: wa-socchinoke-de — はそっちのけで is neglecting a duty to do something else and sounds critical; はさておき is a neutral shift of topic.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.japanese: 冗談はさておき、そろそろ本題に入りましょう。
examples.english: Joking aside, let's get down to the main topic.
examples.reading: じょうだんはさておき、そろそろほんだいにはいりましょう。

examples.japanese: 味はさておき、この店は雰囲気だけは抜群にいい。
examples.english: Taste aside, this restaurant's atmosphere alone is outstanding.
examples.reading: あじはさておき、このみせはふんいきだけはばつぐんにいい。

materials.prompt: 〜はそっちのけで・〜をそっちのけで
materials.answer:
neglecting; ignoring (one thing to do another)

そっちのけ means shoving something off to the side, and 〜はそっちのけで / 〜をそっちのけで marks a person ignoring or neglecting something that deserves attention in order to throw themselves into something else. 宿題はそっちのけで = ignoring the homework. It carries a mildly critical tone toward the person doing the neglecting.
materials.reading: はそっちのけで・をそっちのけで
materials.notes:
Casual in tone and usually critical: it faults someone for neglecting a duty in favour of something else.

Unlike 〜はさておき (a neutral pivot in topic), そっちのけ implies a responsibility is being wrongly abandoned.

Synonyms: mo-kamawazu — もかまわず is doing something heedless of X; そっちのけ specifically means neglecting X in order to pour oneself into something else.

Related: wa-sateoki — はさておき neutrally postpones a topic; はそっちのけで faults someone for abandoning what they should be doing.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Noun＋はそっちのけで／をそっちのけで

examples.japanese: 息子は宿題をそっちのけで、朝からずっとゲームをしている。
examples.english: Ignoring his homework, my son has been playing games all morning.
examples.reading: むすこはしゅくだいをそっちのけで、あさからずっとゲームをしている。

examples.japanese: 彼は自分の仕事はそっちのけで、同僚の相談にばかり乗っている。
examples.english: Neglecting his own work, he does nothing but give advice to his colleagues.
examples.reading: かれはじぶんのしごとはそっちのけで、どうりょうのそうだんにばかりのっている。

materials.prompt: は〜となっている
materials.answer:
is (formally) set as; has become; stands as ~

〜となっている presents something as an established, official state — a rule, schedule, or settled result — in a formal, impersonal tone. 受付は10時からとなっております = reception is set from 10. It is like になっている but more formal, and is common in announcements, documents, and signs. The 〜は marks what the arrangement is about.
materials.notes:
となっている is the more formal, official-sounding version of になっている, common in notices and rules.

It describes a settled state or arrangement, not an action happening right now.

Related: naru — なる marks a change into a new state; 〜となっている presents the resulting state as an established, formal arrangement.

Related: koto-ni-naru — ことになる settles that something has been decided; 〜となっている states the standing arrangement in formal, notice-like language.

Related: te-iru — 〜ている marks an ongoing state; となっている is that state framed formally as an official arrangement.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Topic ＋ は ＋ Noun ＋ となっている
Sentence［plain form］＋ こととなっている

examples.japanese: 館内での飲食は禁止となっています。
examples.english: Eating and drinking inside the building is prohibited (by the rules).
examples.reading: かんないでのいんしょくはきんしとなっています。

examples.japanese: 会議は来週の月曜日からとなっております。
examples.english: The meeting is set to start from next Monday.
examples.reading: かいぎはらいしゅうのげつようびからとなっております。
