materials.prompt: はともかく
materials.answer:
setting ~ aside; regardless of ~; never mind ~, the point is

〜はともかく sets a topic aside as not the point right now, shifting the focus to what follows — 'never mind X, the real issue is Y'. Often 〜はともかく(として). X is downplayed as secondary here, not dismissed as unimportant in general.
materials.reading: はともかく
materials.notes:
It parks X as 'not what matters now' and moves to a more important Y; it doesn't claim X is worthless overall, only that we're leaving it aside here.

After a question-like clause it takes か: 行くかどうかはともかく ('setting aside whether to go').

Related: o-towazu — を問わず means 'regardless of any value of X'; はともかく sets one specific X aside to focus on Y.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

Sentence ＋ か ＋ はともかく（として）

examples.reading: あじはともかく、このみせはねだんがやすくてたすかる。

examples.japanese: 結果はともかく、最後まで全力を尽くしたことに意味がある。
examples.english: Regardless of the outcome, there is meaning in having given it my all to the end.
examples.reading: けっかはともかく、さいごまでぜんりょくをつくしたことにいみがある。

materials.prompt: は
materials.answer:
as for ~ (topic)

は marks the topic of a sentence — the thing you are talking about — and the rest of the sentence comments on it. It sets the stage, roughly like "as for ~", and is one of the first particles a learner meets.
materials.reading: は
materials.notes:
Although written with the hiragana は, as a topic particle it is pronounced wa.

は marks the topic (often already known), while が introduces or identifies a subject; 私は学生です presents "me" as the topic, 私が学生です answers "who is the student?"

Related: ga — が identifies or introduces a subject; は sets up a known topic to comment on.

Related: mo — も replaces は to mean "also / too" instead of marking a plain topic.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I am a student.
examples.reading: わたしはがくせいです。

examples.japanese: 東京は人が多いです。
examples.english: Tokyo has a lot of people.
examples.reading: とうきょうはひとがおおいです。

materials.prompt: 〜わ〜わで
materials.answer:
what with ~ and ~ (a pile-up of, usually, troubles)

〜わ〜わで lists two or more things — typically mishaps — that pile up at once, and the closing で leads into the resulting (bad) state. Each item ends in わ: 財布は落とすわ、電車は遅れるわで散々だった = what with losing my wallet and the train being late, it was awful. It conveys an exasperated 'one thing after another' feeling and is common in spoken complaints.
materials.notes:
The listed items are usually negatives piling up, and the final で introduces the resulting (bad) situation.

This わ is a listing particle, not the sentence-final feminine わ — here it always comes in the paired わ〜わ pattern.

Related: wa-feminine — Shares the syllable わ but is unrelated: the feminine 〜わ is a single sentence-final softener, not a paired listing of troubles.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: What with losing my wallet and the train being delayed, I've had really rotten luck today.

examples.reading: パソコンはこわれるわ、しりょうはみつからないわで、しごとがまったくすすまなかった。

materials.prompt: は〜より…です
materials.answer:
A is more ~ than B

This is the basic comparison pattern: A は B より [adjective] です says that A is more ~ than B. A is the topic, B より marks the thing compared against, and the adjective states how A wins out.
materials.reading: はよりです
materials.notes:
より attaches to the standard of comparison (B), which is the one being beaten: 電車より速い means "faster than the train".

To shift the spotlight onto the winner, the same idea can be phrased as B より A のほうが.

Synonyms: yori-hou-ga — より〜のほうが says the same comparison but puts the focus on the item that comes out ahead.

Related: yori — より is the "than" particle at the heart of this pattern.

Related: no-naka-de-ichiban — This compares two nouns; の中で〜が一番 picks the top of a whole group.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Noun-A ＋ は ＋ Noun-B ＋ より ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective ＋ です

examples.english: Today is colder than yesterday.
examples.reading: きょうはきのうよりさむいです。

materials.prompt: 訳あり
materials.answer:
having (unspoken) special circumstances

訳あり literally 'there is a reason' describes someone or something as carrying special circumstances that are deliberately left unstated — often awkward, delicate, or something that lowers value. 訳ありの二人 = a couple with a complicated backstory; 訳あり商品 = goods discounted for some (minor) flaw. It behaves like a noun/na-adjective modifier (訳ありの〜, 訳ありだ) and hints at a story without telling it.
materials.reading: わけあり
materials.notes:
訳あり implies there is a reason but pointedly leaves it unspoken — usually something awkward, delicate, or that reduces value.

It modifies like a noun/na-adjective (訳ありの関係, 訳あり品); there is no matching 訳なし used the same way.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: That person seems to be carrying some kind of complicated past.
examples.reading: あのひとは、どうやらわけありのかこをかかえているらしい。

examples.reading: このみせでは、わけありひんをやすくうっている。

materials.prompt: わけだ
materials.answer:
that's why ~; so that means ~; no wonder ~ (a natural conclusion)

〜わけだ presents something as a logical consequence you've pieced together from what's known — どうりで寒いわけだ = no wonder it's cold. It can also restate or interpret ('so you're saying...'). It signals a conclusion that follows naturally from the facts.
materials.reading: わけだ
materials.notes:
It draws a conclusion that follows from the situation, unlike から／ので, which simply supply a reason.

Keep it apart from わけではない (partial denial) and わけにはいかない (can't afford to).

Related: wake-dewa-nai — わけではない softly denies a conclusion; わけだ affirms one as the natural upshot.

Related: koto-ni-naru — ことになる is 'it works out / it's been decided that'; わけだ presents a conclusion drawn from reasoning.

Related: node — ので simply states a reason; わけだ points to the conclusion that reason leads to.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: わけではない
materials.answer:
it doesn't (necessarily) mean that ~; it's not the case that ~ (partial denial)

〜わけではない gently denies a conclusion someone might jump to — 'that doesn't mean...', 'it's not that...'. 嫌いなわけではない = it's not that I dislike it. It denies part, not all, and often heads off a likely misunderstanding. Casual: わけじゃない.
materials.reading: わけではない
materials.notes:
It's a soft, partial denial ('not necessarily so'), far weaker than わけがない ('no way that's true') or a flat 〜ない.

It typically corrects an assumption the listener might otherwise make.

Synonyms: kanarazushimo — 必ずしも〜ない is 'not always/necessarily'; it often teams up with わけではない for the same partial-denial nuance.

Synonyms: to-iu-mono-dewa-nai — というものではない denies that a general claim always holds; わけではない denies a specific inferred conclusion.

Related: wake-ga-nai — わけがない is a total 'impossible'; わけではない only chips away at part of a conclusion.

Related: wake-da — わけだ affirms a natural conclusion; わけではない denies one.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

な-adjective ＋ な／Noun ＋ という ＋ わけではない

materials.prompt: わけがない
materials.answer:
there's no way that ~; it's impossible that ~ (logical impossibility)

〜わけがない strongly denies that something could be true, on the basis of reasoning — そんなことあるわけがない = there's no way that's true. It is more emphatic and logic-driven than はずがない. The casual form is わけない.
materials.reading: わけがない
materials.notes:
It denies that something can be true (a logical conclusion); 'no means to do it' is ようがない.

It is a stronger, more confident version of はずがない.

Synonyms: hazu-ga-nai — はずがない is a softer 'shouldn't / can't be'; わけがない is a more forceful, reasoned 'no way'.

Related: wake-dewa-nai — わけではない is a partial 'it's not that ~'; わけがない is a full-on 'that's impossible'.

Related: you-ga-nai — ようがない denies any means to do something; わけがない denies that something is true.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: わけにはいかない
materials.answer:
can't (bring myself to) ~; can't afford to ~ (for social or moral reasons)

〜わけにはいかない says you can't do something — not because it's physically impossible, but because duty, circumstances, or social pressure won't allow it. 休むわけにはいかない = I can't just take the day off. With a negative verb, 〜ないわけにはいかない flips to 'have no choice but to'.
materials.reading: わけにはいかない
materials.notes:
The impossibility is social or psychological, not physical; for 'no means to do it' use ようがない.

The double negative 〜ないわけにはいかない means 'must do', so watch the form carefully.

Related: nakereba-naranai — なければならない is a plain 'must'; 〜ないわけにはいかない is 'must' pushed by duty or obligation.

Related: shikanai-no-choice — 〜しかない is 'have no choice but to' from lack of options; わけにはいかない blocks an option on social grounds.

Related: you-ga-nai — ようがない is physical/means-based impossibility; わけにはいかない is being unable for social or moral reasons.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［dictionary form］＋ わけにはいかない
Verb［ない form］＋ わけにはいかない（＝ must do）

examples.english: It's a request from a teacher I owe a lot to, so I can't turn it down.
examples.reading: おせわになったせんせいのたのみだから、ことわるわけにはいかない。

materials.prompt: 割に
materials.answer:
considering ~; for ~; despite ~ (more/less than expected)

割に（は） compares something against a standard or expectation and points out that reality doesn't match it — X considering Y, or X despite Y. 値段の割においしい = tasty for the price. It weighs an amount or degree against what the first part would lead you to expect, and flags the gap.
materials.reading: わりに
materials.notes:
It highlights a gap between expectation and reality; when the result actually fits what you'd expect (as befitting), use だけあって instead.

Unlike plain のに ('although'), 割に specifically measures a degree or amount against the standard the first part sets up.

Synonyms: noni-although — のに simply marks 'although X, unexpectedly Y'; 割に weighs the result against the level X would lead you to expect.

Synonyms: kuse-ni — くせに also flags an unexpected mismatch but adds blame or scorn; 割に stays neutral.

Antonyms: dake-atte — だけあって says the result fits the standard ('just as you'd expect from X'); 割に says it runs against that standard.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: このレストランはねだんのわりにりょうがおおいです。

examples.japanese: 彼はたくさん練習した割に、あまり上手になっていない。
examples.english: Considering how much he practiced, he hasn't gotten very good.
examples.reading: かれはたくさんれんしゅうしたわりに、あまりじょうずになっていない。

materials.prompt: わざと
materials.answer:
on purpose; deliberately; intentionally

わざと is an adverb saying an action was done on purpose, usually with awareness of the effect it would cause — often a teasing or negative one. 彼はわざと負けた = he lost on purpose.
materials.reading: わざと
materials.notes:
It describes acting intentionally, often with a mischievous or unkind slant.

Don't confuse it with わざわざ ('go to the trouble of / go out of one's way'), which is about special effort, not sneaky intent.

Related: wazawaza — わざわざ is going out of your way to do something with effort; わざと is doing something on purpose, often slyly.

Related: tsumori-de — 〜つもりで is 'with the intention of'; わざと flags that the act itself was deliberate.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.japanese: 弟を笑わせようと、わざと変な顔をした。
examples.english: To make my little brother laugh, I made a silly face on purpose.
examples.reading: おとうとをわらわせようと、わざとへんなかおをした。

examples.english: She deliberately ignored my question.

materials.prompt: わざわざ
materials.answer:
to go out of one's way to; to take the trouble of doing

わざわざ is an adverb that marks an action as a special, deliberate effort — one that went beyond what was strictly needed, like making a special trip or taking extra trouble. It often acknowledges someone's kindness (thanks for going to the bother), and can also gently point out that such effort wasn't really necessary.
materials.reading: わざわざ
materials.notes:
Don't confuse it with わざと ('on purpose'): わざわざ is about the extra trouble taken and is usually well-meant, while わざと is about acting deliberately to bring about a particular (often unwanted) result.

It frames the effort as beyond the minimum; using it can imply you notice the bother involved, so it carries a warmer or more pointed nuance than a plain verb.

Related: wazato — わざと is doing something deliberately to cause a result (often a bad one); わざわざ stresses the extra trouble taken, usually with goodwill.

Related: te-made — 〜てまで frames effort as going 'so far as to' an extreme; わざわざ simply notes that a special effort was made.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: わずかに
materials.answer:
slightly; barely; merely; only a little

わずかに means 'slightly, only a little, barely'. As an adverb it describes a very small degree or change (わずかに動く = move a fraction), and before a quantity it means 'merely, only just' (わずか二年 = a mere two years). Throughout, it emphasizes how small or scarce the amount is.
materials.reading: わずかに
materials.notes:
When modifying a quantity it usually drops に: わずか二年, not わずかに二年.

It highlights smallness or scarcity of degree/amount; it is not the 'only' of identity or scope (that role belongs to だけ／のみ).

Related: dake — だけ limits to 'only ~ and nothing else'; わずか(に) stresses that the quantity or degree itself is tiny.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Thanks to the treatment, the pain eased slightly.
examples.reading: しょちのおかげで、いたみがわずかにやわらいだ。

examples.english: In a mere two years since opening, that shop spread across the whole country.

materials.prompt: を
materials.answer:
direct object particle

を marks the direct object — the thing a transitive verb acts on (what you eat, read, buy). It can also mark the place a motion verb moves through or leaves (公園を歩く, 家を出る). Though written を, it is pronounced "o".
materials.reading: を
materials.notes:
を is pronounced the same as お ("o"), but this particle is always written を.

Intransitive verbs take が, not を — say ドアが開く for "the door opens", not ドアを開く.

Related: ga — が marks the subject that acts; を marks the object acted on.

Related: ni — に marks a destination or target; を marks the thing the verb acts on.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: I read the newspaper every morning.
examples.reading: まいあさしんぶんをよみます。

examples.japanese: 公園を散歩します。
examples.english: I take a walk through the park.
examples.reading: こうえんをさんぽします。

materials.prompt: をください
materials.answer:
please give me ~

Politely asks for an object by naming it, marking it with を, and adding ください: "please give me ~". Use it to request a thing — in a shop or at a restaurant. To ask someone to do an action instead, use the て form plus ください.
materials.reading: をください
materials.notes:
をください requests a thing (a noun); to request an action, attach ください to the て form: 待ってください.

Put a number and counter before ください to ask for a quantity: 切符を二枚ください.

Related: te-kudasai — てください requests an action; をください requests a thing.

Related: morau — もらう describes receiving; をください is how you politely ask to receive.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.english: Excuse me, water please.
examples.reading: すみません、みずをください。

examples.japanese: この赤いりんごをください。
examples.english: I'll take this red apple, please.
examples.reading: このあかいりんごをください。

materials.prompt: や
materials.answer:
and (such as); things like

や links nouns as examples from a larger set, meaning "things like A and B (among others)". Unlike と, which lists everything, や implies the list is not complete. It often finishes with など ("and so on") to make that "among others" sense explicit.
materials.reading: や
materials.notes:
や joins only nouns, and hints there are more items; と joins nouns exhaustively (exactly these).

You can add など after the last item to underline "and such".

Synonyms: to-and — と lists nouns exhaustively; や implies the list is only a sample.

Related: nado — など pairs with や to spell out "and so on".

Related: mo — も adds "also" to a set; や lists example members of a set.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: There are things like eggs and milk in the fridge.
examples.reading: れいぞうこにたまごやぎゅうにゅうがはいっています。

materials.prompt: 〜や否や
materials.answer:
as soon as; the moment that; no sooner ~ than

〜や否や attaches to a dictionary-form verb to mean 'the instant that ~, no sooner ~ than': ベルが鳴るや否や = the moment the bell rang. The second clause reports what happened immediately and unexpectedly right after. It is a literary, written expression; the following clause states an actual past event, not a plan, request, or command.
materials.reading: やいなや
materials.notes:
It is literary; in ordinary speech 〜とすぐに or 〜たとたん is more natural.

The second clause must be a factual, usually past, occurrence — not a command, request, or the speaker's own intention.

Synonyms: ga-hayai-ka — が早いか is likewise literary 'the moment ~', but stresses that the second action began almost before the first was even finished.

Synonyms: ta-totan — たとたん(に) also means 'the moment ~', often with surprise, but is less literary and follows the た-form.

Synonyms: nari — 〜なり means 'as soon as ~' where the same subject moves straight into the next action; や否や allows a different subject or an external event to follow.

Related: to-douji-ni — と同時に means 'at the same time as ~' (simultaneity); や否や stresses immediate succession right after the first event.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: The moment the bell rang, the students dashed out of the classroom.

examples.english: No sooner had she heard the news than she rose from her seat and left the room.
examples.reading: そのしらせをきくやいなや、かのじょはせきをたってへやをでていった。

materials.prompt: 〜やしない
materials.answer:
there's no way ~; definitely doesn't/won't (emphatic negative)

〜やしない is a colloquial contraction of 〜はしない, used to deny something emphatically — 'there's no way ~, definitely won't ~'. It attaches to the verb stem: 分かりやしない = there's no way anyone understands, できやしない = it just can't be done. The tone is exasperated or dismissive, brushing off a possibility as out of the question. It belongs to casual, spoken language.
materials.reading: やしない
materials.notes:
It comes from 〜はしない (わ／や sound change) and is casual and emphatic; avoid it in formal contexts.

It rejects a possibility outright with feeling, stronger than a plain 〜ない.

Related: totemo-nai — とても〜ない says something is impossible to do; やしない emphatically denies that it happens or holds at all.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: やがて
materials.answer:
before long; in time; eventually

やがて is an adverb meaning 'before long, in time, eventually'. It presents something as coming about through the natural passage of time — the situation moves toward the stated outcome without much delay. It has a narrative, written flavor and describes an approximate near future rather than a fixed time.
materials.reading: やがて
materials.notes:
It marks a natural, not-too-distant progression of time; it is not 'finally, after much effort', which is ついに.

It names an approximate near future, so it does not pair with an exact clock time or date.

Related: tsui-ni — ついに marks an endpoint reached at last, often after long effort; やがて is 'before long', stressing a smooth passage of time.

Related: kekkyoku — 結局 sums up how things turned out in the end; やがて simply says the next stage arrives soon.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: Before long, even the children's laughter had faded away.
examples.reading: こどもたちのわらいごえも、やがてきこえなくなった。

examples.english: If you keep making an effort, results will come in time.
examples.reading: どりょくをつづけていれば、やがてけっかはついてくるだろう。

materials.prompt: やら〜やら
materials.answer:
what with ... and ... (and other things)

やら〜やら lists two representative items — nouns, verbs, or adjectives — while implying there are others besides. It often carries a nuance of things being troublesome, chaotic, or overwhelming, so it suits situations of busyness or mixed feelings: 荷物やら書類やら = 'what with luggage and papers and all'.
materials.notes:
It tends to convey that the listed things pile up into something troublesome or confusing, unlike the neutral listing of とか.

The items should be of the same type (two nouns, two adjectives), and the pattern implies 'and others', not an exhaustive list.

Synonyms: toka-toka — とか〜とか lists examples neutrally; やら〜やら adds a sense of trouble, disorder, or being overwhelmed.

Related: tari-tari — 〜たり〜たり lists representative actions neutrally; やら〜やら lists items with an exasperated or busy nuance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun ＋ やら ＋ Noun ＋ やら
Verb／Adjective［plain form］＋ やら ＋ Verb／Adjective［plain form］＋ やら

examples.reading: ひっこしのひは、にづくりやらてつづきやらでいちにちじゅうばたばたしていた。

materials.prompt: やれ〜やれ
materials.answer:
what with ~ and ~ (listing burdens or complaints)

やれ〜やれ〜 lists one troublesome thing after another, usually with a tone of exasperation at how much is piling up: やれ会議だやれ報告書だ = what with meetings and reports and everything. Each item is often a noun + だ, and the string is frequently rounded off with と before a verb like 忙しい. It conveys the speaker's weariness at a barrage of demands, and is colloquial.
materials.notes:
Do not confuse this listing construction with the standalone interjection やれやれ ('good grief', a sigh).

It carries a complaining, put-upon tone, listing burdens rather than neutral choices.

Related: nari-nari — なり〜なり lists alternatives to choose from ('either A or B'); やれ〜やれ lists grievances piling up, with a weary tone.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.reading: やれかいぎだ、やれほうこくしょだとおわれて、じぶんのしごとがいっこうにすすまない。

materials.prompt: 〜やすい
materials.answer:
easy to do; prone to (readily happens)

〜やすい attaches to the ます-stem and means an action is easy or comfortable to do — 食べやすい = easy to eat, 分かりやすい = easy to understand. It can also mean something readily happens (割れやすい = breaks easily). The compound conjugates like an い-adjective (やすかった, やすくない).
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 使いやすい, not 使うやすい.

The whole compound inflects as an い-adjective: past 〜やすかった, negative 〜やすくない.

Antonyms: nikui — 〜にくい is the neutral 'hard to' — the opposite of 〜やすい.

Antonyms: zurai — 〜づらい is 'hard to (and uncomfortable)' — an opposite of 〜やすい with an added strain nuance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: This app is very easy to use.

materials.prompt: よ
materials.answer:
emphasis / informing particle

よ at the end of a sentence tells the listener something you think they don't already know, or drives your point home — like adding "you know" or "I'm telling you". It presents new information or reassurance from the speaker to the listener.
materials.reading: よ
materials.notes:
よ presents information the speaker assumes is new; ね instead seeks the listener's agreement about something shared.

Overusing よ can sound pushy, so save it for when you are genuinely informing or reassuring.

Related: ne — ね seeks the listener's agreement; よ informs them of something new.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: よほど・よっぽど
materials.answer:
considerably; to a great extent; far more

よほど is an adverb meaning 'to a considerable degree, much (more)'. It often draws an inference that a situation must be extreme from the evidence at hand (よほど疲れていたのだろう = 'must have been really tired'), and it also strengthens comparisons (よほどいい = 'far better'). よっぽど is the more colloquial, emphatic form.
materials.reading: よほど・よっぽど
materials.notes:
In the inference use it commonly pairs with のだろう／らしい: よほど〜のだろう = 'must have been quite ~'.

よっぽど is casual; it also colors a suppressed impulse — よっぽど言おうかと思った = 'I very nearly said it'.

Synonyms: sazo — さぞ guesses sympathetically at how someone must feel; よほど also infers a strong degree but is not limited to feelings and can intensify comparisons.

Related: hodo — ほど marks a degree or extent as a benchmark; よほど is a fixed adverb meaning 'to a considerable degree'.

Source references: jlptsensei

examples.japanese: 彼は挨拶もせずに帰ってしまった。よほど機嫌が悪かったのだろう。
examples.english: He left without even saying goodbye. He must have been in a really bad mood.

examples.reading: このみせのほうが、えきまえのみせよりよっぽどやすい。

materials.prompt: より
materials.answer:
than; compared to

より marks the standard you compare against — the 'than X' in a comparison. It attaches right after the noun used as the yardstick: 去年より暑い = 'hotter than last year'. The thing that comes out higher is usually marked with は or のほうが.
materials.reading: より
materials.notes:
より comes right after the standard being beaten: 電車は車より速い, so 車より sits next to 速い.

To pick the top out of three or more, use 一番, not より (which compares two things).

This より (comparison) is different from the formal より meaning 'from'.

Related: yori-hou-ga — より〜のほうが is the fuller 'B is more ~ than A' frame built on this より.

Related: ichiban — 一番 picks the single best of three or more; より compares just two things.

Related: no-naka-de — の中で names the group; pair it with 一番, not より, for the outright top.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: よりほかない
materials.answer:
have no choice but to; no option besides

〜よりほかない (also よりほかはない) attaches to a dictionary-form verb to say there is nothing besides doing it — 'no choice but to ~'. It marks the sole remaining option with a tone of resignation, when no better alternative is available.
materials.reading: よりほかない
materials.notes:
Keep the preceding verb in dictionary form: あきらめるよりほかない.

It is a near-synonym of よりしかたがない and ざるを得ない; all express a reluctant, unavoidable choice.

Synonyms: yori-shikata-ga-nai — よりしかたがない means the same 'no choice but to'; the two are interchangeable in most contexts.

Synonyms: zaru-o-enai — ざるを得ない is a more formal, written way to say one cannot help but do the action.

Related: shika-nai — 〜しかない likewise limits things to one option; よりほかない adds a resigned, no-alternative nuance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: より〜のほうが
materials.answer:
B is more ~ than A

Compares two things and states which one has more of a quality: "compared to A, B is more ~". A takes より ("than") and B takes のほうが ("the ~ side is more"). The order of the two parts is flexible, but the item marked のほうが is always the one that wins the comparison.
materials.reading: よりのほうが
materials.notes:
のほうが marks the item that is "more"; より marks the baseline it beats — swap them and the meaning flips.

To pick the top out of three or more, use 一番 instead of this two-way comparison.

Synonyms: wa-yori-desu — は〜より…です makes the same comparison with A as the topic instead of のほうが on B.

Related: yori — より on its own is the "than" that this fuller pattern is built around.

Related: ichiban — 一番 picks the single most out of three or more, not a two-way comparison.

Related: no-naka-de-ichiban — 〜の中で〜が一番 says which is the most within a group; this compares just two.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Noun-A ＋ より ＋ Noun-B ＋ のほうが ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective

materials.prompt: よりしかたがない
materials.answer:
have no choice but to; nothing to do but

〜よりしかたがない (also よりしかたない) attaches to a dictionary-form verb to say there is no option other than doing it — 'there's nothing to do but ~'. It resigns the speaker to the only remaining course of action, usually reluctantly, when circumstances leave no alternative.
materials.reading: よりしかたがない
materials.notes:
The verb before より stays in dictionary form: 歩いて帰るよりしかたがない, not 帰ったより.

It carries a tone of reluctant resignation; it is nearly identical in meaning to よりほかない and ざるを得ない.

Synonyms: yori-hoka-nai — よりほかない is a near-identical twin; both mean 'no choice but to', with よりほかない sounding a touch more formal.

Synonyms: zaru-o-enai — ざるを得ない ('cannot help but') is a more formal, written equivalent attaching to the ない-stem.

Related: shika-nai — 〜しかない also says 'the only option is ~'; よりしかたがない specifically frames it as resigned helplessness.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: よりも
materials.answer:
(more) than ~; rather than ~ (comparison, with emphasis)

よりも is より 'than' with emphatic も, marking the standard of comparison and stressing the gap — 去年よりも暑い = even hotter than last year. The thing being compared against comes before よりも (Aよりも B = B, more than A).
materials.reading: よりも
materials.notes:
よりも is より with added emphasis; largely interchangeable, but よりも highlights the contrast more.

The point of comparison sits before よりも, so 'A よりも B' means B outdoes A.

Synonyms: yori — より is the plain 'than'; よりも is the same with emphasis on the difference.

Related: yori-hou-ga — 〜より〜ほうが frames a two-way choice ('B is more ~ than A'); よりも just marks the standard being beaten.

Related: to-iu-yori — というより corrects a description ('rather than say A, it's B'); よりも compares degrees or preferences.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 予定だ
materials.answer:
be scheduled to; plan to (an arranged plan)

予定だ marks something as a set, on-the-calendar plan — a schedule already arranged rather than a whim. Verbs attach in the dictionary form (行く予定だ) and nouns take の (旅行の予定だ). It is more concrete and official-sounding than つもり.
materials.reading: よていだ
materials.notes:
予定だ is an arranged, scheduled plan; つもり is a personal intention. A booked trip is 予定, a private resolve is つもり.

Nouns take の before 予定: 旅行の予定です.

For a plan that fell through, 予定だった means 'was supposed to (but…)'.

Synonyms: tsumori — つもりだ is a personal intention rather than a fixed, arranged schedule.

Related: you-to-omou — ようと思う is 'I think I'll', looser than a set 予定.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ようだ
materials.answer:
it seems that; it appears (from evidence)

ようだ expresses a conjecture the speaker draws from what they can see, hear, or otherwise sense. It is a fairly objective 'it seems / it appears', grounded in evidence rather than a wild guess. It attaches to plain forms; nouns take の and な-adjectives take な before よう.
materials.reading: ようだ
materials.notes:
Nouns need の, not だ: 学生のようだ, not 学生だようだ.

ようだ rests on the speaker's own observation. For something you only heard from someone else, use そうだ (hearsay) or らしい.

In casual speech みたい replaces ようだ with the same meaning: 雨が降ったみたい.

Synonyms: mitai-da — みたい carries the same 'it seems' sense but is casual and spoken; ようだ is more neutral.

Related: souda-appearance — そうだ reads an impression straight off appearances; ようだ reasons from evidence.

Related: rashii — らしい leans on outside or secondhand information; ようだ on the speaker's own observation.

Related: you-ni-you-na — The same よう builds ように・ような for 'like / similar to'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ようでは・ようじゃ
materials.answer:
if (things go / continue) this way ... (bad result)

〜ようでは presents a situation — often an undesirable habit or state — and says that if it holds, a negative consequence follows: こんな簡単な問題も解けないようでは… = 'if you can't even solve a problem this simple ...'. The second clause is typically a warning or a judgment that things won't work out. ようじゃ is the casual contraction.
materials.reading: ようでは・ようじゃ
materials.notes:
It leads to a negative evaluation or outcome ('won't succeed / no good'); it is not used to introduce a happy result.

Do not confuse it with ようではないか (a 'let's ~' exhortation); ようでは here is a conditional 'if this way'.

Related: you-dewa-nai-ka — Looks similar but opposite in use: ようではないか urges 'let's do ~', while ようでは warns 'if it's like this ~'.

Related: kagiri — 〜限り says 'as long as X holds, ~'; ようでは narrows this to an undesirable state leading to a bad result.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: まいばんこんなにおそくまでざんぎょうするようじゃ、そのうちからだをこわしてしまうよ。

materials.prompt: ようではないか
materials.answer:
let's ...; why don't we ... (formal exhortation)

〜ようではないか is a formal, rhetorical exhortation built on the volitional — 'let us ~, shall we not ~'. The speaker calls on the listeners to join in an action, so it is common in speeches, editorials, and appeals. ようじゃないか is the more colloquial variant of the same call to action.
materials.reading: ようではないか
materials.notes:
It attaches to the volitional (乗り越えよう＋ではないか); this is exhortation, distinct from the conditional 〜ようでは ('if this way ~').

The tone is oratorical and formal; in ordinary conversation a plain volitional or 〜ましょう is more natural.

Related: janai-ka — じゃないか seeks the listener's agreement ('isn't it?'); ようではないか builds on the volitional to urge joint action.

Related: you-to-omou — ようと思う is one's private intention to act; ようではないか openly rallies others to act together.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.reading: こんなんなときこそ、みんなでちからをあわせてのりこえようではないか。

examples.reading: このうつくしいまちのしぜんを、わたしたちのてでまもろうではないか。

materials.prompt: 〜ようが〜まいが・〜ようと〜まいと
materials.answer:
whether one does or not; regardless of whether ~

This pattern pairs a volitional (〜よう) with the negative volitional まい to mean 'whether one does ~ or not': 行こうが行くまいが = whether you go or not. The main clause holds true regardless of which side is the case. まい attaches to the dictionary form of godan verbs (行くまい) and to either form of ichidan/する verbs (食べまい／食べるまい, しまい／するまい). It is emphatic and somewhat formal.
materials.notes:
Keep the two verbs the same: the affirmative volitional (〜よう) plus its negative counterpart (〜まい).

まい follows the dictionary form for godan verbs (書くまい) and the stem or dictionary form for ichidan verbs (食べまい／食べるまい); for する both するまい and しまい occur, for 来る both 来るまい and 来まい.

Synonyms: you-ga-you-to — 〜ようが／ようと (single) means 'no matter (how/what)'; the 〜まい version explicitly spans the do/not-do alternatives.

Synonyms: ni-kakawarazu — にかかわらず says 'regardless of ~' about a noun or fixed set; ようが〜まいが frames the two poles as verb alternatives.

Related: mai — まい on its own is the negative volitional ('probably won't / won't'); here it forms the negative half of the 'whether or not' pair.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［volitional］＋が／と＋（same verb）＋まいが／まいと

materials.prompt: ようがない
materials.answer:
there's no way to ~; it's impossible to ~ (no means available)

The ます-stem plus ようがない says there is no method or means to do something, so it simply can't be done — 連絡しようがない = there's no way to get in touch. It stresses a missing means rather than a lack of ability. Also written 〜ようもない.
materials.reading: ようがない
materials.notes:
Attach it to the stem: 直しようがない, not 直すようがない.

It means 'no means to do it'; 'no way that [it's true]' (logical) is わけがない.

bunpro lists N2

Related: wake-ga-nai — わけがない denies that something could be true (logic); ようがない denies there's any means to do it.

Related: koto-ga-dekiru — ことができる is 'able to do'; ようがない is the flat 'no way to do it at all'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ようが〜ようが・〜ようと〜ようと
materials.answer:
whether ~ or ~ (either way, it makes no difference)

Two volitionals in a row — 〜ようが〜ようが or 〜ようと〜ようと — list two contrasting possibilities and declare that neither affects the outcome: 笑おうが泣こうが = whether you laugh or cry. It also works with adjectives via their volitional-style forms (高かろうが安かろうが = whether expensive or cheap). The main clause stands unchanged no matter which of the two holds. It is emphatic and somewhat formal.
materials.notes:
Both slots take a volitional form; the two possibilities are usually contrasting (laugh/cry, expensive/cheap).

The main clause must be unaffected by either alternative; it states something that holds either way.

Synonyms: you-ga-mai-ga — ようが〜まいが spans a do/not-do pair; ようが〜ようが lists two positive alternatives, both irrelevant to the outcome.

Synonyms: you-ga-you-to — 〜ようが／ようと (single) means 'no matter (what/how)'; doubling it names two specific possibilities.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: い-adjective［かろう］＋が／と＋い-adjective［かろう］＋が／と

materials.prompt: 〜ようが・〜ようと
materials.answer:
no matter what/how; even if; regardless of ~

A single volitional followed by が or と means 'no matter ~ / even if ~': 何を言われようが = no matter what I'm told, どうなろうと = no matter what happens. It concedes any possibility and states that the main clause holds all the same. With adjectives it uses かろう (どんなに苦しかろうと), and with nouns/な-adjectives であろう (誰であろうと). It is emphatic and more formal than ても.
materials.reading: ようが・ようと
materials.notes:
が and と are interchangeable here; both mean 'no matter ~'.

It is emphatic and somewhat formal; plain ても is the more everyday 'even if'.

Synonyms: temo — ても is the everyday 'even if ~'; 〜ようと／ようが is more emphatic and formal, stressing 'no matter what'.

Synonyms: you-ga-you-ga — doubling it (ようが〜ようが) lists two specific alternatives; the single form concedes any possibility at all.

Related: mo-kamawazu — もかまわず means 'without regard for ~ (and acting anyway)'; 〜ようと states that the outcome holds no matter the case.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: ようか〜まいか
materials.answer:
whether or not to do (deliberating)

〜ようか〜まいか expresses inner deliberation about whether to do something or not: 行こうか行くまいか = 'whether to go or not'. It joins the volitional (I'll do) with まい (I won't / negative volition), so the speaker is weighing two courses and wavering. It has a slightly literary, reflective tone.
materials.notes:
The same verb appears twice — once in the volitional, once with まい: 話そうか話すまいか, not a mixed pair.

For する and くる, expect しようか／するまい（すまい）and こようか／くるまい（こまい）rather than an added -oumai form.

Related: mai — まい alone states 'won't / probably not'; ようか〜まいか pairs it with the volitional to show two-way deliberation.

Related: you-to-omou — ようと思う states a formed intention to act; ようか〜まいか is the earlier stage of still wavering between doing and not.

Source references: jlptsensei
structures: Verb［volitional］＋ か ＋ Verb［dictionary form］＋ まいか

materials.prompt: 〜ようものなら
materials.answer:
if one were to (even slightly) do ~, dire consequences would follow

〜ようものなら takes a volitional-form verb and warns that if that action were so much as attempted, something serious or disastrous would happen. The consequence is heavy and often exaggerated: 少しでも文句を言おうものなら大変なことになる = if you dared to complain even a little, all hell would break loose. It expresses the speaker's sense that the situation is so touchy that the smallest move triggers an outsized reaction.
materials.reading: ようものなら
materials.notes:
Distinguish the two ものなら: with the volitional (言おうものなら) it means 'if one were to, with dire results'; with the potential (できるものなら) it means 'if one could'.

The result clause is negative and often hyperbolic — the point is how extreme the reaction to a small act would be.

Synonyms: mono-nara — The potential-based ものなら (できるものなら) expresses a wish 'if only one could'; ようものなら uses the volitional to warn of dire results.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: ような気がする
materials.answer:
to have a feeling that ~; it somehow feels like ~

〜ような気がする expresses a vague, intuitive impression — you sense something without solid proof. 忘れ物をしたような気がする = I have a feeling I forgot something. It is softer and more subjective than 〜と思う.
materials.reading: ようなきがする
materials.notes:
It voices an uncertain hunch, weaker than 〜と思う (a considered opinion).

With a noun, insert の: 学生のような気がする.

Related: you-da — ようだ draws a reasoned 'it seems' from evidence; ような気がする is a looser inner hunch.

Related: you-ni-mieru — ように見える is 'looks like' from what you can see; ような気がする is an inner impression, not a visual one.

Related: mitai-da — みたいだ is a casual 'seems like'; ような気がする foregrounds your own gut feeling.

materials.prompt: ように祈る
materials.answer:
to pray / hope that ~ comes true

ように祈る expresses a hope or prayer that something will come about. The ように clause names the wished-for outcome — usually something outside your control — and 祈る ('pray') or 願う ('wish') voices the hope. It is common in well-wishes and set phrases.
materials.reading: ようにいのる
materials.notes:
The wished-for verb is non-volitional — a state or event you cannot force: 合格できるように祈る, not a plain action you would just do yourself.

In spoken well-wishes the 祈る is often dropped: 早くよくなりますように ('hope you get well soon').

ますように (polite stem ＋ ように) is the common set shape for a heartfelt wish.

Related: you-ni-iu — ように言う relays a command to someone; ように祈る voices a personal hope.

Related: you-ni-so-that — Same ように frame, here filled by a wished-for result rather than a plain purpose.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: ように言う
materials.answer:
to tell / ask someone to do ~

ように言う reports an instruction or request passed to someone: the ように clause holds what they were told to do, and 言う (or 頼む, 伝える) delivers it. It is the standard way to relay a command indirectly, without quoting the exact words.
materials.reading: ようにいう
materials.notes:
For a negative instruction, use the ない form before ように: 遅れないように言う ('tell them not to be late').

This reports a command indirectly. To quote the exact words, use 「…」と言う instead.

言う can be swapped for 頼む (request), 伝える (pass on), or 注意する (warn), keeping the same ように frame.

Related: you-ni-te-hoshii — ように〜てほしい voices your own wish; ように言う reports an instruction given to someone.

Related: you-ni-inoru — ように祈る hopes for an outcome; ように言う relays a command.

Related: you-ni-so-that — Same ように frame, here filled by a request rather than a plain purpose.

Source references: bunpro

to look ~; to appear ~ (judging from how it looks)

materials.prompt: ようになる
materials.answer:
to come to ~; to reach the point where

ようになる describes a change over time — you reach a state or ability you did not have before. It pairs naturally with potential verbs (話せるようになる = 'become able to speak') and marks arriving at a new normal. The negative なくなる shows losing a habit or ability.
materials.reading: ようになる
materials.notes:
For 'stopped doing / can no longer', use なくなる, not ないようになる: 食べなくなった rather than 食べないようになった.

ようになる is a change that unfolds; ようにする is a conscious effort. 泳げるようになった (came to be able to swim) vs 泳ぐようにする (make a point of swimming).

ようになる highlights a gradual shift, so it pairs especially well with potential verbs.

Related: you-ni-suru — ようにする is deliberate effort; ようになる is the change itself coming about.

Related: koto-ni-naru — ことになる is a decision or arrangement being settled; ようになる is a gradual change in ability or habit.

Related: rareru-potential — Potential verbs pair with ようになる to say you've become able to do something.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ように
materials.answer:
so that; in order to (a state comes about)

ように states the purpose behind an action — you do the main action so that some situation will come about. The clause before ように is usually a state or a potential / negative verb (something you cannot directly will), like 聞こえる, わかる, or 忘れない. It contrasts with ために, whose front clause is a deliberate action.
materials.reading: ように
materials.notes:
ように takes a non-volitional verb (potential, negative, or change of state): 見えるように. For a goal reached by deliberate action, use ために: 車を買うために.

No の or な before this ように — it attaches straight to the plain verb.

The two clauses can have different subjects, which suits ように but is awkward for ために.

jlptsensei lists N3

Related: tame-ni — ために gives a purpose reached by deliberate action; ように, a state you aim to bring about.

Related: you-ni-suru — ようにする turns such a goal into an ongoing effort to do something.

Related: you-ni-naru — ようになる describes that aimed-for state actually coming about.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ようにする
materials.answer:
to make sure to; to make an effort to

ようにする says you deliberately arrange your behavior so a certain thing happens (or does not). It expresses making an effort or keeping a conscious habit: 毎日運動するようにする = 'make a point of exercising daily'. With ている (ようにしている) it stresses an ongoing habit you keep up.
materials.reading: ようにする
materials.notes:
ようにする is a conscious effort you make; ようになる is a change that happens on its own. 早起きするようにする (I make myself get up early) vs 早起きするようになった (I've come to get up early).

For a firm one-time decision, ことにする fits better; ようにする leans toward ongoing effort or habit.

The ている form ようにしている marks a habit you are keeping up, not a single act.

Related: you-ni-naru — ようになる is the change coming about on its own; ようにする is the effort you make.

Related: koto-ni-suru — ことにする is a firm decision to do something; ようにする is ongoing effort or habit.

Related: you-ni-so-that — The same purpose ように, here completed by する into a personal effort.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ように～てほしい
materials.answer:
want someone to act so that ~ comes about

This pattern layers a ように purpose clause onto a てほしい request: you name the outcome you are hoping for with ように, then say you want someone to act toward it with 〜てほしい. It makes the wish gentle and outcome-focused — you care about the result, not just the bare action.
materials.notes:
The ように clause usually takes a non-volitional verb (potential, negative, or change of state): 遅れないように, 間に合うように.

てほしい voices a want directed at another person; you cannot use it for your own actions.

The negative want is 〜ないでほしい: 心配しないでほしい ('I don't want you to worry').

Related: te-hoshii — てほしい alone just states 'I want you to do X'; here ように adds the goal behind it.

Related: you-ni-iu — ように言う reports telling someone to do it; ように〜てほしい voices your own wish.

Related: you-ni-so-that — Shares the purpose ように 'so that', here completed by a want.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: ようによっては
materials.answer:
depending on how one does or looks at it

ようによっては is 'manner' よう (verb stem + よう, as in 考えよう・使いよう) followed by によっては 'depending on'. It says that a different — often more favorable — result is possible depending on the way you approach or interpret something. 考えようによっては = depending on how you look at it; 使いようによっては = depending on how you use it. It frequently introduces a reframing that turns a seemingly negative thing into something acceptable.
materials.reading: ようによっては
materials.notes:
This よう is the 'way/manner' nominalizer (考えよう, 言いよう), not the volitional; don't read it as ようにも or ようとする.

It usually sets up a positive reframing — 'seen a certain way, it's actually fine' — rather than a neutral list of possibilities.

Related: you-nimo-nai — Both use よう, but ようにも〜ない is the volitional ('even if I try'); ようによっては is the manner noun ('depending on the way').

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ように・ような
materials.answer:
like; similar to; as if

This よう compares one thing to another: ような modifies a noun ('a ~ like X'), ように modifies a verb or adjective ('in a ~ way, like X'). It draws a resemblance or gives an example. Nouns connect with の: 夢のような ('dream-like').
materials.reading: ように・ような
materials.notes:
ような goes before a noun, ように before a verb or adjective: 子どものような笑顔 vs 子どものように笑う.

Nouns need の: 山のように, not 山ように.

This is the 'resemblance' よう; the same shape also builds ようだ ('it seems') — context tells them apart.

Synonyms: mitai-da — みたい is the everyday spoken version of this 'like / similar to' comparison.

Related: you-da — The predicate ようだ 'it seems' is built on the same よう.

Related: rashii-typical — らしい (typical of) says something is a fitting example; ように just draws a resemblance.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ようにも〜ない
materials.answer:
even if one wanted or tried to, one can't (because circumstances block it)

〜ようにも〜ない says that even if you had the will to do something, external circumstances make it impossible. The same verb is usually repeated: the volitional form + にも sets up the intention, and its potential negative closes off the possibility. 起きようにも起きられない = I want to get up but can't. The barrier is a real-world obstacle (illness, lack of information, no time), not a lack of desire — the desire is precisely what is being frustrated.
materials.notes:
The verb is normally repeated: volitional + にも, then its potential negative — 出かけようにも出かけられない, not 出かけようにない.

The blocking reason is an external circumstance; the will to act is present, which is what makes the impossibility frustrating.

Related: you-to-suru — ようとする describes making the attempt; ようにも〜ない says the attempt is blocked by circumstances so it can't be carried out.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 要するに
materials.answer:
in short; to sum up; essentially

要するに is an adverbial phrase that introduces a concise restatement of what was just said — 'in short, essentially, to put it briefly'. The speaker boils a longer account down to its core point, often cutting through detail to the conclusion that really matters.
materials.reading: ようするに
materials.notes:
It restates the essence in fewer words; it is not a cause-and-effect 'therefore', so it summarizes rather than draws a logical consequence.

What follows is the speaker's own paraphrase of the gist, so it usually condenses several points into one.

Synonyms: tsumari — つまり restates 'in other words'; 要するに specifically frames the restatement as a boiled-down summary of the essentials.

Synonyms: to-iu-koto-da — ということだ concludes 'it amounts to ~'; 要するに opens the sentence to signal a summary is coming.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ようと思う
materials.answer:
I think I'll ~; I'm thinking of ~ing

Volitional verb ＋ と思う states a personal intention the speaker has more or less just formed. It is softer than declaring a fixed plan — it presents the decision as your current thinking. Use ようと思っている for an intention you have been holding for a while.
materials.reading: ようとおもう
materials.notes:
Attach it to the volitional (行こう), not the dictionary form: 行こうと思う, not 行くと思う (which just means 'I think he'll go').

ようと思う reports the speaker's own intention; you cannot use it to state someone else's will directly.

と思っている suggests a longer-held intention; plain と思う, a decision made at the moment of speaking.

Synonyms: tsumori — つもりだ states a firmer, more settled intention; ようと思う is more 'I've just decided'.

Related: yotei-da — 予定だ is an arranged, on-the-schedule plan; ようと思う is looser personal thinking.

Related: tsumori — つもりだ is a firmer intention already held; ようと思う leans toward a fresh decision.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ようとしない
materials.answer:
won't (even) try to ~; makes no effort to ~

The negative of 〜ようとする: 〜ようとしない says someone shows no willingness to do something, often with a note of criticism or frustration — 話を聞こうとしない = won't even listen. It usually describes another person's stubborn refusal to act.
materials.reading: ようとしない
materials.notes:
Uses the volitional stem (食べよう, 聞こう), not the dictionary form.

It implies they could act but choose not to — stronger than a plain 〜ない (which just states they don't).

Antonyms: you-to-suru — ようとする is making the effort to do something; ようとしない is refusing to make any effort.

Related: you-to-shita-ga — ようとしたが is 'tried but failed'; ようとしない is 'won't even attempt'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ようとしたが
materials.answer:
was about to / tried to ~, but ~ (and it didn't work out)

The past volitional 〜ようとした plus が／けど marks that you were on the verge of doing something, or attempted it, but were interrupted or it failed — 出ようとしたが = I was about to leave, but... Because of が, a thwarted outcome usually follows.
materials.reading: ようとしたが
materials.notes:
Built on the volitional (出よう, 言おう), not the dictionary form.

With が, an interrupted or failed result normally follows, so the subject is someone who meant to act.

Related: you-to-suru — ようとする is the base 'try to / be about to'; ようとしたが adds a past attempt that fell through.

Related: tokoro-datta — ところだった is 'was just about to (nearly)'; ようとしたが centers on an attempt that got blocked.

Related: you-to-shinai — ようとしない is 'won't even try'; ようとしたが is 'did try, but failed'.

Source references: bunpro

materials.prompt: ようとする
materials.answer:
to try to ~; to be about to ~ (on the verge of)

The volitional plus とする means either making an effort to do something (立ち上がろうとする = try to stand up) or being right on the point of something happening (日が暮れようとする = the sun is about to set). Context decides which reading applies.
materials.reading: ようとする
materials.notes:
Built on the volitional (帰ろう, 出よう), not the dictionary form.

Different from 〜と思う (stating an intention) and 〜つもり (a settled plan): ようとする is the attempt or the imminent moment itself.

Antonyms: you-to-shinai — ようとしない is the negative — refusing to make the attempt that ようとする describes.

Related: you-to-omou — 〜ようと思う states an intention you've formed; ようとする is actually attempting or being on the verge.

Related: ru-tokoro-da — 〜るところだ is 'about to do' as a scheduled next step; ようとする can also mean caught in the very moment of starting.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ゆえに
materials.answer:
therefore; hence; because of; for the reason that (formal)

ゆえに expresses cause and consequence in formal, literary, or logical language. As a conjunction at the head of a sentence it means 'therefore, hence'. Attached to a noun (＋ゆえ／のゆえに) or a plain clause (＋がゆえに) it means 'owing to ~, because of ~': 経験の浅さゆえに = owing to inexperience. It is the register of reasoned argument and classical style, far more formal than から or ので.
materials.reading: ゆえに
materials.notes:
This is formal/literary; in everyday speech から, ので, or だから are the natural choices.

When it attaches to a noun, no の is strictly required (若さゆえ), though のゆえに also occurs.

Synonyms: kara — から is the everyday 'because'; ゆえに expresses the same causal link in formal, literary, or logical writing.

Synonyms: tame-ni — ため(に) gives a neutral cause or purpose; ゆえに is more formal and belongs to reasoned or classical style.

Related: node — ので softens a reason as objective and polite; ゆえに is markedly formal and literary.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

examples.english: His judgment, owing to his lack of experience, was naive in places.

examples.english: This is an unprecedented undertaking. Therefore, careful examination is called for.
examples.reading: ぜんれいのないじぎょうである。ゆえに、しんちょうなけんとうがもとめられる。

materials.prompt: 〜ざる
materials.answer:
not ~ (classical/literary negative, before a noun)

〜ざる is a classical negative ending equal to 〜ない before a noun. It survives in modern written and set expressions — 絶えざる努力 = ceaseless effort, 予期せざる事態 = an unforeseen situation. It attaches to the ない-form base (the あ-stem) of a verb, with する → せざる and くる → こざる. Mostly literary or fixed-phrase, not everyday speech.
materials.reading: ざる
materials.notes:
〜ざる comes before a noun (絶えざる努力); the clause-ending / adverbial form is 〜ず.

Irregular: する becomes せざる, not しざる.

It is literary; in ordinary sentences use 〜ない.

Synonyms: nu — 〜ぬ is the classical negative that ends a clause or precedes a noun; 〜ざる is a parallel attributive form.

Related: zaru-o-enai — ざるを得ない ('have no choice but') is built on this same ざる base, fixed with を得ない.

Source references: bunpro
structures: Verb［ない form, drop ない］＋ ざる
する → せざる／くる → こざる

examples.english: An unforeseen situation arose.
examples.reading: よきせざるじたいがおきた。

materials.prompt: ざるを得ない
materials.answer:
have no choice but to ~; cannot help ~ing

〜ざるを得ない attaches to a verb's ない-form base to say the speaker is forced by circumstances into the action, often reluctantly — 認めざるを得ない = have no choice but to admit it. Formal in tone, with する → せざるを得ない.
materials.reading: ざるをえない
materials.notes:
Formed on the ない-base minus ない: 行かない → 行かざるを得ない.

Irregular: する → せざるを得ない, not しざるを得ない.

It conveys reluctant compulsion by outside circumstances, not a free personal choice.

Synonyms: yori-hoka-nai — よりほかない also means 'nothing to do but'; ざるを得ない stresses reluctant compulsion by circumstance.

Synonyms: nai-wake-niwa-ikanai — ないわけにはいかない is 'can't not do', driven by duty or social obligation; ざるを得ない is driven by unavoidable circumstances.

Synonyms: shika-nai — 〜しかない is a plainer, more colloquial 'have no choice but'; ざるを得ない is more formal.

Related: zaru — 〜ざる is the classical negative base on which this fixed pattern is built.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［ない form, drop ない］＋ ざるを得ない
する → せざるを得ない

examples.japanese: 台風で、旅行を中止せざるを得なかった。
examples.english: Because of the typhoon, we had no choice but to cancel the trip.
examples.reading: たいふうで、りょこうをちゅうしせざるをえなかった。

examples.japanese: これだけ証拠があれば、事実を認めざるを得ない。
examples.english: With this much evidence, I have no choice but to admit the facts.
examples.reading: これだけしょうこがあれば、じじつをみとめざるをえない。

materials.prompt: 前者は・後者は
materials.answer:
the former ~ ; the latter ~

前者 means "the former" (the first of two things mentioned) and 後者 means "the latter" (the second). Used together, they let you refer back to two items without repeating them: 前者は安く、後者は速い = the former is cheap, the latter is fast. It's a formal pairing, common in writing and comparisons.
materials.reading: ぜんしゃは・こうしゃは
materials.notes:
前者／後者 work only when exactly two things have been named; for three or more, refer to them by name instead.

後者 is read こうしゃ; don't read this pair as the time words 前 (before) / 後 (after).

Related: ippou-de — 一方で contrasts two sides of a situation; 前者／後者 point back to two specific items already named.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: Comparing trains and buses, the latter is often the cheaper one.
examples.reading: でんしゃとバスをくらべると、こうしゃのほうがやすいことがおおい。

materials.prompt: 全然～ない
materials.answer:
not at all

全然 in front of a negative predicate denies something completely: 全然読めない = 'can't read it at all'. It is the everyday, conversational way to make a negation total.
materials.notes:
In casual speech 全然大丈夫 ('totally fine') is common, but in tests and careful writing 全然 pairs with a negative.

全然 denies completely; for a milder 'not very', use あまり〜ない.

Synonyms: sukoshi-mo-nai — 少しも〜ない is an equally total denial, a touch more formal.

Synonyms: mattaku-nai — 全く〜ない (N3) is the stiffer, more written 'not at all'.

Related: amari-nai — あまり〜ない is partial ('not much'); 全然〜ない is total.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ぞ・〜ぜ
materials.answer:
emphatic masculine sentence-final particles

ぞ and ぜ are rough, masculine sentence-final particles that add force to an assertion. ぞ can be aimed at oneself as resolve or at others as a warning (負けないぞ = I won't lose; 危ないぞ = watch out). ぜ is directed at a listener to press a point or urge agreement (もう行くぜ = come on, let's go). Both belong to casual, informal speech and sound blunt or tough.
materials.reading: ぞ・ぜ
materials.notes:
Both are informal and masculine-sounding; they are out of place in polite or formal speech.

ぞ can be muttered to oneself as resolve, whereas ぜ is always aimed at a listener.

Source references: jlptsensei

materials.prompt: 〜ずじまい
materials.answer:
ended up never doing (and the chance is gone)

〜ずじまい combines the negative ず with 仕舞い ('the end') to say a period closed with the action never done — and the speaker regrets it: 結局行かずじまいだった = in the end I never did go. The chance is understood to be lost now. It follows the ない-stem (する becomes せずじまい), almost always appears in the past (〜ずじまいだった), and pairs naturally with 結局 or とうとう.
materials.reading: ずじまい
materials.notes:
する becomes せずじまい — ×しずじまい is wrong.

It implies the opportunity has closed and carries regret; for a neutral 'didn't do', plain しなかった is enough.

It normally reports a finished period, so the past 〜ずじまいだった is the usual form.

Related: sokonau — 〜そこなう marks missing a particular chance to do something; ずじまい looks back on a whole period that ended without it.

Related: zu-tomo — ずとも is a concessive 'even without doing'; ずじまい reports that the doing never happened, with regret.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro
structures: Verb［ない stem］＋ずじまい（だった）

examples.reading: きょうとにさんねんもすんでいたのに、けっきょくきんかくじにはいかずじまいだった。

materials.prompt: ずに済む
materials.answer:
to get by without having to do; to be spared doing

ずに済む attaches the classical negative ず to a verb to say that some troublesome action turned out to be unnecessary — the situation was settled without it. The nuance is relief that an unwanted effort, expense, or bother was avoided. する becomes せずに済む.
materials.reading: ずにすむ
materials.notes:
する becomes せず, not しず: 電話せずに済む.

It says the action turned out unnecessary (a fortunate avoidance), not merely that you chose not to do it; for a plain 'without doing', use ずに or ないで on their own.

Synonyms: te-sumu — て済む says a matter is settled by doing/being something; ずに済む is the negative side — settled without having to do it.

Related: zuni — ずに plainly means 'without doing', with no sense of avoided trouble; ずに済む adds the relief that the action proved unnecessary.

Related: naide — ないで is the colloquial 'without doing'; ずに済む specifically frames it as escaping an unwanted task.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ずにはおかない・〜ないではおかない
materials.answer:
will inevitably cause; will not rest until

〜ずにはおかない declares that a force will not let things end without the verb happening. With causative or emotive verbs, the subject is often a thing whose power inevitably affects people: 聴く人を感動させずにはおかない = it cannot fail to move listeners. With a personal subject it voices fierce determination: 謝らせずにはおかない = I won't rest until I make him apologize. It is emphatic, formal, and written in flavor; する becomes せずにはおかない.
materials.reading: ずにはおかない・ないではおかない
materials.notes:
Don't confuse it with ずにはいられない, which is the speaker's own uncontrollable urge; ずにはおかない is an external force or resolve that will inevitably bring the action about.

In the 'inevitable effect' use the verb is typically causative (感動させる, 考えさせる) and the subject is often a work, event, or statement.

する becomes せずにはおかない.

Related: zuni-wa-irarenai — ずにはいられない is an internal urge you cannot suppress; ずにはおかない is an outcome the force of things will not fail to produce.

Related: zu-niwa-sumanai — ずには済まない says circumstances oblige you to act; ずにはおかない says the action will inevitably be brought about.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ずには済まない・〜ないでは済まない
materials.answer:
cannot get away without doing; will have to

〜ずには済まない says the matter cannot be settled unless the action is taken — social or moral circumstances leave no way out: 謝らずには済まない = an apology is unavoidable. 済む means 'to be settled', so the pattern literally reads 'it won't be settled without doing'. Typical contexts are apologies, compensation, and explanations that society demands. It follows the ない-stem (する → せずには済まない) and is formal in tone.
materials.reading: ずにはすまない・ないではすまない
materials.notes:
The pressure is external — social or moral obligation; for an inner emotional urge, use ずにはいられない.

Its counterpart ずに済む means the opposite: you got by without having to do it. Keep the two apart.

する becomes せずには済まない.

Antonyms: zu-ni-sumu — ずに済む means you managed to get by without doing it — the mirror image of ずには済まない.

Related: zu-niwa-okanai — ずにはおかない is an inevitable effect or fierce resolve; ずには済まない is an obligation circumstances impose.

Related: zuni-wa-irarenai — ずにはいられない is an emotion you cannot hold back; ずには済まない is a duty you cannot dodge.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ずとも
materials.answer:
even without doing; even if not

〜ずとも is a literary concessive: even without doing the verb, the main clause still holds. 言わずとも分かる = you needn't say it — I understand anyway. It is the classical equivalent of 〜なくても, built from the negative ず plus concessive とも, and する becomes せずとも. Today it appears in written style, formal speech, and set turns of phrase, lending a dignified or aphoristic ring.
materials.reading: ずとも
materials.notes:
It is literary register — in conversation, 〜なくても is the natural equivalent.

する becomes せずとも: 説明せずとも, not ×しずとも.

It attaches to verbs; for nouns and adjectives, use でなくとも or くとも patterns instead.

Synonyms: temo — 〜なくても is the everyday equivalent; ずとも says the same in classical, written style.

Related: made-mo-nai — までもない judges an action unnecessary ('no need to'); ずとも concedes its absence and moves on.

Related: koto-nashi-ni — ことなしに states that something happens without the action; ずとも concedes 'even if it doesn't happen'.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜ずくめ
materials.answer:
nothing but; entirely; full of

Noun＋ずくめ means the whole of something consists of that noun through and through: いいことずくめ = nothing but good things, 黒ずくめ = (dressed) all in black, 規則ずくめ = rules upon rules. It attaches to a limited group of nouns — colors, ごちそう, いいこと, 規則, 異例 — and, unlike だらけ, it happily describes good things as well as oppressive ones. It often characterizes a period, an outfit, or an organization.
materials.reading: ずくめ
materials.notes:
Only a conventional set of nouns takes ずくめ (黒, いいこと, ごちそう, 規則, 異例...); you cannot coin freely with it.

It is not inherently negative — いいことずくめ is common; for 'covered in something undesirable', だらけ is the right choice.

Standard orthography is ずくめ, not づくめ.

Synonyms: darake — だらけ means 'full of / covered in' something undesirable (泥だらけ, 間違いだらけ); ずくめ can be entirely positive.

Synonyms: mamire — まみれ is physical smearing over a surface (汗まみれ); ずくめ says the whole content or makeup is that thing.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ずに
materials.answer:
without doing ~

ずに attaches to a verb's negative base to mean "without doing ~" — 朝ご飯を食べずに家を出た = went out without eating breakfast. It's the more formal, written equivalent of ないで. The one irregular form is する → せずに.
materials.reading: ずに
materials.notes:
する becomes せずに, not しずに.

ずに is more formal and written; ないで is the everyday spoken choice.

Synonyms: naide — ないで is the everyday spoken "without doing ~"; ずに is the same meaning in a formal, written register.

Related: koto-naku — 〜ことなく is a formal "without ever ~ing"; ずに is the plainer "without doing (this time)."

Related: zu-ni-sumu — 〜ずに済む builds on ずに to mean "get by without having to ~."

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ずにはいられない
materials.answer:
can't help but do; can't keep oneself from doing

ずにはいられない says you can't stop yourself from doing something — the urge or feeling is too strong to hold back. 笑わずにはいられない = can't help laughing. It's the formal, written partner of ないではいられない, and する becomes せずにはいられない.
materials.reading: ずにはいられない
materials.notes:
する becomes せずにはいられない, not しずにはいられない.

It describes a feeling or urge you can't suppress — usually your own; it's not for an outside obligation like "must, because the rules say so."

Synonyms: nai-dewa-irarenai — ないではいられない means exactly the same; ずにはいられない is its more formal, written form.

Related: zaru-o-enai — 〜ざるを得ない is being forced to act by circumstances; ずにはいられない is an inner urge you can't hold back.

Related: te-tamaranai — 〜てたまらない is an unbearably strong feeling; ずにはいられない is an action you can't stop yourself from taking because of one.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: 〜づらい
materials.answer:
hard to do (often uncomfortable or a strain for the doer)

〜づらい attaches to the ます-stem and means an action is hard or uncomfortable to do — often because doing it puts some strain or awkwardness on the speaker. 言いづらい = hard to bring myself to say; 歩きづらい = hard to walk. The compound behaves like an い-adjective (づらかった, づらくない).
materials.notes:
〜づらい often carries a sense that the difficulty is unpleasant or a burden on the doer; 〜にくい is more neutral and also fits purely objective difficulty.

Attach it to the stem: 読みづらい, not 読むづらい.

Synonyms: nikui — 〜にくい is the neutral 'hard to'; 〜づらい adds that the difficulty is uncomfortable for the doer.

Synonyms: gatai — 〜がたい is stronger — 'nearly impossible to' — and more formal or literary.

Antonyms: yasui — 〜やすい means easy or comfortable to do — the opposite of 〜づらい.

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ずつ
materials.answer:
each; apiece; at a time; in steady increments

ずつ follows a quantity to mean "that much each" or "that much at a time" — 一つずつ = one apiece, 少しずつ = little by little, 三個ずつ = three each. It spreads an amount evenly across people or occasions, or marks steady, equal increments.
materials.reading: ずつ
materials.notes:
ずつ needs a quantity word in front of it (一つ, 少し, 千円); it doesn't attach straight onto a plain noun.

Related: goto-ni — 〜ごとに marks "every unit" (一日ごとに = every day); ずつ marks "this much each / at a time."

Source references: jlptsensei, bunpro

materials.prompt: ずっと
materials.answer:
by far; way (more); far and away — in comparisons

In a comparison, ずっと intensifies the gap — "by far," "way more," "far and away." AよりずっとB stresses that B beats A by a wide margin, not just barely. Note this is a separate sense from the ずっと that means "the whole time / continuously."
materials.reading: ずっと
materials.notes:
This comparative ずっと emphasizes a big difference; the same word also means "continuously / the whole time," so let the context tell them apart.

Related: yori — より marks the thing compared against; ずっと intensifies how wide the gap is.

Related: ichiban — 一番 picks the top of a whole group (superlative); ずっと stresses the margin between just two things.

Source references: bunpro

examples.english: Walking is far more pleasant than going by train.
examples.reading: でんしゃでいくより、あるいたほうがずっときもちいい。
